en: Preface to the *Souxuan lu* (Record of Searching for the Profundities) of the *Chunyang shan Sifenlü chao* (Commentary on the Four-Part Vinaya from Mount Zhongnan).
Written by the Śramaṇa Shi Chengguan of Daxingtang Monastery in the Capital.
*Śīla* means pure precepts. They are that by which one restrains evil and exerts oneself in conduct, fixing the will upon integrity and constancy. Purity here does not require pearls or jade.
The *Dian* (Epitaph). It illuminates with the light of the sun and moon, opening up the level ground of the One Ultimate and guarding the lofty ramparts of the myriad virtues.

Since the Buddha-sun sank in the west and this wind blew to the east, he who has guided the seven assemblies to stand far apart and who has manifested as one born in accordance with the four reliances is Master Xuan.

His virtue moved both humans and devas; his learning encompassed both the internal and external [teachings]. He was the one who distinguished the various schools... [text fragment] ...of the various sections.

This school transmits the single source with impartiality, upholding the grand framework of the Tripiṭaka and providing a model for a thousand generations. Its phrasing is concise yet its principles reach their ultimate depth;

its meaning is perfect and its applications are manifest. For those who enter its gate, Perfect Enlightenment is as if present. Nevertheless, those who have drawn from this stream to compose commentaries have each exhausted their own particular capacities.
Five hundred years later, there was the Vinaya Master Zhìhóng of Gūsū, who was truly the Zísì (Wang Bi) of the Śākyamuni lineage.

The meaning was granted by Heaven; the text was perfected through study. Lamenting the verbose branches of the words of many exegetes and grieving that the simple and direct principles were obscured, this record was compiled.
Errors were excised to polish the truth; the obscure was sought to reach the profound. It illuminates with sincere precedents and reflects with clear explanations.
Drawing upon the models and plans of the worthy, it gathers and unfolds them further. Thus, the clouds of delusion are dispelled from the moon of wisdom, and the sky of meaning—
He has purified the literary stars and sifted through the works of antiquity and the present to establish the beauty of his own school.

The tradition of Zhongnan Mountain has not vanished, and the compositions of the Wu River flow on forever. Having come to my door, he advanced toward the profound mysteries; having gained access to their subtle refinements, he beheld their deep pathos.
I have thus inscribed these few lines to commemorate his excellence, hoping that future students will know that the source of their lineage has its origin here.
Return to the Source.
*Sousuanlu Jie Sifenlü Shanfan Buque Xingshi Chao Lu*,
Volume One (including the preface, from the beginning through the sixth section).
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Zhìhóng of Shuānglín Monastery in Wú County.
The expansion and contraction [of the teachings] accord with the capacities and circumstances of beings; differences and similarities arise from emotional attachments and views.

Thus, while the sages of the Western Heaven [India] verified the Great Canon and established it as five schools, the practitioners of this Eastern Land, through their realization and experience, have integrated the four divisions back into a single system. Previously, they were divided individually...

Distinguishing their differences, I now bring together their similarities and differences. I shall preface this with what has been heard from the nine successive dynasties as the cause for its inception.

I will summarize the profound purport of the Tripiṭaka to provide a basis for this composition. Regarding the seven classes of practitioners mentioned by others, the teaching extends throughout the entire transformation;
first taking my own school as the foundation, I shall clarify the secondary practices in accordance with the essence of the precepts. I will extract passages of common view from various schools.
The sutras and śāstras adopt the explanations found in the Vinaya; where certain matters exist but the textual expression is insufficient, they provide definitive resolutions to ensure completeness.

They encompass various paths to elucidate what precedes them, and unify distinct categories to follow after. Though the matters are difficult to comprehend, they are presented from beginning to end without abbreviation.
The categories are easy to understand and mutually illuminate one another without being prolix; the text is concise and the practice is divided accordingly, with chapters grouped by category.

At that time, those who received the transmission possessed sharp faculties and understood it clearly. Since then, however, students have become muddled in their understanding and remain ignorant; though they search extensively through commentaries and records, their doubts and obstacles remain many.

One must consult the *Karmavācanā* and the *Śīlacittotpāda*, for their principles correspond and accord. Now, I have searched out those profound meanings to bring them into comprehensive harmony with this work.
The text: In cases where the meaning was not yet clear, I re-examined the passages cited by ancient authors; where the phrasing and principles were appropriate, I have recorded them in full.

Where I had previously obtained an exegesis of the text, and where the revealed principles were complete, I have necessarily included them. Thus, the headings for "Searching the Profundities" (Souxuan) were provisionally titled.

This work consists of ten scrolls, of which three fascicles have been completed. It is my hope that those who embody the essence of the masters will examine the intent behind my choices of inclusion and exclusion. Now, within the text...
All that is cited here clearly reveals their names; their explanations of the meaning are not in vain, and they serve as a reliable basis for the performance of rituals.
The *Karmavācanā*, the *Śīlacitta*, the *Lìqǐngzhòngyí*, and the *Jiètàjīng* were all composed by the Master of the Commentary (Zhishou).
Regarding the record by Vinaya Master Ci of Ximing Monastery, when the text mentions "Ci" or "Xi," these both refer to [Master] Rong of Puzhou.
Vinaya Master Ji; Vinaya Master Daoshen of Quanzhou; Vinaya Master Jing of Nanquan Temple; Vinaya Master Tansheng of Jingzhou;
as for the one from Dangyang mentioned in the text, it is Vinaya Master Lin of Huzhou; Vinaya Master Hai of Dashi Temple; Vinaya Master Ling’e of Chongsheng Temple;
Vinaya Master Chongfu of Guangyan Temple; and Vinaya Master Yan of Fahua Temple in Yuezhou.

Regarding the text titled *Fupian* (Supplementary Chapters): these are by Master Dajue of Huayan Monastery in Hangzhou, Master Bianchang of Lingyin Monastery in Hangzhou, and Master Yixuan of Xingning Monastery in Changzhou. Regarding the text titled *Zhongzhong* (Deciding the Mean):
this is by Master Yiwei of Tianzhu Monastery in Hangzhou. As for the citation "Lingshan and Tianzhu," this refers to Suzhou Baoshou [Monastery].
Regarding the Vinaya Master Faxing of En Temple, he cites [the master] from Zhiling as being this person.
Regarding the Vinaya Master Tanyi of Kaiyuan Temple in Yuezhou, he cites [the master] who "gave rise to the aspiration" as being this person.

Furthermore, regarding Vinaya Master Lì and Vinaya Master Huaiqian of Samadhiraja Temple in Runzhou, they cite [the masters] Jizheng and Samadhiraja respectively as being these persons. [And there was] Vinaya Master Qingyan of Shuanglin Temple in Hangzhou.
Regarding the citation "Fuyang," this refers to Vinaya Master Langran of Cihesi in Runzhou. Regarding the citation "Cihesi," this refers to Vinaya Master Daoheng of Kaiyuansi in Suzhou.
As for the rest, they are either recorded in this text or cited within the subsequent section on the interpretation of meanings.

Consequently, their titles and positions were made public. However, there were some who were recognized for their insights but did not receive official titles; we have merely recorded their insights while omitting their names.
According to the extant records and notes, these have circulated in the world; as for those beyond our current knowledge or hearing, their number is unknown.
Relying on the names to draw out the meanings, this merely indicates the successive transmission of the precepts.
Now, in order to explain the text, it shall be divided into five major sections: first, clarifying the Teacher who expounds the doctrine; second, clarifying the scriptural treasury that is expounded.
The first [section] on the compilation and preservation of the Threefold Canon is divided into six parts:
first, explaining the meaning of "Buddha"; second, discerning the number of bodies; third, clarifying the essence and characteristics of the bodies;
fourth, the differences in the lands where they reside; fifth, identifying which body is the speaker; and sixth, reconciling the non-difference between the three and the one. Regarding what is said:
"Buddha" is called *buddha* in Sanskrit; it is also transliterated as *futu*, *foduo*, *butuo*, *buto*, or *futu*. These are merely errors in the transmission of the sound.
Since this term has no direct equivalent in Chinese, it is translated according to its meaning as "The Awakened One" (*jue-zhe*), for it possesses two meanings.

To speak of "awakening through observation" (*juecha*) refers to the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*); the four abodes [of ignorance] are like thieves, which the noble awakening alone knows. To speak of "awakening through realization" (*juewu*)...

Regarding this, in contrast to the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), ignorance is like sleep; only the Sage alone awakens from it. There are two types of ignorance: ignorance that deludes one regarding phenomena (*vastu*), which is awakened by clearly perceiving the three realms of existence;

and ignorance that deludes one regarding principle (*tattva*), which is awakened by realizing the true nature of dharmas. Both are termed "awakening" because they involve awakening through penetration. Furthermore, there are three types of awakening:

first, self-awakening, which distinguishes one from ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*); second, awakening others, which distinguishes one from those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*); and third...

This awakening is complete. It differs from that of other bodhisattvas; there are ten further aspects that cannot be fully described. Question: Is such an awakened Buddha possessed of mind, or is he without mind?
If he possesses mind, then he is subject to delusion and craving. If he is without mind, by what means can he be called "awakened"?
Since awakening itself lacks substantiality, who is it that awakens to self and others? What is now called "awakening" is, in fact, emptiness. For...
With an empty mind free from discursive thought, one thoroughly penetrates the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) and realizes its true nature.

Following conventional designations, this is termed "awakening" (*bodhi*). Thus, the *Awakening of Faith* states: "What is called awakening refers to the essence of the mind being free from discursive thought.

This state of being free from discursive thought is equal to the realm of empty space, pervading everywhere without exception. The single characteristic of the dharma-realm is precisely the Tathāgata’s impartial Dharma-body. Relying upon this dharma..."
The body is called "awakening" (*buddha*). Such awakening is the meaning of "Buddha. Second, regarding the determination of the number of Buddha-bodies:
Question: How many bodies does a Buddha possess? Answer: A Buddha has three kinds: the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), the Reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*), and the Transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*).

The essence of the Dharma-body is originally unborn; it wondrously transcends all marks and cannot be said to exist. It is perfectly endowed with all virtues and cannot be said not to exist. It abides...

The mind is immediately at variance [with reality]. Only by departing from discursive thought does one accord with it. To be deluded by it is to revolve in birth and death; to awaken to it is to attain the quiescence of *nirvāṇa*.

Because it is that upon which great merit relies, it is called the *dharmakāya*. As for the *saṃbhogakāya*, it is accomplished through the myriad practices; its marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) are boundless.
It is called the *saṃbhogakāya* because it receives the fruit as a recompense for the cause. Third is the *nirmāṇakāya*, which exists within the *dharmakāya* and *saṃbhogakāya*—

These [manifestations] flow forth to accord with the capacities of ordinary and small-minded beings. Thus, a sutra says: "The Buddha’s true Dharma-body is like empty space; it manifests forms in response to things, like the moon reflected in water.
Therefore, when there is a stimulus, he appears born in a royal palace; when there is gratitude [for the end of the age], he displays extinction at the twin śāla trees.

His spiritual transformations are unfathomable, and his manifestations have no fixed direction. When one traces his footprints, he seems to come and go, yet when one speaks of his essence, it is profoundly still."
However, they are eternally abiding. The Dharma-body is named Vairocana; the Reward-body is named Rocana; the Transformation-body is named Śākyamuni. Third, to distinguish their essence:
the Dharma-body refers to the principle of the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*), which is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), untainted (*anāsrava*), eternally abiding, and immutable.
The Reward-body refers to that which is induced by cultivation; it is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and untainted, and is considered eternal through its continuity. The Transformation-body refers to...

Responding to conditions as they arise, that which is conditioned and subject to outflows is impermanent by nature; this is the distinction between the three bodies. Fourth, regarding the difference in their abodes:
the Dharma-body dwells in the Constant Quiescent Light, the Reward-body resides in the Lotus Treasury World, and the Transformation-body dwells in the Sahā world;
this is called the distinction of lands. Fifth, as for which body of the Buddha is capable of preaching: [The question asks: Since the Buddha...
There are three bodies (*trikāya*). By which body is this Vinaya teaching spoken? Answer: It is spoken by the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body). How is this known?
Because [the Buddha] manifested his traces in the royal palace, returned to the truth beneath the Bodhi tree, and proclaimed [the Dharma] at the Deer Park.

Thus, the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* says: "As for the *nirmāṇakāya*, it constantly turns the wheel of Dharma. In its six assemblies, three of them share the same body and land without distinction. Question: Above, you have distinguished the three bodies.
There is a distinction. Why is it that the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states, "This body of mine is now the Dharma-body," while the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* states, "The Buddha-body is the Dharma-body"?
If the bodies were necessarily not distinct, then one would know that there is no difference between the [Buddha] and the layman [Vimalakīrti].
Therefore, the *Samantabhadra Sūtra* says: "Śākyamuni is also named Vairocana, who pervades all places. As for that Buddha...

The dwelling place is named the Constant, Quiescent Light (Nityapraśāntaprakāśa). Thus, one should know that it is three yet always one; it is one yet always three. Where there is one, there are three;
where it is not three, it is not one. Therefore, though born in the royal palace, he was not born; though extinguished at the twin śāla trees, he did not perish.

Second, the explanation of the treasury of the teachings taught [herein] is divided into two parts: first, the enumeration of the numbers; second, the explanation of the names. First, regarding the enumeration of the numbers: based on...
There are two types of persons: bodhisattvas and śrāvakas. With respect to the Dharma, there are three: namely, Sūtra, Vinaya, and Abhidharma.

Second, regarding the explanation of the names: first, the explanation of the general name "Piṭaka" (Basket/Storehouse); second, the explanation of the specific designations for persons and dharmas. As for the term "Piṭaka," the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:
"Regarding these three and two, why are they called 'piṭakas'? The answer is: they are called piṭakas because they are able to contain [or collect] all that ought to be contained."
It is called a "piṭaka" (basket) because it contains meaning; thus, the three [types of teaching] are themselves the piṭakas. This is an *karmadhāraya* (appositional compound).

Second, the explanation of the individual names is divided into two parts: first, the separate explanation of persons and dharmas; second, the analysis of how the three piṭakas of dharmas subsume the two piṭakas of persons. The first part is further divided into two.
To prioritize the person over the Dharma: the term "Bodhisattva" is an abbreviation of the Sanskrit sound. In its full form, it should be called *bodhisattva*.
Since there is no corresponding Chinese word for it, the Sanskrit term is retained. The language of the Qin (Chinese) prefers brevity;
thus, "bodhi" has "ti" removed and "sattva" has "tva" removed, hence it is called "Pusa" (Bodhisattva). "Bodhi" is translated here as "Dao" (the Way); "sattva" is said to mean "having" (*you*).
"Sattva" (sentient being) refers to those who possess the emotional capacity to seek the Way. Thus, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "Bodhi" is the object of focus, which is the fruit sought;

"sattva" refers to the seeker who is capable of seeking, one who has made the great vow to seek Great Bodhi—this is a *tatpuruṣa* compound meaning "a sattva who seeks bodhi. Furthermore, it says: "Bodhi is the object sought; sattva is the [seeker]..."

They deliver sentient beings. Through wisdom, they seek supreme enlightenment above; through compassion, they rescue sentient beings below. Because the name is established based on their objective, they are called *bodhisattvas*.
As for those called *śrāvakas* (Hearers): it refers to when the Buddha preaches the Dharma; because they hear the sound and awaken to the Way, they are called *śrāvakas*. As the *Lotus Sūtra* says:
"If there are sentient beings who possess the nature of wisdom within, [they follow] the Buddha, the World-Honored One..."

"Venerable One, those who hear the Dharma and accept it with faith, who apply themselves with diligent vigor, and who desire to swiftly escape the triple world to seek their own nirvāṇa—this is called the Śrāvaka-yāna.
Question: "The Bodhisattvas and the Śrāvakas each have their own distinct Piṭaka established. Why is no such Piṭaka established for the Pratyekabuddhas?"
Answer: According to the *Samantaprabhā-sūtra*, there are three types of *piṭaka*: first, the Bodhisattva; second, the Pratyekabuddha; and third, the Śrāvaka.

However, according to the first chapter of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, the Pratyekabuddha-piṭaka is not established as a separate category, because the teachings and principles of those Pratyekabuddhas are fewer than those of the Śrāvakas.

Because it is the majority, they are collectively termed the Śrāvaka Piṭaka. Furthermore, as for the Pratyekabuddhas, they realize only the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) and sever the grasping at a self;

since their realization is identical to that of the Śrāvakas, they are subsumed within the Śrāvaka Piṭaka. Question: Since the Sūtras establish [the category] while the Treatises do not, is this not a contradiction? Answer:
The reason the Treatises do not establish it is because they subsume them within the Śrāvaka Piṭaka based on the identity of their realized principle.

I have heard that those established as such in the sutras do so because of differences in their spiritual capacities; their faculties may be sharp or dull, and while they rely to some extent upon the teachings, the names of those teachings differ.

Because they speak only of the twelve links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), they are established separately. As for the term "Pratyekabuddha" (Solitary Realizer): "dependent" (*pratyaya*) refers to the object of observation, and "awakened" (*buddha*) refers to the observing wisdom.

Because these individuals realize the Way by taking dependent origination as their basis, they are called Pratyekabuddhas. There are two types of them: first, [the *khaḍgaviṣāṇakalpa* (rhinoceros-like) ...]
The Pratyekabuddha (Solitary Realizer) appears in an age when no Buddha is present. Thus, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:

"Always delighting in tranquility and not wishing to dwell in company, having perfected the preparatory practices (*prayoga*), they awaken by themselves without a teacher and forever transcend the three realms; therefore, they are called 'Solitary Realizers' (*pratyekabuddha*).

Because such a person has cultivated the roots of merit conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya-kuśalamūla*) over many lifetimes until they are sharp, they merely observe that the grasses and trees of the world sprout in spring and grow in summer.
Seeing autumn’s decay and winter’s falling leaves, one awakens to impermanence; thus, through spontaneous realization and verification, there is no need for external instruction.
This refers to the *pratyekabuddhas* of the two classes who appear during the time of a Buddha; they attain awakening only after hearing the Buddha preach the Dharma. Thus, a sutra says:

"For those seeking the state of a *pratyekabuddha*, one teaches the Dharma corresponding to the twelve links of dependent origination. Second, regarding the Dharma, there are three categories: first, the *sūtra* (scriptures); likewise...

It is called *sūtra*. *Sūtra* and *suttanta* are both Sanskrit terms, differing only in their phonetic weight; in this vernacular [Chinese] they are translated as "sūtra" (*jing*). "Sūtra" means "constant.

The Tripiṭaka Master of the Tang dynasty translated it as "Agreement-Sūtra" (*qiejing*). "Agreement" (*qi*) refers to being in accord: that is, the teaching which expresses (*abhilāpa*) accords with the principle expressed (*abhidheya*), and it accords with the spiritual capacities of sentient beings;
therefore, it is called an "Agreement-Sūtra. Furthermore, "sūtra" has the meaning of "pervading" and "gathering. Thus, the first fascicle of the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* says:
Because it can penetrate and encompass, it is called a *sūtra*. This is because the Buddha’s holy teaching penetrates and upholds the meanings that ought to be known;
thus, it is correctly translated as "thread. Just as a thread can string flowers together so that they are not scattered by the wind, so too is the *Sūtra*:

it gathers the meanings explained so that they do not disperse, like a thread stringing flowers or like warp-threads holding the weft. Thus, *sūtra* is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional compound) meaning "the collection itself."
According to the *Abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra*, there are five meanings: first, "fountain," because its flavor is inexhaustible; second, "manifestation," meaning it reveals the ultimate truth;
third, "production," meaning it gives rise to sublime goodness; fourth, "plumb line," meaning it establishes the distinction between the deviant and the correct;
fifth, "garland," meaning it strings together the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*). Second, as for the *Vinaya*, it is also called *Viniścaya*.
That [piṭaka] is also called *vinaya*. This term is translated as "discipline" (*lü*). Discipline means "dharma"; it is named after its teaching.
A detailed explanation of the title is provided elsewhere. Third is *abhidharma*, which is also called *abhidhamma*. This term is translated as "treatise" (*lùn*).

It is called a "treatise" because it investigates principles, establishes what is correct, and distinguishes characteristics through questions and answers. It is also called the "Incomparable Dharma. *Abhi* means "without" (*wu*), and *dharma* means "comparison" (*bi*).

*Dharma* means "dharma. It is therefore called the "Incomparable Dharma" (*anupama-dharma*), referring to the untainted (*anāsrava*) dharma. Because it is supreme among forms of wisdom (*prajñā*), and because there is no other dharma superior to this dharma, it is called the "Incomparable Dharma.
The Tripiṭaka Master of the Tang dynasty says: *Abhidharma* is translated here as "Dharma in Opposition" (*pratidharma*).

Regarding the term "Dharma in Opposition," it refers to untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) acting as the cognizing subject that opposes [and discerns] the principle of Nirvāṇa and the Four Noble Truths.

The phenomena that are confronted are called *abhidharma*. Thus, the *Abhidharmakośa* states: "Pure wisdom along with its attendants is called *abhidharma*, as well as the wisdom and treatises by which this [wisdom] is attained.
Of these two phrases, the former refers to *abhidharma* in terms of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

The second phrase refers to the Abhidharma in relation to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). Regarding the term "ultimate" (*paramārtha*): that which is untainted (*anāsrava*) is called ultimate, while that which is tainted (*sāsrava*) is called conventional.

As for the inclusion of the two persons within the characteristics of the Dharma, this distinguishes the sense of inclusion by correlating the three baskets of the Dharma with the two baskets of the persons.
Question: Among the three baskets, to which vehicle’s persons does the Vinaya-piṭaka belong? Answer: As for the Vinaya-piṭaka...
The Śrāvaka-piṭaka is comprised therein; the remaining two piṭakas are subsumed under the Bodhisattva-piṭaka. Alternatively, each of the three piṭakas may contain both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna elements:
the Mahāyāna tripiṭaka is subsumed under the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, while the Hīnayāna tripiṭaka is subsumed under the Śrāvaka-piṭaka.
The Third Council on the Maintenance [of the Teaching] consists briefly of three sections: first, the time of the council; second, the maintenance by the five masters;
and third, the separation into schools. Regarding the first, the council: the compilation of the Buddha’s bequeathed words is termed "council" (*saṃgīti*). "Council" means to compile and arrange.
According to their respective categories, they were gathered together in one place and inscribed upon palm leaves; therefore, it is called a "compilation" (*saṃgaha*). As for...

This section is divided into two parts: first, the exposition of the circumstances surrounding the compilation; second, the exposition of the time and place. The former consists of two sub-sections: first, the exposition of the circumstances;

second, the exposition of the compilation. Regarding the first, the circumstances: when the Tathāgata appeared in the world, he bestowed teachings according to the capacities of beings, benefiting them as infinitely as the sands of the Ganges.

When his mission was fulfilled and it was time for him to pass away, he was about to enter *nirvāṇa*. He entrusted the upholding of the True Dharma to Kāśyapa and Upāli, desiring that they should gather [the teachings].
The Buddha’s sincere words were transmitted through the *palm-leaf* (palāśa) manuscripts; thus, the *Dharmaguptaka-dharmakośa-āgama* (付法藏傳) states:

The Buddha told Kāśyapa, "You should now know that for immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, for the sake of sentient beings, I have diligently practiced asceticism and single-mindedly sought the unsurpassed, supreme Dharma.
My former vows are now fulfilled. I am about to enter *nirvāṇa*; therefore, with this profound..."
“I entrust the Dharma to you. You should, in the future, respectfully follow my intention, widely proclaim and disseminate it so that it shall not be severed.
Kāśyapa replied, “Excellent! I accept these instructions and shall uphold the True Dharma. Thereupon, Kāśyapa took his leave of the Tathāgata.
He went to the Piṇḍola Cave on Vulture Peak Mountain, where he practiced walking meditation and tranquil dhyāna, proclaiming the sublime Dharma and delivering all sentient beings.
Later, when the World-Honored One was about to enter nirvana, he emitted a supreme radiance and the great earth shook violently.
He then thought to himself, "Could it be that the Tathāgata intends to enter nirvana and is manifesting these signs? He immediately entered samādhi and, with his divine eye...
He beheld the Tathāgata by the side of the Hiraṇyavatī River amidst a grove of *śāla* trees, having relinquished his life-force in his entirety.

Having made this observation, he was deeply distressed and displeased, thinking: "How sudden is the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata! The eye of the world has been extinguished; unwholesomeness increases!
He then proceeded with his followers toward the city of Kuśinagara. According to the *Buzhishu* (Commentary on the Sectarian Tenets), seven days after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa...
One day, Kāśyapa was unaware [of the Buddha's passing] and set out for the city of Kuśinagara with his followers.
On the way, he encountered a non-Buddhist brahmin named Upaka. Kāśyapa asked him, "Where have you come from? He replied, "I have come from the city of Kuśinagara.
He asked again, "Do you know my World-Honored One? He replied, "I do. He asked again, "Is he still alive? He replied, "He is no longer in the world."
"Yes. It has already been seven days since his parinirvāṇa. All the devas and humans have made grand offerings, and it was from that place that I obtained these *mandārava* flowers.
Upon hearing this, Kāśyapa was displeased. Then, having heard these words, all the bhikṣus were overcome with great sorrow and distress;
they threw themselves to the ground, wailing and sobbing, their tears falling like rain. The Vinaya says: At that time...
There was the Śākya son Upananda, who spoke among the assembly, saying: "Venerable ones, stop for a moment;
do not be so deeply distressed. We have now attained liberation from that mahallaka. While he was alive, he frequently instructed us on what should and should not be done;
now we may act as we please. And so they did as they wished.

[He] acted [as follows]. Desiring to stop [the funeral rites], there were also non-Buddhists who reviled and disparaged the Dharma and Vinaya of the Śramaṇa Gautama, comparing them to smoke and so forth.
When Kāśyapa heard this, he was displeased. The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states: After Kāśyapa had cremated the Buddha’s relics, he assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them, saying:
"Previously, while I was traveling on the road, I heard the words of non-Buddhists and the evil bhikṣu Upananda."

The fourth period of translation. This section has two parts: first, clarifying the periods of the successive translations of the Vinaya text; second, identifying the time and place of the composition of the *Shan-chien* (Exposition).

According to both the records and the diagrams, it is said that the translation by Jueming consisted of forty-five fascicles, together with one fascicle of the *Sifen-jieben* (Four-Part Prātimokṣa). Later, Faling retranslated it and expanded it into sixty fascicles.
Next, to clarify the time and place of the compilation of the *Shō*, there are two parts: first, clarifying the reasons for the compilation of the *Shō*;
second, identifying the time and place of its composition. Question: Since the time of Vinaya Master Sengcong, the commentaries on the *Fuguang* and *Yuanshou* have flourished extensively.

For what reason did you further compose the *Sìchão* within the school you yourself studied? Was it because you were dissatisfied with the conduct of former practitioners, or was it intended as a meritorious achievement?

This is a heterodox view. Answer: The intent of what I have composed is fully clarified in the preface. Now, as this *Biànchāo* (Discerning Extracts) arises, I shall briefly cite its structural framework to manifest its four aspects.

First, it clarifies that certain ancients did not rely on the Vinaya at all when propagating and maintaining the teachings, but instead conducted affairs solely through their own intellectual ingenuity.
Second, although the former masters relied upon the Vinaya-piṭaka, their expository teachings were not clear, resulting in errors in the practices they explained.
Third, I lament that the commentaries of the ancient teachers did not manifest [the rules] for application in worldly affairs; how could they suffice as a model for future learners?

Fourth, although the *karmavācanā* texts of both ancient and modern times clarify worldly matters, they are either too prolix or too abbreviated to be of practical benefit to beginners. I shall now briefly cite [from them].
There are four points. It is essential that this *Zhaochao* (Excerpts) be compiled; is this not a meritorious task, rather than promoting heterodox views?

This will be explained in detail below in the "Preface on the Occasion of the Composition. Fearing prolixity, I shall not elaborate here. Second, the section distinguishing the time and place of the compilation, which has two parts:

first, distinguishing the time and place of the initial compilation; second, clarifying the time and place of the revision. Nanshan said: "In the sixth month of the ninth year of the Wude era of the Tang dynasty..."
This was the time. It was compiled at Fengde Monastery on Mount Zhongnan in the capital; this was the place.

At that time, as the government was purging the ranks of the monastic community, there was no concern for public reputation. Thus, I closed my door and arranged the material according to what I had studied.

My sole intention was practical application; I wrote with direct brushwork for clarity, without striving for ornate prose. Therefore, the language is often clogged and crude; I trust those with discernment will understand.
The scholar understands that my aspirations are entrusted herein. Regarding the second point, the time and place of the re-revision:

according to the *Biographies of Nanshan*, in the eighth year of the Zhenguan era, while traveling to visit famous mountains, he arrived at Yici Valley in Shi Prefecture and consequently re-revised the *Shichao*.
He also annotated the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, the *Karmavācanā-vibhāṣā*, and other works; as he examined and lectured on them one after another, the five assemblies marveled at his extraordinary mastery.

Within the fifth section, "Exegesis According to the Text," there are two parts: first, the introductory section on the judgment of the teachings (*p'an-chiao*); second, from "The Four-Part [Vinaya]" onwards, the exegesis based on the text itself.

The first three [sections]. First, clarifying the reasons for the structural classification (*kepan*). Second, distinguishing between existence and non-existence. Third, summarizing all virtues to judge the differences among the commentaries (*chao*).

Regarding the first, the reasons: Question: The Buddha’s teachings were transmitted from the West; who in this land classified them into these three distinct parts? Answer: The Bodhisattva Dao’an possessed extraordinary wisdom.
He exhausted the source of profound meanings and was ahead of others regarding even what had not yet sprouted. He analyzed the fundamental teachings and summarized—
It is divided into three sections. When the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* subsequently arrived, it was found that the Eastern language and the Western text were indeed in perfect accord.

Now, teachings do not arise in isolation; they must have a cause. The treatise refers to this as the "Section on the Causes and Conditions for the Arising of the Teaching," which in this land is called the "Introduction.

Once the conditions for arising are manifest, there must be a fulfillment of what was intended. The treatise refers to this as the "Section on What is Expounded in the Holy Teachings," which in this land is called the "Main Body" (the Correct Teaching).

Not only does this bring benefit to the present, but it is also hoped that its influence will extend to the future. The *Śāstra* refers to this as the "Section on Following the Teaching and Practicing It," while here it is termed "Circulation" (*liutong*).
From that time onward, all have followed this classification.

Second, regarding the determination of presence or absence: however, among the various sacred teachings, some are complete while others are incomplete. For instance, the *Avataṃsaka* and the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* explain only the introduction and the main body;

the *Avalokiteśvara Chapter* contains the middle and the conclusion; and the *Heart Sūtra* lacks both the beginning and the end entirely. As for the *Śrīmālādevī Sūtra* and other such scriptures, they mostly possess all three divisions.
Therefore, when judging and classifying the teachings, one must not treat them as being identical.

The third section has two parts: first, an introduction to the ancient [traditions]; second, the establishment of the present [position]. Regarding the introduction to the ancient: it summarizes how various virtuous masters differ in their categorization of the *Chao* (Excerpts).
Whether from remote antiquity or recent times, whether among former sages or later scholars, their structural analysis (*kepan*) of the text of the *Chao* does not deviate from two basic intentions.

Some divide it into three sections, taking the "Distinct Teaching" (*biejiao*) as their basis; others establish only two categories, following the original text of the *Chao*. For now, regarding the three sections: they are the Introductory, the Main, and the... [text continues].

The commentary states: According to the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, the first ten sections constitute the introductory portion (*nidāna*). From the second section, "Establishing the Thesis" (*zhìzōng*), through the twenty-ninth, these together constitute the main body (*samyak-artha*).
The thirtieth section, "Various Schools’ Separate Practices," constitutes the dissemination portion (*pariṇāmana*). How is this known?

Regarding the division into three parts in the *Chao* (Commentary), it follows the *Jie-mo-su* (Karmavācanā-vyākhyā). That treatise contains ten chapters, which the author of the *Chao* himself has categorized.
This is divided into three sections. The first, the "Collection on the Conditions for the Dharma" (*Jífáyuánchéng*), constitutes the introduction (*nidāna*).

The second, from "The Binding and Liberation of the Various Realms" (*Zhūjiè jiějiě*) downward through the eight chapters, constitutes the main body (*śarīra*). The third, the single chapter "Miscellaneous Dharmas for Sustaining the Teaching" (*Záfa zhùchí*), constitutes the dissemination (*parīndanā*).

Since that [text] takes miscellaneous dharmas as its dissemination, these various sections circulating separately serve to encourage study; this is what is meant by "dissemination. Thus it is established. Next, [the text] establishes...
Second, Fuyang and others state that there are only two sections, with the introduction being exactly as before, and no section on circulation (*liutong*).

They establish this by saying: "As when the Buddha preached a sutra, there are three reasons for establishing the section on circulation: first, because he spoke directly in accordance with the capacities of the audience;

second, because at the conclusion of the preaching, there was an audience to whom the teaching was entrusted; and third, because at the conclusion of the preaching, the fourfold assembly relied upon his instructions and practiced accordingly."

Therefore, the *Shu-yao* does not include it; thus, it was not established [as a separate section]. As for what the ancients established—encouraging study so that one might know—it is for the purpose of circulation.

The Buddha ordained that all disciples must learn and know these Three Baskets of the Holy Teachings. Since failing to study them constitutes an offense against the precepts, why would this alone be an exception?
There is no such principle. If that were the case, and it were not established as a section on circulation, it should not have been transmitted to later students.

Answer: Generally, there are two ways of disseminating [the teachings]: first, encouraging study; second, entrusting [the teachings]. Encouraging study as a means of dissemination occurs throughout all meanings.
Now, this commentary begins from the introductory section and concludes with the main body of the text;
by clarifying the meaning according to the text, it aids both the new and old students and encourages them to practice it. This is "encouraging study" as a means of dissemination.

Next, regarding the establishment of the present [text], it is divided into two parts: first, the formal exposition; second, a comparative analysis of the two prefaces found in the *Sūtra*, the *Vinaya*, and the *Śāstra* (Commentary), as well as their points of agreement and difference.
First, concerning what is established here: since the original text of the *Śāstra* already possesses its own structural divisions (*ko-fen*), why is it necessary to establish separate ones?

The title refers to the "Preface to the *Śāstra*. Second, the "Garment" (*yi*) refers to the ten topical gates (*shí mén*) as the preface; the principle of having a preface is clear. In the upper scroll, the chapters are established to set forth the fundamental tenets (*biāo zōng*).
The Commentary (Zhù) further states: "The initial presentation of the essential body (zōngtǐ) constitutes the text of the main teaching (zhèngzōng), which may be relied upon;

however, as there is no established section for the propagation (liútōng), I have not yet ventured to divide it. Furthermore, the Sub-commentary (Chāo) itself divides the sections based on approximately three lines of text, without setting forth a position for the propagation.

Moreover, according to the beginning of the 'Miscellaneous Essential Practices' (Zá yào xíng piān), the conclusion of the preceding section introduces the following one, stating: 'If the stages of the journey are mutually inclusive, they possess the aforementioned [elements]...'"
The various sections are categorized and subsumed under three divisions. Within these three divisions, it is impossible to extract a single chapter to serve as a "Circulation Section" (Prakīrṇaka).
If one were to establish this based on the *Karmavācanā* (Jie-mo), the *Karmavācanā-vyākhyā* (Jie-mo-su) states that they are distinct and cannot be classified together.

The original *Vinayavibhāṣā* (Chao-ben) says: "How could one dare to arbitrarily judge the Buddha’s scriptures? Since even [the extant versions] are not complete, how could fabricated works be identical? One must certainly request..."

Regarding the division into "upper" and "lower": if one seeks it according to the text, it cannot be established [as such]. In principle, the "most excellent" (the *uttara*) portion should be the primary focus. Furthermore, there are those who wish to establish three divisions;

these should also be sought based on the text of the *Chao* (the *Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā*). The first two follow the previous method; the third, however, is based on the opening section of the *Zazaxingpian* (Chapter on Miscellaneous Essential Practices), which categorizes and collects them systematically to form the *Pravāraṇā* (or *Pravibhāga*) division.

This too constitutes the structural framework of this school. It differs from the former approach in that it selects only a single chapter, allowing for both perspectives to coexist according to one's inclination.
Second, distinguishing between the two prefaces of the Sūtras and the Vinaya; the *Chao* (Commentary) treats them likewise. Regarding the two prefaces of the Sūtras:

the first is called "Certification of Faith" (*zhèngxìn*), referring to the six factors of accomplishment beginning with "Thus have I heard. The second is "Setting Forth" (*fǎqì*), such as when the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states:

"At that time, the Elder Subhūti asked the World-Honored One," and so forth. Regarding the two prefaces of the Vinaya: the first is "Encouraging Faith" (*quànxìn*), referring to [the account of] Dharmatrāta...

The Venerable Upāli, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, extracted the four divisions (*caturvarga*) from the great *Vinaya-piṭaka*. Fearing that people might not believe it, he exhorted them to give rise to faith at that time;

thus [the text] says, "I prostrate and pay homage to all Buddhas," and so forth. Second, regarding the originator: it refers to Śāriputra, who, relying on a place of tranquility, gave rise to a thought.
He contemplated how long the Dharma of previous Buddhas had remained and requested the Buddha to establish the precepts extensively so that the Dharma would endure for a long time.

Because it abides [in the Dharma], it is called "initiation. Regarding the two prefaces of the *Chao* (Commentary): the first preface states that the study of the precepts (*śīla-śikṣā*) is the life-force of the Buddha-Dharma;

its power to sustain and maintain the teaching is profound. Although the Buddhas and the four reliances (*catur-niśraya*) have propagated and upheld it without fail, because we now dwell in the degenerate age of the Semblance Dharma (*sāṃprata-yuga*), the times have become increasingly diluted and thin.

Those who faithfully observe and revere them are rare; those who follow the practices of former masters often remain confused regarding the guidance of the teachings. As for the compositions of the ancients, their complexity or brevity fails to meet the needs of the present time.
One must initiate this sentiment to compose the *Xingshichao* (Commentary on Monastic Practice). Thus it is said: "With a brilliant resolve, I have set forth my pen to fully unfold [this work].
This constitutes the source of its inception; therefore, it is the "Preface of Inception.

Second, the various teachings selected for inclusion in the *Chao*, their ritual matters and practical applications, and their categories are arranged according to their affinities and given as titles at the head. These encompass the great framework of the Tripiṭaka and synthesize...

The extensive expositions of the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Abhidharma are categorized into ten thematic sections to clarify how the teachings were established according to the capacities of beings. These regulations and prohibitions truly apply to future generations.
Regarding the determination of the original source, when there is no text in one’s own school, it is permitted to adopt from other divisions.

When the Vinaya indicates that something should be heard but does not provide a full explanation, one need not concern oneself with the literal phrasing; rather, one should directly cite essential statements and sublime expressions. Thus, it enables people of the time to see the essence of the *Chao* (Commentary).

[Supplement]: It is known that this was permitted by the Buddha; the present *Chao* (Excerpts) cites it here as proof that it is indeed trustworthy. I have thus divided this preface into two parts, corresponding to the "Proof" (*zhèng*) and "Encouragement" (*quàn*) aspects of faith.

Therefore, one should know that the two prefaces of the *Sūtra*, *Vinaya*, and *Chao* are all identical in their inspiration through proof and encouragement; there is only a slight difference in the arrangement of the preceding and following sections.

Regarding the "Correct Teaching" (*zhèngzōng*), there are three types of proximate meanings, which differ in three respects according to the capacity of the audience, the principle (*lǐ*), and the phenomenon (*shì*). [The distant...]

[The Master] said: "It is accomplished through cultivation that is free from faults; it is not otherwise. Question: In the Sūtras and Vinaya, the testimony of faith (*śraddhā*) always precedes the introduction (*nidāna*).
Why, then, in this *Śāstra-ṭīkā*, is the introduction placed first and the testimony of faith placed after? Answer: Indeed, the original Sūtras state that the introduction comes first.

However, when the Buddha was approaching his parinirvāṇa, he left instructions that the testimony of faith should be placed [at the beginning]. In the Vinaya, it is Śāriputra who provides the introduction.

The original [text] was also placed at the beginning. When the five divisions were established, it was only then that the "Encouragement of Faith" (*Kuan-hsin*) was appended. The present *Ch'ao* (Excerpts) is not like this;

its author composed the *An-ssu ching-lü* (Unsurpassed Sūtra and Vinaya) himself and left behind instructions for its division into two parts, treating them as identical to the Buddha’s initial preaching of the Vinaya and Sūtras. This was originally intended to be the primary [section].

Later, fearing that people of the time would have little learning and not realize that these abridgments, deletions, and supplements were all authorized by the Buddha, he therefore placed [the *Kuan-hsin*] next.

To cite the authentic texts and provide proof so as to inspire faith, this shall come later. The preceding various meanings have concluded the introductory section on the classification of the teachings (*śāsana-vibhāga*).
Now begins the second part: the exegesis according to the text. This is divided into two sections; first, from the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* onwards, up to the tenth [chapter].
The Preface constitutes the introductory section (*nidāna*). The second part, *The Compendium of Ritual Procedures for the Vinaya of the Four-Part School:

A Condensation of the Excessive and a Supplement for the Deficient*, consisting of thirty chapters in its upper volume, constitutes the main body (*saddharma*). This first section is now divided into two parts: first, an explanation of the general exposition of the preface;

second, from "Now, as for the virtue of the precepts" onwards, a detailed interpretation based on the two orders (*dvivarga*). The first of these two has two sub-sections: first, an explanation of the title of the work composed; second, [the section on] Jingzhao.

The following section identifies the person capable of composing this work. It consists of two parts: first, an explanation of the general title of the newly compiled *Shō*; second, a clarification within the annotations that distinguishes it from previous individual compositions. Question:

Since ancient times, in all commentaries on titles (*hikika*), one first explains the title and only then proceeds to the structural divisions (*kō*) of the introduction (*jo*) and the main body (*shō*).
By what teaching does the present work depart from this, first dividing the introduction and the main body, and only then presenting the title within the introduction? May this be permitted?

Does this title then belong to the introduction? Answer: It is indeed highly significant. This general title encompasses the general introduction, which contains the overall purport of the entire commentary (*chao*).
From the beginning of the three volumes of the main body (*zhengzong*) onwards, all likewise follow the general name;

however, as for the "volumes" (*juan*), they differ according to their specific divisions—upper, middle, and lower—whereas the "titles" (*ti*) pertain to the general, being nothing other than a pruning of the redundant and a supplementation of the deficient.
If the ritual procedures were omitted, and if the general title were not raised, whose preface would this be? And by what name would the upper, middle, and lower volumes be established?

Therefore, one knows that without the general, there is no way to encompass the specific; thus, all [the general elements] are listed in the general title. Without the specific, the general cannot be realized;
therefore, beneath the general, the preface and the distinctions of the upper, middle, and lower volumes are listed. This is...

One gives rise to views based on the literal text, rather than following the recorded words with a distracted mind. Question: According to the ancients, they first explain the general title and subsequently divide the text into the introduction and the main body;
what fault is there in this? Answer: Regarding the division and judgment, it is not convenient. If one were to first explain the general name of the *Chao* (Commentary)...
The single character "xu" (序, sequence) serves as a distinct heading for the section on the introduction; thus, from this point onward, the text should be divided into two sections:

first, clarifying the introductory section (*nidāna-vibhāga*); second, examining the main body (*śarīra*). If one were to divide it in this manner, it would distinguish [the main text] from the commentaries and the titles of the chapters.
However, since the title remains after the division of the sections, this is not convenient. Furthermore, according to the ancients, one first provides a general explanation of the title and—
To assign a title and rank, and then subsequently divide the text into the Introductory (Nidāna) and Main (Saddharma) sections, would be most inconvenient.

Since the title of the Introduction has already been explained, it is logically inconsistent to further establish a separate section for the "Introductory Division" (Nidāna-vibhāga). Furthermore, the author certainly did not intend such a division.

Because of these various objections, this section was composed. Question: This title belongs to the Introduction; therefore, the annotative notes may simply differ from the title of the Introduction. Answer: [As follows...]
Regarding the distinct introductory notes found at the beginning of each of the three volumes, although their phrasing appears different, they serve the same purpose.

The first volume uses the term "author" (*zuòzhě*), which is not without its designated name and title; the middle volume uses "composer" (*zhùshùzhě*), which frequently establishes a name for distinction;

and the last volume uses "annotator-compiler" (*zhùzhuàn*), which is by no means lacking in a name or heading. Thus, these are the general introductory distinctions found at the head of all three volumes, regardless of the specific wording.
The introduction and the main body differ from those of the ancients. According to the divisions established above, there is no detail that is not fully accounted for.

Upon reaching the conclusion of the lecture, when the topical outlines are restated and summarized, one merely summarizes the introduction and the main body without restating the titles; thus, it appears as if there are no titles. This requires further discernment. Within this, there are two parts:

first, explaining the general name of the *Śāstra*; second, separately explaining the single character "xu" (introduction) by establishing its topical headings, thereby distinguishing it [from other works].

As for the ordering and the assignment of names and ranks, there is no need to labor over them with detailed regulations; they shall merely be briefly described as occasion demands. This is not a matter of minute detail;
let the masters consider this in its general scope.
In both ancient and modern expositions of titles, there are two modes of judgment: the extensive and the concise. Regarding the concise, Master Fu stated:

"The *Sifen lü* (Four-Part Vinaya) cites the general title of the fundamental school; 'Deletions of the Redundant' (*Shanfan*) and so forth signify the specific name of the composition. In Sanskrit, it is called *Caturvargika*."

This [work] consists of four parts. "Four" refers to the number; "parts" (fen) refers to branches. Taken together, these four branches form a single compendium; hence it is called the *Caturvarga* (Four Parts).
In Sanskrit it is called *Vinaya*, which is translated here as "Law" (*lü*). "Law" means the Dharma.
Its seven branches encompass purity, enduring the cold of the evergreen pine; its six prohibitions are upright and luminous, free from the flaws of even a white jade disc. It is solemn and austere.

Because it is observed, it is called "Dharma" (the Teaching). "Four Parts" (*caturvarga*) is a specific designation for that which is divided; "Vinaya" (Discipline) is the general name for what is contained within.

When the general and the specific are both indicated, it is named the *Caturvargika-vinaya* (The Vinaya in Four Parts). "Deleted" (*shan*) means to excise. "Redundant" (*fan*) means excessive. [The text] weeds out disordered phrasing and truncates superfluous branches;
it removes the spurious and retains the authentic, so that the meaning is abundant while the words are concise. "Supplemented" (*bu*) means to augment. [It fills] the omissions...

This [work] is brief. It widely gathers what is upright and substantial, collecting scattered pearls. Although its radiance may be slightly dimmed, its great contribution is not yet sufficient for practice.

To manifest the words and clarify the actions, it is said that the principle is simple; the principle is quiescent, empty, pervasive, and perfectly interfused—this is its intended meaning. This is for the purpose of guarding body and speech.
The *Yanshi Chao* (Excerpts on the Practice of the Vinaya) is an abridgment. Its elegant prose is layered with brilliance and its subtle meanings are clearly elucidated.
It serves as the title for this composition and stands at the head of all its constituent chapters; therefore, it is called the *Sifenlü [Shanbu Suishu Yiji] Chao*.
Second, the extensive explanation has two parts. First, the ten characters [from "The Four-Part Vinaya"] cite the general title that permeates the entire work.

Second, the single character "Preface" (xu) subsumes the specific headings of the two prefaces; this constitutes the preceding section, for which the character "Preface" must be appended to the brief explanation above.
If one follows the subsequent section, it states: "The second, the extensive explanation, is divided into two parts. First, the three characters 'The Four-Part Vinaya' (*Sifen lü*)."
This raises the fundamental tenets of what has been studied. The seven characters following "Delete the Redundant" (*shānfán*) indicate the general title of the present work.

Regarding the interpretation of these fundamental tenets by masters of both past and present, there are differences in their concise expositions. The *Língshān Wèn* (Questions from Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa) asks: "Between this *Sifen lü* (Four-Part Vinaya) and the [Mūla-]Vinaya, which came first?
It answers: "The Vinaya should come first, as it was spoken by the Buddha himself; furthermore, it has been transmitted through five patriarchs as a single Vinaya Piṭaka."
The name "Four-Part" (*Caturvarga*) arose later; it is a derivative term. If that is so, the *Vinaya* (Discipline) should logically precede it. Why, then, is it placed after the *Caturvarga*? Answer:
Those of both ancient and modern times have universally maintained that this was done for the sake of distinction. The *Jixin shu* (Commentary on the Mind of Precepts) states:

"The 'Four-Part' is a title that reveals its specific doctrine, distinguishing it from other schools. 'Vinaya' is used to distinguish it from the other Piṭakas; it is the general designation for the *Vinaya*, not a separate [category]."
It is spoken of as "four parts" (caturvarga) to manifest the whole; for without the whole, there would be no way to encompass the particulars, and thus it is called *vinaya*.

These four parts are both particular and whole: they are particular in relation to other schools (*nikāya*), and they are whole insofar as they collectively subsume the four parts. The meaning of *vinaya* is likewise so.
This collectively subsumes the five divisions and specifically distinguishes them from the other treasuries (*piṭakas*).

Regarding the first two [points], I shall first explain the two characters *sifen* (four parts) and subsequently resolve the single character *lü* (vinaya). Regarding the first three [points], I shall initially clarify the correct interpretation.

Second, the refutation of [erroneous] interpretations; third, the clarification of the distinctions between persons and dharmas. Regarding the "four divisions," the *Dharmatara-śāstra* (Fu fǎ zàng zhuàn) states:
"One hundred years after [the Buddha’s passing], Upagupta had five disciples, each adhering to a particular view as their standard.
Consequently, they divided the Great Canon into five treatises, and the four distinct titles arose from this. An ancient master said: "Dharmānanda..."
The Master of the Vinaya, at the Great Canon’s eighty recitations of the Vinaya, transmitted the text four times, exhausting all the characteristics of what is explained;

hence it is called the *Catuṣpariṣat*. Specifically, the twenty fascicles of the Bhikṣu Prātimokṣa constitute the first part; the fifteen fascicles from the Bhikṣuṇī Vinaya onwards constitute the second part;
the fourteen fascicles from the *Varṣā* (Rainy Season Retreat) onwards constitute the third part; and from the *Vihāra* (Dwellings) onwards—

It consists of eleven fascicles and constitutes the fourth division. Ling Shan states: "This is named according to its recitation; the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* and other vinayas are all the same. Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says:
"In the kingdom of Mathurā, the original Vinaya consisted of eighty sections (*bhāṣya*). The treatise itself explains this as follows:
Regarding the "Eighty Sections" (Asīti-bhāṣā): this is a name derived from the recitation, namely the Vinaya of the Eighty Recitations (Aṣṭaka-bhāṣā-vinaya).
Next, concerning the identification of those that are not commentaries, the Tripitaka Master Yi Jing stated: "This was likely brought as a Sanskrit original by a Tripitaka Master of that time."

There are four recensions; this [text] was produced according to these four recensions, and is therefore called the *Caturvarga* (Four-Part Vinaya). The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* and other vinayas likewise judge it thus.
They establish the following reasoning: when Upāli presided over the council, he had to ascend the seat eighty times before his recitation was finally completed.
How could it be that the Master of the Vinaya recited a single section four times without such a principle? Regarding those who derive their names from counting-sticks (*sè*), the *Fazhengpò* states:
"For instance, when Jue Ming came from the West, he was able to recite the Sanskrit original; as he reached this point, he translated it immediately.

How could there have been four counting-sticks, resulting in four names? Furthermore, the Tripiṭaka Master Furuo of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* was also able to recite the original text, yet there were no Sanskrit [manuscripts].
"Ten bundles of leaves"—how could this be called the *Daśabhāṇavāra* (Ten Recitations)?

Therefore, we know it is not [the same]. Third, to clarify the distinction between the person and the Dharma: Question: Are these four parts (*caturvarga*) the name of a person or the name of the Dharma? Answer: The "four parts" is the name of the Dharma.
If one were to follow the person who upholds it, one should call it the *Dharmaguptaka*. However, here we set aside the person and follow the Dharma; therefore...

Regarding the term "Four-Part" (Sifen): if both the school and the person are designated together, it refers to what is titled in the *Karmavācanā* as the *Sifen lü Tanwude jiemobu* (The Four-Part Vinaya, Dharmaguptaka Karmavācanā).
"Dharmagupta" is a Sanskrit term; according to Fei Changfang’s *Lidai sanbao ji*, in the Wei language it means "Dharma-Treasury" (Fazang).
Among the eighteen schools, he is named Dharmarakṣa; among the twenty schools, he is named Dharmagupta; in the *Śīlaskandhaka-vibhāṣā*, he is named Dharmottara;
in the *Karmavibhāṣā*, he is named Dharmādarśa; or he is called Dharmasamya, and so forth.
The second section, the explanation of the *Vinaya*, is divided into three parts: first, the translation of the names; second, the interpretation of the meaning of *vinaya*;

and third, the subsumption [of these meanings] under the six types of grammatical analysis (*ṣaḍ-vyākhyāna*). Regarding the first, the translation of the names, the *Śīlaskandha-śāstra* states: "To enumerate the various names collectively, there are three kinds.

First, in Sanskrit it is called *vinaya*, which is translated here as 'law' (*lü*). Second, in Sanskrit it is called *śīla*, which is translated here as 'precept' (*jiè*). Third, in Sanskrit it is called *prātimokṣa*."
This is called "individual liberation" (prātimokṣa). Question: Since there are three names [for this discipline], what is the intention behind designating it specifically as "vinaya"?
Answer: "Vinaya" means teaching; it is that which can give rise to understanding and practice. The Great Sage bestowed the teaching, fully enumerating the paths of conduct.

The five assemblies rely upon these provisions to maintain perfect virtue; therefore, it is called "precept" (śīla). By relying on the precepts, one eradicates transgressions until they are extinguished; therefore, it is called "liberation" (mokṣa). This is...
Thus, both the practice of cause and effect arise from the teachings; therefore, the Vinaya teachings are cited here to encompass these two. Next, regarding the explanation of the meaning:

the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) asks, "What is the meaning of 'precept' (*śīla*)? The meaning is defined as "to warn" or "to admonish. It is so called because it warns and exhorts the three types of action (*trikarma*).
“Staying far away from conditions that are non-virtuous” clarifies its cause. Regarding what is called “liberation” (*vimukti*), as cited in the treatise:

the precepts of the path are named liberation, while the precepts of the ritual act are named individual liberation (*prātimokṣa*). There are two obstacles to the purity of the precepts: first, unwholesome karma; second, afflictions (*kleśa*).

The precepts purify the obstacle of karma, which may be eliminated by awaiting wisdom; in view of what is removed by this specific portion, they are called “individual liberation. Subsequently, wisdom eliminates the afflictions. Now...
It is called "ultimate" and is named "liberation. Regarding the term *vinaya*, the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states:

"In ancient translations, *vinaya* was all rendered as 'extinction' (*mie*), because the seven types of *vinaya* serve to pacify the four kinds of disputes. Now, for what reason is it translated as 'discipline' (*lü*)? 'Discipline' (*lü*) means 'dharma.

It is named after its teaching, which distinguishes between the heavy and the light, and determines what is permitted or prohibited, and what constitutes observance or violation. Since that which is not dharma is not fixed, it is correctly translated [as discipline]."
The secular world has nine schools of thought, and the Dharma is one among them. Therefore, all legal matters in the world fall under the jurisdiction of the penal code.
While the Way differs from the secular, its terminology is distinct; yet when it comes to adjudication, one must necessarily rely on established law.

This is why the character for "law" (lǜ) is accompanied by the radical for "pen" (yù): it is to signify the brush. In resolving and determining cases, nothing is settled without the brush; thus, the brush is the instrument of the school of law.

As for the *Xiàng* (Elephant): consider that the disciplinary sections are like the seven types of discipline found in the *Ekottarika-āgama*. The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* also has its proofs regarding the nine matters.

"Anciently they were unified as 'extinction' (*miè*)" refers to their functional efficacy. Extinction means the ability to quell disputes; it is not that the discipline itself is not quiescent. It is like water extinguishing fire.
It is not called "extinction. Therefore, the Vinaya text states: "The classification according to the *piṇḍa* (sections) and *varga* (chapters) all possess established precedents;

as they collectively encompass the principles of the Dharma, what else remains to be discussed? Question: Since the Vinaya uses the Dharma as its instruction and establishes protocols for ritual practice, how does it differ from the other two Piṭakas?

Answer: They are not the same. In the other Piṭakas, the principles are clarified; these principles reside in emptiness and penetration. Whichever gate one enters to reach understanding, it all accords with the contemplation of the Way.

The intent lies in removing obstructions; why restrict oneself to the literal words? The Vinaya, however, is not like this. Its distinctions between light and heavy offenses, and its allowances and prohibitions, are fixed by permanent standards.
To disrupt the constant order and ruin the continuity of the lineage must necessarily be governed by legal statutes. From this perspective, the meaning of the Dharma becomes even more manifest.

Therefore, the Tripiṭaka did not originally exist in this land and cannot be translated [into its local customs]. Although the Vinaya is concise in its principles, its judicial sentencing is entirely inconsistent with our own; yet the application of its statutes possesses a systematic method.
Since the words are similar, I shall now merely translate the intended meaning and stop here. How is this known? "Vinaya" means "Dharma. It possesses ritual propriety from beginning to end;
within the Buddha's teachings, this principle can be established. Therefore, the establishment of the *pien-chu* (sections of the Prātimokṣa) is observed by all three periods of time.

While the methods of conversion may differ, the natural precepts (*prakṛti-śīla*) are eternally fixed. Secular laws are not so; they undergo changes and developments through successive generations. In antiquity, meat was used...

Regarding "punishment" (*xing*): thus the legal codes state that "punishment" means "to complete. Once one's flesh is destroyed, it remains permanently so for the rest of one's life and cannot be restored.

Now, the cane-stick, penal servitude, and banishment are used as substitutes for these ancient methods; therefore, they are not fixed. Question: According to the Buddhist Dharma, can the Vinaya rules be definitively applied by correspondence?

Upon examining the characteristics of its teachings, there are also instances where they are not fixed. For example, the four grave offenses (*caturmahāpatti*) are likened to decapitation; how is this so?

Therefore, regarding the opening of the rite of repentance and the authorization to preside over *karmavācanā*, the views and interpretations of various schools differ in their assessments of what constitutes light or heavy offenses.

How, then, can the Dharma be taught so that the eternal order is permanently established? Answer: Heavy offenses involve either concealment or disclosure, which are two distinct matters; the Dharma permits both opening and closing [of the path], and thus there exists a constant standard.

To sever one's head is a metaphor for lacking the factors of nobility (*ārya-dharma*). Upholding the Dharma requires adhering to the fundamental precepts and rituals; while the application must account for the gravity or lightness of the circumstances according to the specific capacity of the individual, the structural framework of the particular school (*nikāya*) must not be lost.
Based on this very standard, how could it be considered non-Dharmic?

Next, to distinguish the six types of grammatical analysis (*ṣaṭ-vibhakti*): how many analyses do the *Caturvarga* and the *Vinaya* possess? Master E distinguishes two based on the expressive terms (*abhidhāna*):
namely, *karmadhāraya* (appositional compound) and *bahuvrīhi* (possessive compound). Regarding the term *karmadhāraya*: "holding" (*dhāra*) means to sustain; "function" (*karman*) means activity.

The *Vinaya* can sustain the activity of the four categories (*caturvarga*); since the four categories are themselves the *Vinaya*, it is called *karmadhāraya*. Regarding the term *bahuvrīhi*: the "four categories" refers to a number.

Regarding the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Four-Part Vinaya), it is explained by means of a numerical compound (*dvigu*). When focusing on what is expressed (*abhidheya*), there is also an *adhikaraṇa-samāsa* (dependent determinative).

"The precepts of the four parts" is an *adhikaraṇa-samāsa*. Although various commentaries extensively list the categories of the six types of compounds, they are not recorded here as they are not essential to this digest (*piṇḍī*).

Second, the explanation of the general title for this present work. The seven characters are divided into four parts: first, *shānfán* (deleting the redundant); second, *bǔquè* (supplementing the deficient);
third, *xíngshì* (practical application); and fourth, *chão* (extract). Regarding "deleting the redundant" (*shānfán*): Lingshan says, "to prune and eliminate" (*shānxuē*;

*shān* is pronounced *suōjiān*). The *Sāncāng* says, "to delete and remove. The *Shēnglèi* says, "to prune and finalize. Thus, when Confucius "deleted the *Shī* and *Shū* and finalized the *Lǐ* and *Yuè*," this was precisely that practice.
Fazheng said: "The character 'ce' (册) is derived from 'dao' (刀). 'Ce' refers to bamboo slips and wooden tablets, known as *du*.
This was because in ancient times there was no paper, so people wrote on these slips and tablets. Later, Cai Lun invented paper, which replaced those slips and tablets.

When the ancients used their brushes, if a scribe made an error in writing, they would scrape it away with a knife; this conveys the meaning of deletion and correction. However, the general principle of deleting the redundant does not exceed this."

There are two types: the first is "abbreviating" (shānqǔ), and the second is "excising" (chánlú). This is because of verbosity. In the case of the Sacred Teachings, one abbreviates what is redundant and prolix;
as the text says, "that which is not practiced at the time," its meaning is equivalent to "abandonment. In the case of commentaries (zhāngshū), one excises superfluous accounts;

thus it is said, "superfluous accounts must be cut away," so that the general intent may be established. Regarding the three meanings of Mount Lingyan for resolving verbosity, and the four meanings of "Unfolding the Correct" (Fāzhèng)...
Explanation: Because the reasons have not yet been exhausted, we now rely on what is cited in the *Chao-wen* (Excerpts). Buddhist teachings are fully encompassed therein.

Generally speaking, there are nine categories: first, the primary texts of the Vinaya; second, the various schools (*nikāya*); third, the Sūtras of the Hīnayāna; and fourth, the Śāstras of the Hīnayāna.
There are nine categories: first, the five Mahāyāna Vinayas; second, the six Mahāyāna Sūtras; third, the Mahāyāna Śāstras; fourth, the collections of the noble sages;

fifth, the commentaries and sub-commentaries of the ancients; and sixth, the single volume of the *Śāstra* (the *Vinayamātṛkā*). These do not exceed these nine. Regarding the first, the abridgment of the texts of the specific Vinaya divisions:

for example, the two sets of *Prātimokṣa* for monks and nuns, and the twenty *Khandakas*. In explaining each matter, there is always an introductory narrative (*nidāna*) stating that the Buddha was at a certain location.
"Such-and-such a person has committed such-and-such an offense," and so forth. If we speak in terms of the *Prātimokṣa* itself, there are over six hundred sections, none of which are urgent matters.
Furthermore, regarding the *Vinaya-skandha* on the method of receiving the precepts, it clarifies the obstacles and prohibitions (*antarāyika-dharma*), all of which have their own origins (*nidāna*).

Initially, as for the methods of reception, there were those by "Welcome" (*svāgata*), the "Superior Method" (*uttara-dharma*), the Three Refuges, the Eight Precepts, the *Saṃghāvaśeṣa*, as well as the various *Khandakas* such as those concerning the settling of disputes. Since the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa...
Apart from the *karmavācanā*, there are no other [procedural] dharmas; therefore, they have been deleted in their entirety. The text says: "Who can pierce its knots and joints?

Second, regarding the deletion of the various Vinaya schools: one should know that while the *Dharmaguptaka* school contains only the text for convening the assembly, it does not discuss the six characteristics or the distance of the monks' arrival.
Now, the texts concerning the distance of the assembly's gathering from the various schools are selected for deletion, provided they are as follows: [if they can be divided].

[The text] distinguishes [the sources]. Thus, it adopts the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations), whose text states: "In accordance with the village boundary (*grāmamaryādā*), which is the monastery boundary (*vihāramaryādā*);

these cannot be distinguished. For the village boundary, it adopts the text from the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*; for the water boundary (*udakamaryādā*), it adopts the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, etc. All of these are selected through deletion;

as for all other remaining texts not fully included, they were not the intention of the compiler, and therefore they have been deleted. Third, regarding the deletion of Hīnayāna sūtras: the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*...

When assembling the Sangha, one should spread the seats and strike the *gandī*. While the various Vinayas state only that a resident lay attendant (*upāsaka*) or a novice (*śrāmaṇera*) should strike it, there are also instances where a monk (*bhikṣu*) strikes it;
however, these texts are not explicit. Therefore, I have taken the *Ekottarika Āgama* to establish that a monk may indeed strike it.
The *Ekottarika* says: "Ānanda ascended the lecture hall and struck the *gandī*; this was the Tathāgata’s command."

Regarding the drum: Ānanda himself struck it to testify that a bhikṣu may act as such; all other extensive elaborations have been deleted and not included. Fourth, regarding the deletion and inclusion of the Hīnayāna śāstras:

for instance, in the procedure for appointing those with the five virtues (*pañca-guṇa*) for the *pravāraṇā*, the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* merely states that one must possess the two sets of five virtues, but does not mention appointing two persons.
The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* and the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* both prescribe appointing two persons as the rule. In the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*...
Regarding two or more persons, up to a large number, for the purpose of performing the *posadha* (restoration of harmony):

although the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* and other vinayas clarify the number of persons to be appointed and the term "restoration of harmony" (*posadha*), the underlying meaning remains unclear. Therefore, I have excerpted from the *Trisahasra-vidhāna-śīla-śāstra*, which states:
"When appointing two persons, it is so that after the *pravāraṇā* (invitation to admonish) of the Saṃgha has concluded, they may confess their offenses to one another; one must not seek others."
As for the *Pudgalaviniścaya* (Self-Indulgence), because it was not authorized by the rest of the Sangha, all other textual passages that were not exhaustive have been deleted and omitted.
