Fifth, regarding the deletion of Mahāyāna vinaya texts: for instance, within the section on the precept against theft concerning the mutual use of the Three Jewels, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* and other codes extensively explain that the Three Jewels must not be used interchangeably, yet they do not provide the underlying reason why they must not be so used; therefore, these have been deleted.
Regarding the Mahāyāna Vinaya, the *Chao* (Excerpts) quotes from the *Ratnarāśi-sūtra*: "The two types of property belonging to the Buddha-dharma must not be used interchangeably.

This is because there is no one who acts as a master over the Buddha-dharma, nor is there anyone to whom one may submit a formal request for permission. Thus, they differ from the property of the Saṃgha. Consequently, the property of the *sthavira* (permanent endowment) and the *caitya* (provisional lodging) are distinct.

As for the *karmadāna* bhikṣu (bhikṣu in charge of affairs), he must harmonize with the Saṃgha by soliciting their consent (*chanda*) and distributing voting sticks (*śalākā*). Only when they are thus united may these funds be utilized. Self-...
As for external texts that were not exhaustive, they were deleted and not adopted; hence it is said, "the deletion of the prolix.

Regarding the six deletions, as for those Mahāyāna sūtras which state—along with various sections of the Vinaya—that receiving offerings improperly makes it difficult to digest the faithful alms, and that it is better to wrap one's body in iron leaves than to accept clothing and such from those with faith, yet lack methods for treating such ailments through aversion, these were deleted and replaced by extracts from the *Mahāsannipāta*.
The Sūtra says: "When a bhikṣu puts on his undergarment, he should cultivate the perception of it as being smeared with blood, putrid, and loathsome.
When holding his alms bowl, he should cultivate the perception of it as a skull smeared with blood. When receiving milk or curd, he should cultivate the perception of them as pus and blood.

When receiving vegetables, he should perceive them as like hair. Even when entering a dwelling, he should perceive it as a prison. This person will immediately attain the Dharma as it truly is. This is a brief summary.
This text was intended as a skillful means to inspire world-weariness (*saṃvega*). Aside from this, all other incomplete passages were deleted and not included.

Seventh, regarding the selection of Mahāyāna treatises: although various schools all possess the *mānāpya* (probation) for disciplining individuals, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states that the *brahmadanda* (excommunication) rite entails that none of the seven classes of followers may have contact with or speak to the person. Although such a text exists, its meaning and application remain unknown.
For this reason, I have selected and excerpted from the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*. Its text states: "If the mind is violent and unruly, it is subdued by the Dharma of Brahmā.

Since speech exists in the Desire Realm, and the ground [of existence] also extends to the Form Realm, yet there are those who cause affliction and offense through silence, one subdues them through silence.

Aside from these passages, all other incomplete texts have been deleted and not included. Furthermore, I have deleted various collections of the worthy and holy, as well as the five divisions of the Vinaya. Strike!

The fourfold striking consists of three rounds; that is, three strikes each. Since it does not mention "long striking," the *Dharmatāsaṃgraha-avadāna* (付法藏傳) relates the case of King Kaniṣka, who, due to his great slaughter and violence, died and was reborn within a thousand-headed fish. A wheel of swords revolved around his body, cutting him as he was born again.
However, whenever he heard the sound of a bell, the wheel of swords remained suspended in the air. It is because of such causes and conditions that [this practice] was made known.
Long excerpts. Now, taking these long excerpts to suffice for this ritual practice, all other remaining texts have been deleted and omitted.

Ninth, regarding the deletion of the commentaries and treatises of ancient masters: speaking in general terms, I shall cite four types as examples; if considered as a whole, they are far more numerous.

First, in the case of works such as the *Senglao* (Discourse on the Monastery), their prolixity has been deleted. Second, the deletion of redundancy and excessive usage—[the latter] being understood through common knowledge.
The practice of "bell-temples" (zhōng-sì) was established by the laity; they claim that [the temple] is pure as a separate entity from other things, thereby conflating the monastic and the secular.

Third, the confusion regarding the teachings concerning the *prakṛtistha-kṣetra* (natural boundary): within a single summer retreat, one may only receive the formal authorization (*jñapti*) three times, and one must utilize seventy-three paces and a half to assemble the Sangha across the entire monastery to establish purity, yet no monks are left to reside there—such evil practices must not be emulated. Fourth, the deletion of redundant evils: these are not...
Regarding the regulations for the Dharma and the Saṃgha, such passages as those that falsely cite the punishment of five hundred *puṇya* (merits) must all be deleted.
Thus, the *Chao* states: "Extraneous accounts must be excised," and further: "Now we wish to delete its redundancies and errors. Question:

Although the nine categories mentioned above exhaustively encompass the textual material, if one deletes the redundant explanations of ancient masters found in the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*, this may be considered the deletion of the superfluous. However, regarding the various Vinayas and Śāstras of other schools...
[Question: You take passages from the Hīnayāna sūtras to form the body of this commentary; these are all instances of supplementing what was missing.

How can you say that you have "deleted the redundant"? Is such an interpretation not confused? [Answer: It is because I wished to supplement what was missing that I first deleted and selected the texts.

For the time being, let us discuss how I took the essentials and removed the redundant; is this not indeed "deleting"? However, when citing those texts, it is impossible to transcribe them in full; I intend to delete [the superfluous].

The "Exclusionary Sections" (*chuchu*) constitute the elimination of the redundant. The *Chao* states: "Regarding the inexhaustible texts from outside [the core], if one were to insist on tracing their beginnings and ends, that would not be the intention of the compiler.
It further states: "Now, all have been abridged and omitted, retaining only the textual evidence.
The *Chao* itself declares this to be the elimination of the redundant; this is the proof.

Regarding the second point, "Supplementing Deficiencies" (Bùquē): Dāngyáng states that "supplementing" (bù) means to fill in, so as to make the appearance complete in meaning; "deficiency" (quē) means lacking, which carries the sense of being incomplete.

Lìngshān’s *Fourfold Explanation of the Term 'Fā'*, citing the *Zhèngyǐ*, provides three interpretations. However, regarding the text of the *Chāo* (Commentary), the underlying reasons are not yet exhaustive. Question:
Is it because the conduct of ancient practitioners was insufficient, or is it because the Vinaya itself is not comprehensive, such that deficiencies must be supplemented?
[Question: Yes. [Answer: The deeds of the ancients are indeed insufficient to discuss. As refuted in the Preface, not one in a hundred is authentic, due to the divergent tenets of the five masters.
Having gathered these fragmentary texts that have survived, they have been translated here, yet many errors remain. Their practices were inadequate for the times.

Since the original Vinaya text is absent, it is necessary to draw from the Sūtras and Śāstras so that both the capacity of the audience and the teaching are complete; therefore, supplementation is required.

Above, there are nine ways to eliminate redundancies, and there are likewise nine ways to supplement omissions. If the text of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* is not clear, one should take from other schools to supplement it.

If other schools have no such text, one takes from the *Sūtras* of the Hīnayāna to supplement it. If the *Sūtras* of the Hīnayāna have none, one takes from the *Śāstras* of the Hīnayāna to supplement it.
If the *Śāstras* of the Hīnayāna have none, one takes from the *Vinayas* of the Mahāyāna to supplement it. If the *Vinayas* of the Mahāyāna have none, one takes from the *Sūtras* of the Mahāyāna.

Where there is nothing in the Mahāyāna sūtras, I supplement it from the Mahāyāna śāstras. Where there is nothing in the Mahāyāna śāstras, I supplement it from the *Sangīti* (Compendium of the Noble Ones).

Where there is nothing in the *Sangīti*, I supplement it from the commentaries of the ancients. Where there is nothing in the commentaries of the ancients, the author of this sub-commentary has provided supplementation based on the meaning and the principle.

To provide an example of the four types of supplementation for resolving and clarifying [the text], it refers to the fifth section of the introduction, which concerns the meaning of the text for resolving and clarifying.
Consequently, this ensures that the textual matters of the entire *Śāstra* (Commentary) are complete. Thus, the text states: "The three fascicles encompass the text;

there is no detail left unexpounded. This is intended so that it may be practically useful when facing specific circumstances, without the need to consult others. First, the supplementation drawn from various schools.
Regarding the Vinaya, its matters are indeed numerous; let us cite one explanation as an example. For instance, within the *Zixi zhangxing* (Miscellaneous Practices of the Self-Indulgence), it asks:

"When the *an-gu* (rainy-season retreat) is completed, does this mean one may leave one's original location? The answer states: The Vinaya says that if one does not depart after the *an-gu* is completed, one commits an offense. In the Vinaya, it merely states that failing to depart constitutes an offense;

there is no mention of "not having a place to which one is invited" (*wu qingchu*) nor the phrase "not establishing a limit" (*bu zuo xian*) regarding such an uninvited place. Now, we shall take the five [points].

It is supplemented by [quotations from] the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*. The *Pañcavargika* states: "If one does not depart for even a single night after the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat) has concluded, it is permissible.

Or, "If no specific limit was set for the invitation, or if it is not a place where one has formally accepted an invitation, one may remain there. These passages from the *Pañcavargika* are used to supplement the text of the *Caturvargika-vinaya*, ensuring that the ritual procedures are complete.
Second, regarding the selection of texts from the Hīnayāna sūtras: for instance, in the section on the relinquishment of the precepts (*śikṣāpada*), the *Caturvargika-vinaya* states: "If..."
If one does not delight in the holy life (brahmacarya), it is permitted for them to relinquish the precepts and return to the household life.

However, if they later wish to cultivate pure conduct within the Buddha-dharma, they are again permitted to leave the household life and receive the full ordination (upasampadā). Such is the text of the Vinaya. Yet, it is not known how many times one may relinquish the precepts;
there is no such passage in any of the Vinayas. Therefore, the *Ekottarika Āgama* of the Hīnayāna sūtras was consulted to supplement this. The sūtra states: "Seven [circumstances] are permitted..."
To return and abandon [this] would be an error and contrary to the Dharma. Third, regarding the proponents of the Hīnayāna treatises who clarify the seeds of pure production (*viśuddha-jāti-bīja*):

the *Sifen lü* (Dharmaguptaka-vinaya) states that a bhikṣu should not perform the act of purification himself; rather, he should place the object on the ground and have a *kappiya-kāraka* (a "pure person") perform it, after which he may receive it with washed hands. The *Shan-chao* (Commentary) says:

This refers to cases where there is another person present; if no other person is available, there are no scriptural texts in the various schools [to provide for this], so one must supplement the practice with the treatises of the Hīnayāna.

The *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "One performs the preparatory rite oneself. The commentary explains: This does not mean that one may perform the purification by oneself at will; however, performing it oneself is beneficial. For example, regarding a cluster of fruit:
if it has not been purified, eating the skin or the pulp constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense for each instance; yet, if one eats the seeds, it is permissible.
For each individual *pāyattika* offense, if one now touches it with fire only once, one incurs only a single *dukkaṭa*. By combining them into a single heap of fruit, they all become pure at once;
thus one is spared from many offenses. Is this not beneficial? Therefore, I have taken that text to supplement these ritual procedures. Fourth, regarding the adoption of the Mahāyāna Vinaya:
for instance, in the case of stealing light items belonging to the five groups of renunciants who have recently passed away, the four-part Vinaya [states as follows].
The treatises contain no explicit text on this matter; thus, we take the *Śrāmaṇerakārikā* (Shansheng) to supplement these ritual procedures. Regarding the *Śrāmaṇerakārikā*:

it records the Buddha’s explanation to the elder Śrāmaṇera of the characteristics of guarding the precepts. In the *Yijing tu* (Diagram of the Translation of Scriptures), it is classified as a Mahāyāna Vinaya. The Vinaya states:

"If one steals the minor belongings of a deceased bhikṣu, if the *karman* has not yet been performed, one incurs an offense of light gravity relative to the Saṃgha of the ten directions. Nanshan says: "This refers to calculating the person..."
Because it does not reach five [monks]. If the *karman* has already been performed, one incurs a grave offense in relation to the *saṃgha* present before one.

Nanshan says: This means that because the number of people is limited, it can reach five. If, at the time of death, one steals items entrusted by the deceased according to their instructions, the offense is established in relation to the person to whom they were given.
Fifth, regarding those who take up Mahāyāna sūtras: fish and meat are prohibited in all Vinayas.
Regarding the five types of formal meals (*pañca-bhojanāni*): this constitutes the abrogation of the previous teaching. Now, that teaching is likewise abrogated;
we shall instead adopt the Mahāyāna sūtras to supplement these ritual practices. The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* states: "From this day forward, I do not permit my disciples to eat meat.

For those who eat meat sever the seed of great compassion (*mahāmaitrī*) and become objects of resentment for all living beings—whether moving in water, on land, or through the air. Therefore, I forbid their consumption. This is explained at length therein. Furthermore:
It is said: "As for the previous instruction regarding the eating of meat, this refers not to the flesh of the four types of birth, but merely to manifesting in bodily form.

This is for the sake of saving sentient beings. Regarding the sixth point, concerning those who uphold the Mahāyāna treatises: as in the section on the clear measurements for binding the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*), there are immeasurable texts from both Sūtra and Vinaya, both major and minor.
In the Vinaya, it simply states: "On the fourteenth day, when the precepts are recited, one should arrive beforehand on the thirteenth day; one must not receive [the precepts] [on the day itself]."
In order to clarify the measurement of the *yojana*, Nanshan stated: "Although there are textual references, they do not specify the number of *li*.
Both the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* and the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* state that three *yojanas* constitute the measure, yet neither mentions the size of a *yojana*.

Therefore, one should supplement this with the explicit text of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*. The treatise says: 'There are three kinds of *yojanas*: the smallest is forty *li*; thus, it is known that the measure can be extremely large.'"

[The distance is] one hundred and twenty *li*. This is based on the *Vinaya*, which states that it is the distance traveled in one day. Seventh, regarding the inclusion of the *Āryasaṃgha* (the assembly of noble ones):
as in the inquiry concerning leprosy (*kuṣṭha*) among the prohibitions, the *Vinaya* lacks a clear decision. Citing the *Sudarsana-vinaya*, it says: "Do not ask whether it is red, white, or black.

If it increases in a private place, it is [considered] increasing; if it does not increase in a private place, it is the opposite. Yet they did not realize that such a foul disease had already brought disgrace upon the Buddha.
Regarding the Dharma: what benefit is there in permitting its reception? Thus, it is cited from the *Sangha of King Aśoka* (Yùwáng jí): "There was a Srotāpanna with scabies and an Arhat with wounds;

because there is the benefit of attaining the fruits [of the path], their reception [of robes] is permitted in private places. This passage is taken to prove that permission for reception is beneficial.
Eighth, taking the commentaries of ancient masters: furthermore, during the middle of the summer retreat, if one must leave the boundary due to a matter, whether by water or land...

Regarding the difficulty concerning the severance [of the precepts] and so forth: one does not lose the summer retreat (*varṣa*) by returning to one's own realm. Question: Is there no textual authority in the Vinaya-piṭaka regarding this? Answer: There is no such text;

therefore, one must supplement it with the commentaries of former masters. Nanshan says: "In the past, the ten *tong* (patriarchs) and various masters of the Gao Qi dynasty collectively deliberated and all declared that the summer retreat was maintained.
This is because it was due to difficult circumstances and not a fault of the person. Regarding the ninth point, the definitive resolution, there are many types. First, the Vinaya contains...

Regarding matters: first, when applied in practice, both the text and the meaning are absent; one must resolve and clarify them by citing examples. Second, they are absent from the Vinaya texts but logically ought to exist; one must resolve and clarify them through reasoning.
Third, the meaning exists but the text is absent; one must resolve and clarify them. Fourth, the text exists but the meaning is absent; one must resolve and clarify them.
For now, we shall take those cases where they are absent from the Vinaya texts, logically ought to exist, and where both text and meaning are lacking.

To resolve this according to principle, it is explained as follows: Among the various schools of the Vinaya, there are texts stating that those suffering from insanity, pain, or mental derangement are "not to be counted" (*agaṇanīya*) when performing legal acts (*dharmakarma*), because such individuals do not understand them.
This, however, does not constitute the meaning of being "not to be counted" in the strict sense.

That is to say, among the various schools of this Vinaya, there are no texts or doctrinal explanations regarding those who are intoxicated being "not to be counted. Thus, the *Shouji Chao* (Record of the Essentials), in the section on "Those to Be Counted," states: "The meaning..."

Furthermore, there is the case of an intoxicated person. Such a person’s mind is disordered; this is no different from the aforementioned pain and affliction. By bringing that textual passage here, the matter is resolved.
Regarding the principle that a drunken person is not [fully] qualified to participate in the legal procedures of the Saṃgha, this is no different from what was stated previously.

By bringing that principle here, the present point is established. Although there is no explicit textual authority for such a case in the Vinaya, it is logically consistent that it should exist, as will be explained below. Question:

Regarding the Vinaya texts of one's own school (*sva-nikāya*), it is reasonable to supplement any omissions. However, why take the trouble to supplement omissions found in other schools, as well as in the sūtras and śāstras?
Answer: If there are deficiencies in the practical application (*pravṛtti*) of one’s own school, one takes [rules] from various schools to supplement them.

If there are deficiencies in those various schools, one cites sūtras and śāstras to supplement them, so that a single school may become complete and its practical application free of deficiency. This does not mean taking the literal text [of others].

Supplementing the Treatises on the *Buchu jing* (Sūtra on Supplementing). Question: Since the commentaries of the ancients already state that [the *Buchu jing*] does not convey the intended meaning of the entrustment (*niṣyanda*), it would follow that one should not adopt it.
Why, then, is it adopted? Answer: Both [traditions] harbor strengths and weaknesses. One adopts the best among the good and excludes the worst among the inferior.
Thus, the *Chao* (Commentary) states: "Long-standing views must be recorded to assist broad knowledge; spurious accounts must be excised to..."
This completes the general meaning.

Regarding the three components of the character *xing* (行): there have been many interpretations throughout ancient and modern times. As for the explanation based on the literal characters, Master Fazheng states: the left side is the radical *chě* (彳), and the right side is *chù* (亍, pronounced *chì yù*).

Therefore, it is called "practice" (*xing*). This refers to the manner of advancing alternately with the left and right feet. Now, this "practice" refers to the practice of taking up and employing [the Way]. Dangyang said:
"To encounter a matter and immediately act upon it is therefore called 'practicing affairs' (*xingshi*). The text states: "To encounter a matter and immediately act upon it."

How could one still harbor doubts regarding sin and merit? There are three kinds of matters: first, the *dharma*, which refers to the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*), the invitation for criticism (*pravāraṇā*), and so forth;
second, the matter of persons, such as receiving the precepts and repenting of offenses; third, the matter of things, such as the ground-covering cloth.
Because one acts in accordance with these three types of matters, it is called "performing the ritual" (*xing shi*).

Regarding the term *chao* (extract/compilation), there have been many explanations throughout past and present. Initially, it has two meanings: first, the sense of utility, which refers to excising redundant text;
second, the sense of firm stability, as when a meritorious official is granted an iron seal, which is also called a *chao*, because it causes his family to remain stable and unbroken for generations.
As for the term "chao" (抄): when it reaches later times and its circulation becomes long-established and firm, it becomes like the constant classics of the sūtras.
Thus, the following passage says: "Taking the mean between the prolix and the concise, how could the principle be obscured? This is precisely its meaning. K'o said: "Chao means 'to abridge.
To briefly extract the essential meanings from one's own school as well as from various other sections, without exhausting the full text, is what is called 'chao. There is...

People say that the character "shao" (少) is formed by placing a "gold" radical (金) on the side of "sha" (少). Regarding the Sublime Teachings of the Tripitaka, the wondrous interpretations of the ancients are all like adamant.
By citing essential statements and sublime phrases, they directly reveal their meaning; it is for this reason of being "few" (少) that the text says:
"I have firmly caused the original text to be abridged so as to encompass its various meanings."

Regarding the second section, which provides a specific heading that encompasses both orders (*dvi-pakṣa*): the term "order" (*xu*) refers to the general title of the entire work, as it correctly subsumes this preface.
Consequently, according to the preceding classification, if one follows the subsequent classification, it should be stated as: "The second heading, specifically explained in three parts.
First, from the beginning up to the tenth gate, the general intent of the *Commentary on the One-Part [Vinaya]* serves as the Introductory Section (*nidāna-bhāga*). Second, the Four-Part..."
Descending twenty-seven lines, the text distinguishes the mutual inclusion of the paths of practice, establishing the orthodox tradition for ritual conduct.

Descending three lines from "The Three Followings of the Śrāmaṇera," it clarifies the comprehensive categorization of distinct classes, thereby expanding upon the benefits of its subsequent circulation. Of these three sections, this is the first. Within it, there are two parts:

first, the heading that indicates the sequence; second, from "Now" (*fu*) onwards, the detailed analysis and explanation according to that sequence. As for the term "sequence" (*xu*), it refers to the introductory heading of the title.

The *Fǔpiān* states: The *Yīlǐ* says, "The East School (*xiáng*) and the West Hall (*xù*). The school of the Yù dynasty was called *xiáng*; the school of the Xià dynasty was called *xù*. Guō Pǔ’s commentary states:

"Xù" means to distinguish between the internal and external. This means that by means of this sequence, one dwells on the outside while distinguishing what is within, thereby manifesting the fulfillment of worldly affairs.
Ē says: In the *Kǎogōngjì*, it is glossed as "to unfold. This refers to unfolding the great meaning of a section of the transcribed text.

This refers to the "yi" (intention/purpose). Furthermore, the *Mao Shi* states that "xu" means a preface or introduction. This indicates that it provides a preface describing the reasons for composing the *Chao*, as well as the general outline of the Tripiṭaka, to serve as a basis for reliance.
The second [point] distinguishes this from the separate compositions of antiquity; it is also part of the previous classification.

However, according to the subsequent judgment, it is not classified here, but is merely briefly described. Thus, it is divided into two sequences, both of which still exist today, so that the discerning may know them.

Regarding the phrase "from the author to the distinct [sections]," there have been many explanations by both ancient and modern scholars. I shall cite the interpretation of Cihe (Cíhé), who states: "It is not that there is no author."

This phrase belongs to the commentaries (chao) composed by the ancients; as people have produced many such commentaries, this [phrase] serves as a double citation to indicate the name and clarify the distinction.

This phrase belongs to the present-day Nanshan school; the commentaries of various people differ from one another. By distinguishing it from these, the meaning of the double exclusion is established. Thus, it should be known.
The *Jian* (Selection) must necessarily simplify the *Zhaochao* (Excerpts), and the *Jianchao* (Simplified Excerpts) must necessarily be accompanied by the person [who selected them].

If this is so, since "selection" (*jian*) refers to the commentary notes (*zhuzhu*), they should be placed beneath the name; why then are they placed in the middle? Answer: The reason the notes are placed in the middle is that one wishes to include the *Chao* above and include the person below.
For this purpose, it is now complete, and there is no error. However, my current intention is not thus. The author of the *Chao* relies upon what he has studied.
When compiling the *Sifen chao*, it is sufficient simply to call it the *Sifen lü chao*.
What is the purpose of further designating it as the *Shanfan buque xingshih chao*? The commentary on the *Chao* states: "It is not that there are no authors;
that is to say, among those who have composed *chao* within the school they studied, there are indeed many—such as Li Yin, Yunhui, Yuan Hong, Shengshou, and others, all of whom relied [upon this]."

Within the school of study, commentaries (*chao*) were composed; now, titles such as "Deletions of the Redundant" (*Shanfan*) are designated to distinguish them from other commentaries, hence it is said that "the title is established to manifest the distinction.
This does not yet differentiate [the author] from others; it is only upon reaching the formal titling that one distinguishes [the work] by means of the person.
Furthermore, the commentary in the middle fascicle states: "The authors of these works are many; their titles are established to distinguish them simply.

The lower fascicle states: "The commentaries and compositions are not few; their titles and headings are placed at the beginning of the three fascicles. The phrasing of the notes is entirely distinct, establishing a difference from the ancient copies (*gucāo*).

The intent before and after is no different; for instance, when explaining the preceding text using the notes, one must likewise follow the ancient style, merely distinguishing it from the copied text. Regarding the meaning...
This is not a convoluted approach that follows one's own arbitrary whims.

Regarding the second point, the identification of the person capable of composing the work, this also follows the previous section. Many commentators of the *zhushu* (commentaries) lament that the *jiangchao* (lecture notes) are overly detailed;
however, according to the later judgment, they should simply provide a brief explanation. Knowing this to be of the same intent, I have preserved both versions.

Now there are also two interpretations, the extensive and the concise. First, regarding the concise version: "Bianchang" refers to [the author]. "Jingzhao" indicates the location where the Son of Heaven resides.
"Chongyi Temple" is an alternative name for a *vihāra* (monastery). "Śramaṇa" is a general term for those who have left the household life. "Shi" [refers to the lineage of Śākya].

Thus, [he] is a descendant of the Benevolent One (Munīndra). [The name] "Somakha" is the Dharma-name of the compiler. Because he follows what was left behind by the sages and worthies, it is called a "composition.

The second part, the Extensive Explanation, is divided into six sections: first, identifying the capital city; second, explaining the name of the monastery; third, interpreting the term *śramaṇa*; fourth, manifesting...
The Śākya clan. Fifth, the enumeration of names and titles; sixth, the clarification of the composition. Regarding the term "Jingzhao" (Capital Prefecture): according to the *Erya*, it means "great.
It refers to the capital where the Son of Heaven resides, a place toward which the great multitudes converge and return. Fazheng says: "Jingzhao" signifies a vast accumulation of numbers;
specifically, ten billion is a "zhao," and ten zhao is a "jing. Thus, "jingzhao" carries the meaning of "multitude. It is also called "Jingshi" (Capital City). "Shi" (City) — [text continues].
It is a "zhòng" (multitude). Thus we know that both "shī" (teacher) and "zhào" (augury/sign) carry the meaning of "multitude.
The *Baihūtong* states: "Jīngshī" is the designation for a capital city of a thousand *lǐ*. The *Wángzhì* says: "The realm of the Son of Heaven extends four thousand *lǐ* in each direction.
Such various names do not exceed the sense of the great capital where the multitude gathers; hence it is called Jīngzhào. Regarding the two Chóngyì Temples, according to the two capitals...
The *Taji* (Record of Stūpas and Temples) states: Within Changshou Ward of the Western Capital, this site was originally the residence of Yu Quan, Duke Yanshou of the Sui dynasty.
In the second year of the Wude era of the Tang, Princess Guiyang established it for her husband-in-law, Zhao Cijing.

Because the wife had established it for her husband, it was named Chongyi. "Si" (temple/monastery) means a gathering or an office; it is where those of a similar kind are gathered together in one place, as if—
The various agricultural offices, such as the Taichangsi (Ministry of Rites), were originally pure-practice monasteries where companions lived together; thus, they were called "si" (monasteries).
Subsequently, by imperial decree, he was assigned to Ximing Monastery along with the Abbot. Intending to compile a commentary (*chao*), he then entered Fengde Monastery on Mount Zhongnan.

The name of the temple is taken from its original location. Regarding the term *śramaṇa*, Zhongchao states that it is a general designation for those in black robes and a common name for those of pure conduct.
Lingshan says that according to the complete Sanskrit text, it is *śramaṇa*, which here means "one who has stilled the mind.
Thus, the *Śūramgama-sūtra* (Ruiying jing) states: "One who stills the mind and reaches the source is called a *śramaṇa*. It further states:
"Śramaṇa" is a corruption of the Sanskrit term. According to the *Abhidharmakośa* and *Vibhāṣā*, "śramaṇa" is a name for its fruit, referring to the four fruits of śrāmaṇya.
Thus, that treatise states: "The noble fruits are called śramaṇas, and are also called brāhmaṇas, and are also called the Brahma-wheel, because they are turned by the True Brahmā.
As for the term "Śākya," it refers to the descendants of Śākyamuni. Question: It was stated above that...
"Śramaṇa," you now further refer to as "Śākya. Is this not a violation of a heavy offense? Answer: It is for the sake of distinguishing [the specific from the general].

The term "śramaṇa" mentioned above is the general name for those who have left the household life; even those who have left the household life among non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) are also called śramaṇas. Therefore, the subsequent rule regarding eating in a group states:

"When śramaṇas are giving food, one should know that it refers to those who have left the household life within the Śākya lineage," for even those who have left the household life [among others] are also called [śramaṇas].
He is a śramaṇa. Therefore, I shall now set forth the *Śin-ming* (Explanation of Names) to distinguish him. Ling Shan says:

"To claim 'Śākya' as one's surname by mere verbal recitation, without understanding its origins—how laughable! Thus, secular texts say: there are those who do not know their grandfather’s name, nor do sons know their father’s taboo name.

For this reason, I have briefly set forth this account. If expressed in full Sanskrit, it should be called Śākyamuni; however, people of this land prefer brevity, so [the name] is retained [in its abbreviated form].
This is the explanation of *Śākyamuni*. However, the monks of the Jin and Wei dynasties all followed their teachers' surnames, resulting in various discrepancies.
Master Dao’an said: "The Great Master’s original and ultimate honorific is Śākya; thus, they were all designated by the clan name Śākya. Later, the *Ekottarika Āgama* arrived.

As for the result, it is said that when the four rivers flow into the sea, they no longer retain their original names; likewise, those of the four castes who leave the household life all call themselves sons of Śākya.

Since both monks and nuns inherit this clan name, it is essential to understand its origins. According to the *Shier you jing* (Sūtra on the Twelve Wanderings), at the beginning of the Bhadrakalpa of Śākyamuni:
His clan name was Gautama. In times immeasurable in the past, there was a Bodhisattva who served as a great king.

Having lost both his father and mother at an early age, he abdicated the kingdom to his younger brother and left the household life to study the Way. Wandering through deep mountains, he sought teachers and friends until he encountered a Brahmin of the Gautama clan.
He followed him to study the Way, and the teacher said to him: "You should cast off your royal robes and follow me."
“Dharma-precepts! I shall bestow the Way upon you. He followed these words and received the dharma-precepts; his surname was Gautama.
Having practiced the Way for a long time, his physical appearance changed from its former state. Later, he returned to his native country, yet no one recognized him.

Outside the capital city, within a sugarcane grove, he established a vihāra where he sat in meditation and practiced the Path. At that time, there was a band of thieves who were being pursued by the king; they passed by...
The border guards pursued him, but they could not capture the thief’s person. They then declared that the Bodhisattva had hidden away, seized him, bound him, and impaled him on a wooden stake.
His blood flowed upon the ground. The Great Master Gautama, staying in the deep mountains, beheld this with his divine eye.
He traveled through the air and arrived. He collected the blood from the ground to form a lump of clay, which he carried to his dwelling and consecrated with mantras.
After ten months had passed, a male was formed on the left side and a female on the right; they also took the teacher’s clan name, the Gautama clan.
From this point onward, for eighty-four thousand two hundred and seventy lifetimes, he was a *cakravartin* emperor with a lifespan of eight thousand seven hundred years;
these were all inherited directly from father to son as wheel-turning sage-kings (*cakravartin-rāja*). Only in two lifetimes did he serve as a king of Jambudvīpa.

After [the character] "Song" (宋) minus "Mu" (木) plus "Qu" (取), the king's name was Drumavāha, also known as Uruma. This difference in the Sanskrit pronunciation is due to the shifting of vowel weight.
The same. Thus the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus: "In the past there was a king named King Ummāda. His second queen had four sons:
the first was named Ālokabandhu, the second Cakṣuṣmanta, the third Gajamardin, and the fourth Nimi.
They were wise, sagacious, and martial, possessing great majesty and virtue. His first queen had one son, named..."

Changsheng was stubborn, shallow, and ugly; he was despised by all. His wife thought to herself, "Although my son is the eldest, his talent does not measure up to others, whereas those four younger sons all possess majesty and virtue. By what means can I secure my son's foundation?
She then addressed the King: "Your Majesty’s four sons all possess majesty and virtue, yet although my son is the eldest, his talent does not measure up to theirs. [How may we ensure] our lineage..."
"The great enterprise will surely be usurped. If Your Majesty expels them, my mind will find peace. The King said, "These four sons are filial and fraternal;
they have committed no offense against the state. Why, then, should they be expelled? The Queen spoke again, "These four sons of Your Majesty all possess majestic virtue."
"The fortunes of this great kingdom will surely be extinguished by mutual destruction. The King immediately summoned his sons and commanded them to leave the country.
At that time, the four sons' mother and their sisters born of the same womb all requested to go with them. Many of the people also desired to follow. The King granted them all permission.
They reached the north of the Snowy Mountains and settled in the Śākya forest, where they built a city and established a settlement. The population flourished, and it eventually became a great realm.
In the great kingdom, the king later longed to see him; [the prince] declined and refused to return.
When the king heard this, he sighed three times, saying, "My son possesses such capability. From that time on, they were consequently called the Śākya clan.
Nīla had a son named Aṭṭhila. Aṭṭhila had a son named Koṇḍila. Koṇḍila had a son named Nītha. Nītha had four sons; the first was named...
Śuddhodana; second, Śuklodana; third, Droṇodana; fourth, Amṛtodana. King Śuddhodana had two sons:
first, the Bodhisattva; second, Nanda. King Śuklodana had two sons: first, Ānanda; second, Devadatta.
King Droṇodana had two sons: first, Mahānāman; second, Aniruddha. King Amṛtodana... [text fragment ends]
King Lur-ban had two sons: the first was named Bāba, and the second was named Baddhi.
The Bodhisattva had a son named Rāhula. From Nīla to the Buddha’s own body, there were six generations. Taking virtue as the basis for their clan name, they were of the Śākya lineage.

According to various sūtras, the accounts differ greatly; I cannot describe them all in detail here. When it says "so-and-so," it refers to the name of the author of this compendium. However, regarding the lecture...

Regarding the transmission of the interpretation: some explain it and others do not. If one follows secular etiquette, one avoids the name [of the deceased] and omits it; this is likewise the practice of the gentlemanly tradition.

However, if one follows the names of the Buddhas, one encourages others to recite them. Now, as a child of the Buddha, it is logically appropriate to do so. "Dào" (道) means "Dharma. "Xuān" (宣) is defined in the *Erya* as "pervasive.
This refers to universally transforming those with whom one has a karmic connection by means of the Dharma of the Three Vehicles.
His secular surname was Qian. He was a native of Changcheng in Wuxing. His father was the Duke of [Duoyi], the seventh among ten sons.
The Great Master was the eldest brother of Shi Shen-er-xi. His learning was comprehensive, and his name was Yang. His virtues are difficult to recount in full;

how could a brush ever fully express the profound assistance provided by the dragons and deities? All that he composed, as well as his spiritual communications, are clearly revealed in the *Biographies* (Bi-zhuan).

Regarding the term "zuàn-shù" (composition and narration): according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "zuàn" means to record. According to the *Fazheng* (Correct Pronunciation), "shù" means speech. The Master "narrated" but did not [create].
"Composing" (*zuò*) refers to ancient matters. Question: How does "narrating" (*shù*) differ from "composing"? Answer: Paramārtha says that when the Buddha preached the sutras, it was "composing";

when Kātyāyanīputra composed the treatises, he merely narrated the Buddha’s intent, and thus it is simply called "narrating. If this is so, then a compilation or narration should not be called "composing.
Why then does the *Chaozhu* say, "The author is not non-existent"—is this not indeed "composing"? Answer: It is like [the case of] Kātyāyanīputra...

The *Yanchao lun* (Extended Commentary) explains the Buddha’s words; it is composed by following and synthesizing [the scriptures], and thus may also be called a "composition. This present *Chao* (Excerpts) is likewise:
it compiles and records the holy teachings, and by following and synthesizing them into a coherent text, it may also be termed a "composition.

When the Master [Confucius] said, "I transmit but do not create," he meant that he recounted the deeds of ancients and spoke of them to his disciples, rather than composing anything new; hence he said, "I transmit but do not create. Now...
I have transcribed his narrative into a formal composition, compiling it into three fascicles. This serves to harmonize the two schools and appropriately preserves the author’s original intent;
thus, there is no error. The six preceding sections, though distinct, collectively conclude the second part: the exposition on the names of those who established these teachings.
The preceding section consists of two parts: first, explaining the title of the selected Dharma; second, identifying the person who was able to compose it. These two sections differ.
Having completed the first part—the explanation of the general title of the preface—now follows the second: the detailed interpretation based on the two specific prefaces.

This concludes the previous topical outline. Alternatively, according to the subsequent classification, having completed the explanation of the title of the preface above, now follows the second part.

The commentary is divided into sections in sequence. This section has two parts: first, an introduction to the rise and decline of the training in ethical discipline (*śīla-śikṣā*) and the causes and origins for composing this work;

second, from the listing of the chapters onwards, a description of the general outline of the Three Baskets (*tripiṭaka*), which serves as the basis and authoritative source for the compilation of this sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*).
The *Fazheng* states: "After the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, bodhisattvas composed treatises to expound the sūtras. Although they propagated the holy teachings..."

Fearing that demonic obstacles (*māra-karman*) might arise, one must first take refuge in and pay homage to the Triple Gem, requesting their majestic protection, as stated in the *Awakening of Faith* (*Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra*): "I take refuge throughout the ten directions," and in the *Śata-śāstra*: "I prostrate at the Buddha’s feet," and so forth. Now, why does this present commentary not first take refuge in the Triple Gem, but instead directly extol the virtues of the precepts? Answer: If we consider the period after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, all authors first take refuge in and pay homage to the Triple Gem. However, this present work is composed during the time when the True Dharma has not yet declined; therefore, it does not require such an opening invocation. Furthermore, because the precepts are the foundation for generating the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), they are praised here first. Moreover, since the precepts are the root of the Triple Gem, by extolling the precepts, one simultaneously pays homage to the Triple Gem. Thus, there is no fault. Finally, regarding the phrase "the precepts are the source of the Triple Gem": the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions are the "Buddha-gem"; the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas who have attained the fruits of the path are the "Dharma-gem"; and the Saṃgha of the four assemblies who uphold the precepts is the "Saṃgha-gem. Because these three gems arise from the precepts, the precepts are called the source of the Triple Gem. Therefore, by extolling the precepts, one naturally honors the Triple Gem. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the *Vinaya-mātṛkā-śāstra* states: "The Buddha is the teacher; the Dharma is the teaching; and the Saṃgha is the field of merit. These three are the supreme fields of merit. Now, the compiler of this digest had already previously paid his respects at the time when the masters of the Dharmaguptaka school divided the teachings;

thus, the preface to the Vinaya says, "I bow my head in homage to all Buddhas," and so forth. This is it. Now, following after my teacher, I have appended this to that Vinaya text and shall not separately offer further salutations.

Regarding the first two sections: the first praises the profound and vast virtue of the precepts as the subject matter, noting that concentration and wisdom are not its equal; this is the fundamental principle of this compilation.
"Second, from 'From the Great Master downwards,' [the author] distinguishes the rise and fall of those who propagate [the teaching], thereby articulating the intent behind the composition.
Question: Why is this categorized under both the explained subject—the virtue of the precepts—and the people who propagate it, along with their rise and fall? Answer:

According to the *Chao* (the *Zichiji*), which establishes the fundamental principle, it first clarifies that the precepts are the foundation of the myriad practices; next, it examines whether individuals rely upon the Vinaya or not, concluding: 'Therefore...'"
One knows that rise and fall depend on the person. Now, following their [the masters'] treatises to evaluate this [text], I do not rely upon various commentaries. Of the preceding two [sections]:

the first is a general praise of the virtue and merit of the precepts, manifesting their excellence through metaphors; the second is a specific praise of the wondrous function of the *śīla* (precepts) for the five vehicles, which is peerless and beyond compare.
Regarding the phrase "As for the ultimate image" (*zhìxiàng*), the upper clause is a general praise, while the lower clause manifests it through metaphor. Question: This *Chao* (Digest)...

Why is it that the virtue of the precepts (*śīla*) is praised first? Answer: The precepts are the fundamental principle of a bhikṣu’s practice; all myriad deeds are established in dependence upon them.

This is why they are designated first in this *Xing-shi-chao* (Commentary on the Practice of the Vinaya). This will be explained extensively at the beginning of the section on the "Establishment of the Fundamental Principle.

Consider this. As for the word "Now" (*fu*), it marks the commencement of a discourse. The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states that it has the meaning of initiating a topic and setting forth its subject matter. The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* says: [The following...]

The profound meaning of the *skandhas* is referred to by the term "Fu" (The Master). To speak of "precepts" (*śīla*) alone is to distinguish them from meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*); this is thus a negational definition (*paryudāsa*).

To speak of them together as "the inconceivable virtue of precepts" is to maintain their essential nature and qualities; this is a positive definition (*vidhi*). Regarding the current interpretation, the tradition has been handed down as divided between the monastic and the lay.
First, according to the lay interpretation: the *Zhou Yi* says, "By means of this, one attains purification and fasting. Han Kangbo explains: "Purity..."

The mind is called *śī* (equanimity). To prevent calamities is called *kā* (precept). Some say that "precept" (*jie*) means "caution. Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Yili* states that it means "vigilance.
Regarding the Buddhist interpretation: in Sanskrit it is *śīla*, also called *śīla*. The *Jieshu* (Commentary on Precepts) states: "This [Sanskrit] term is translated as 'precept' (*jie*).

'Precept' (*jie*) is glossed as 'vigilance' (*jing*). Because one uses vigilance to discipline the three karmas and remains far removed from non-virtuous conditions, its causal basis is clarified. *Karma*.
The Commentary states: "Precepts prevent misconduct of body and speech; that which ought to be initiated is not initiated, like repairing a breached city wall.

Regarding "virtue" (*de*): the *Laozi Yinyi* (Phonetics and Meanings of the *Laozi*) says, "Virtue is 'to obtain. It means to obtain [the favor of] things; therefore it is called virtue. The *Zitong* (Compendium of Characters) says:
To obtain [merit] from others externally and to obtain it within oneself internally, such that one is always without loss—this is therefore called *de* (virtue).

The ancient masters all say that "precept" (*śīla*) is a name for the cause, while "virtue" (*guṇa*) is a designation for the fruit. Regarding a bhikṣu who has received these precepts, once he has practiced that cause...
One will certainly attain the fruit. As the *Dìchí jīng* (Śrāvakabhūmi) states: "The thirty-two marks have no cause other than the undifferentiated [practice of] upholding the precepts;
therefore, they are called 'the virtue of the precepts' (*jièdé*). This is a *tatpuruṣa* compound meaning 'the virtue belonging to the precepts.

Regarding 'inconceivable' (*nánxī*), the *Língshān* says: 'This is a double praise of both cause and fruit. This is clarified in the *Fúpiān*, *Huáxián*, *Fùyáng*, and *Jùchù*. In total, there are six meanings. First,"

Regarding the "inconceivable essence": this refers to the moment immediately following the completion of the three *karmavācanās*, when one realizes the essence of non-informative action (*avijñapti*).

It is neither form (*rūpa*) nor mind (*citta*); because it is not form, it cannot be discussed; because it is not mind, it cannot be conceived. Thus, it transcends the realm of thought and deliberation.
After the first reception and before the four relinquishments, the four minds and three natures are constantly present from beginning to end;

they do not depend on external conditions and are, moreover, manifest and inconceivable. Second, the inconceivability of their characteristics: because they arise from the essence as active functions (*saṃskāra*), their modes of activity are not uniform.
This refers to sentient and non-sentient beings, the two truths of emptiness and existence, the eighty thousand dharma-gates, and realms as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Upon each and every such realm, one attains the precepts. As the *Śāṅkhasūtra* states: "Space, the great earth, grasses, trees, and sentient beings" serves as an analogy.
Regarding the third point, the inconceivable majesty and power: the *Vibhāṣā* states that the Buddha possesses majestic power throughout the trichiliocosm.
All of these are the power of *śīla*. Even five hundred arhats, with their powers of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*), were unable to drive away the dragon.
There was one arhat who, through the meditative equipoise of lightness and heaviness, spoke thus: "Worthy-faced One, depart to a distance! Upon hearing this, the dragon immediately left.

All of this is the majestic power of *śīla*. Fourth, the inconceivable protection of evil and gathering of good is precisely because of the virtue of the precepts that one is able to guard against [evil].
It can lead one out of the three evil and perilous paths and enable the attainment of the blissful fruits of the human, celestial, and three vehicles. Fifth, it is honorable, rare, and inconceivable.
This Dharma of precepts was established by the Tathāgata; it is observed by sages and worthies alike, and revered by humans and devas. Only when a Buddha appears in the world does it arise.
This Dharma is established because it is rare; it is something that does not exist among the ninety-six types of non-Buddhist paths.

Furthermore, within the six realms of existence, it can only be received by those in the human realm, as it is difficult for others to achieve. Its causes are profound and its fruits distant, making them difficult to conceive:

through the profound cause of upholding the precepts, one can attain the distant fruit of unsurpassed Bodhi and Nirvana, giving rise to various meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) and so forth. It is the crown [of all teachings].
"Surpassing all forms" uses a metaphor to reveal its ultimate meaning. First, the metaphor is established; second, it is applied to the Dharma. The *Zhou Li* states:
"That which is on the head is called a *guàn* (level tone). This refers to that which binds the hair on the head, and it also takes on the sense of a ceremonial cap or sash.

Thus, the *Liji* says: "At twenty years of age, a man undergoes the capping ceremony (*guàn*, pronounced *guǎn*). It is said [in the West]: "If it is not on the head (level tone), but rather upon the crown (departing tone), it is a ceremonial robe."
The commentary states: "In ancient times, they fashioned the cicada crown (*changuan*). Because the cicada drinks dew and its body is light, they modeled the crown after this and wore it;
thus, it carries the meaning of the gentleman’s admonition for vigilance. Among the various images, 'multitude' refers to the fact that their clothing is not uniform."
Within the Semblance Dharma (*saddharmapratirūpaka*), the holy teachings are not singular; the eighty thousand *dharmamukhas* constitute its manifold manifestations. The *Fuhuan faheshu* states:

"The attire that adorns the physical body has the crown as its preeminent feature; the merit that adorns the *dharmakāya* has the precepts as the supreme among all dharmas such as concentration and wisdom.
Because these two categories are analogous, the crown is used as a metaphor for transcendence."

Second, regarding the separate praise of the sublime efficacy of *śīla* as being peerless and without equal, there are four points: first, it serves as the track for the vehicle; second, it acts as the movement of jewels;
third, among the three trainings (*tri-śikṣā*), one’s own practice (*sva-caryā*) is what is taught for those below;

fourth, in upholding the Buddha-sun and the various dharmas, no other teaching is its equal. The first two are explained together, while the latter two are explained separately. As for the phrase "for the sake of the five," it refers to...
"Voyager" (*hangzhe*) refers to the clear precepts as the precious vehicle; they serve as the guiding rules and the ferry for transport.

Regarding "for the sake of the five vehicles" (*wushengzhe*): first, one explains the five vehicles; next, one clarifies the guiding rules. "Five" (*wu*) is a number. "Vehicle" (*sheng*) has the meaning of transporting and carrying.

By means of these five kinds of dharmas, practitioners are transported, each reaching their respective destination; thus they are called the "five vehicles. This is an *adhikaraṇa-samāsa* (explanatory compound with a numeral). First...
First, enumerating and explaining the names; second, clarifying the meaning of the vehicles (*yāna*). However, the various sūtras and śāstras differ in their enumeration of three or five.

In the *Lotus Sūtra*, there are three: first, the śrāvaka; second, the pratyekabuddha; and third, the bodhisattva. Their definitions are as explained above. Within the teachings set forth therein, the *Abhidharmajñānaprasthāna-śāstra* enumerates five:
the first three are as above, with the addition of humans and devas to make five. "Devas" (heavenly beings) are named for being free from sorrow and affliction, and are constant...
Because they experience happiness. Regarding the term "person" (*pudgala*): the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* states that one who is capable of much gratitude and righteousness is therefore called a person.

The first five [categories] are the persons who are the riders. Next, to distinguish the Dharma which is the vehicle: the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says, "For those seeking the state of a Śrāvaka, he teaches the Dharma corresponding to the Four Noble Truths;
for those seeking the state of a Pratyekabuddha, he teaches the Dharma corresponding to the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination; and for all Bodhisattvas..."
He teaches the Dharma corresponding to the six *pāramitās*. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:

"For those who are to be matured by means of human roots of goodness, he teaches the superior grade of the ten wholesome paths of action (*daśa-kuśala-karmapatha*), as well as the various meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) and wisdom (*prajñā*); this is called the 'Celestial Vehicle' (*devayāna*).

For them, he teaches the inferior grade of the ten wholesome paths of action; this is called the 'Human Vehicle' (*manuṣyayāna*). Generally speaking, the term "vehicle" (*yāna*) has three meanings: first, it refers to that which causes one to proceed...
[The first] increases [virtue]; the second brings afflictions to cessation; and the third brings forth the principle. These three types possess all three virtues:

the increase of practice is the virtue of *prajñā* (wisdom); the cessation of afflictions is the virtue of *vimukti* (liberation); and the manifestation of the principle is the virtue of the *dharmakāya*. If one exhaustively investigates the ultimate principle:

"There is neither two nor three," except for the Buddha’s skillful means of teaching, and so forth. Next, regarding "guidance" (*kai-dō*): "guidance" (*kai*) refers to the rules of conduct. As the *Śāstra* states:

"Because it possesses rules, it is able to produce understanding in sentient beings. Regarding "guiding" (*dō*), the *Zhuo zhuan* says: "To penetrate. It means to lead sentient beings so that they may attain penetration.
Therefore, it is called "guidance. Those who travel by means of the five vehicles merely ride upon the dharmas they have mounted.

If one lacks the *apraṇihita-vinaya* (precept of wishlessness) as well as the five precepts, the eight precepts, and so forth to guard the seven branches of body and speech, one's conduct will deteriorate according to circumstances, and one cannot avoid the evil realms.

Thus, both the vehicle and the precepts must be treated with urgency. By means of these rules of the precepts, one guides the wholesome mind toward concentration (*samādhi*) and the like; concentration and wisdom [arise] within.

Prevention is the external protection of *śīla*. If one merely cultivates contaminated roots of goodness but does not uphold the five precepts, it is like the person during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha who practiced only giving but did not maintain the precepts, such as for the sake of the royal white elephant and so forth.
Therefore, Zhizhi said: "Guided by the precepts, all reach the fruits of the five vehicles. How is this known? As the Introduction to the Precepts (*Śīlaskandha*) says:
If one wishes to be born in the heavens, or to be born among humans, one should always protect the feet of the precepts. For those of the Two Vehicles, as the Preface to the Vinaya says:
"Having eliminated the fetters, there is no obstruction; from bondage and attachment, this liberation arises. Furthermore, the Circulation of the Precept Texts states:

"The Seven Buddhas, as World-Honored Ones, have extinguished and removed all fetters and afflictions (*saṃyojana*). This means that by means of the precepts, one attains the state of a *pratyekabuddha* or a *śrāvaka*. If...
Regarding the discussion of the Buddha, as the verse on the circulation of the precepts says: "With pure precepts and wisdom, one attains the foremost path.
Thus we know that for those of the five vehicles, the precepts serve as the guide. Truly, they are the vessel for the Triple Gem. As the ancients said:
"The virtue of the precepts possesses the function of sustaining and the utility of transporting; it is likened to a ship. The Vulture Peak [Sūtra] says: "Truly..."

It is just like this. "Treasure" (*ratna*) is a metaphorical designation; it is explained by way of enumeration and also carries the meaning of the Three Jewels (*triratna*). Although this is as it has always been, people do not know it unless they study it; therefore, I shall briefly cite it here.

Now, following the fourfold classification in the *Fǔfǎzàng Yìlù* (Record of the Meaning of the Auxiliary Collection), there are: first, the enumeration and explanation of the names; second, the delineation of their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*);

third, the identification of their essence (*svabhāva*); and fourth, the establishment of their sequence. Regarding the first, the enumeration: the ancient and modern views differ, and the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna traditions diverge.

The *Haiyi jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts by Haiyun) establishes four kinds of Triple Gem: first, the Essential Principle (*liti*); second, the Manifested Transformation (*huaxiang*); third, the Sustaining Authority (*zhuchi*); and fourth, the Single Essence (*yiti*).

Regarding the three [kinds] at Vulture Peak, they are identical to the first three mentioned above. Regarding the three in the *Fupian* (Supplementary Chapters), the Single Essence and the Sustaining Authority are the same as before, while the Distinctive Characteristics (*biesiang*) differ slightly.
Within the "Explanation of Names" section, there are two parts: first, the explanation of individual names; second, the explanation of the collective title. The *Jieshu* states: "As for 'Buddha'..."
In Sanskrit, it is called *buddha*, *budha*, *buddha*, *buta*, *butu*, or *butu*. These are merely corruptions of the transmitted pronunciation; there is no such word in that language.

Translated according to its meaning, it is "Awakening" (*jue*). "Awakening" refers to awakening to and discerning reality; it signifies the fulfillment of awakening for both oneself and others, like the blossoming of a lotus flower.
The ten meanings have been explained as previously set forth. As for what is called "Dharma," in Sanskrit it is *dharma*, *damma*, or *dhamma*.

This is merely a different transmission of the same principle. The term *dharma* has two meanings: first, the meaning of "that which maintains its own nature," such as the three aggregates of form (*rūpa*) and so forth, each maintaining its own essence without dispersal;

second, the meaning of "that which serves as a model for generating understanding," referring to phenomena such as impermanence (*anitya*), which can generate the understanding of impermanence and so forth.
Here, we rely on the latter sense. When the Sage expounds the teachings, his intention lies in their being taken up and practiced.
It is like a carriage following its ruts, or a vessel following its mold; the Dharma cannot be perceived by itself, but is established through metaphors.

As for "Saṃgha," it is a term from the Western Heavens (India); the full form is *saṃgha*. Since there is no such word in our own language, we use a corresponding term and call it a "community" (*zhòng*). In terms of substance, four people together constitute the sixfold harmony.
Next, regarding the general designation of "Jewel" (*ratna*), the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: "These three benefit the world... [The text continues with the phrase] "...nearby."
It supports the three realms of existence and distances one from the two types of death; it is rare in this world and uniquely sublime, that which is most highly esteemed as a treasure.
Thus, the *Ratnagotravibhāga* states: "A true treasure is rare in the world; being free from defilement and possessing power, it can adorn the world, excelling and remaining immutable."

The analogy is analyzed according to six meanings: 1. The meaning of rarity: Worldly treasures are absent for those who are impoverished; the Three Jewels are not encountered by those of meager merit.

2. The meaning of freedom from defilement: Worldly treasures are inherently free from blemish; the Three Jewels are utterly detached from all outflows (*āsrava*). 3. The meaning of power: Worldly treasures remove poverty and dispel poison;
the Three Jewels possess inconceivable power common to both [removing suffering and bestowing benefit]. 4. The meaning of adornment: Worldly treasures adorn... [text truncated]

First, the meaning of making the body excellent. The Three Jewels can adorn the *dharmakāya*. Second, the meaning of being superior to the five treasures. Among all worldly treasures, the Three Jewels are supreme;

among all that exists, they are unsurpassed. Third, the meaning of being unchanging. Worldly treasures may be refined but do not change their nature; the Three Jewels, however, remain steadfast through the eight stages of existence (*aṣṭāvasthā*) without falling away.

Although the preceding six points are explained together by means of analogies to establish the point, if one examines the character "treasure" (*ratna*), both are defined as precious and beautiful. This concludes the second section: distinguishing their characteristics.
Regarding these, there are three in the Hīnayāna and two in the Mahāyāna. First, concerning the Hīnayāna, according to the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts):

First is the "principle essence" (*lǐtǐ*). For example, the fivefold body of dharma (*pañcadharmakāya*) is the Buddha Jewel; the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) principle of cessation (*nirodha*) is the Dharma Jewel;

and the merits of Śrāvakas, both those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), are the Saṅgha Jewel. Second is the "manifestation of transformation" (*huàxiàng*). For example, Śākyamuni, who ruled over the trichiliocosm, is the Buddha Jewel.
The propagation and dissemination of the True Teaching constitutes the Jewel of the Dharma. The five groups, beginning with the *pudgalas* (individuals), constitute the Jewel of the Saṃgha.

Regarding the three modes of sustenance (*dhāraṇa*): physical images, stūpas, and temples constitute the Buddha-Jewel; that which is transmitted on paper and silk constitutes the Dharma-Jewel; and the precepts, dharmas, and ritual forms constitute the Saṃgha-Jewel. Regarding the two aspects of the Mahāyāna:
as for the single essence (*tattva*), the *Fupian* (Supplementary Chapters) states: "True Suchness (*tathatā*) is the essence, for all phenomena have Suchness as their nature."
Therefore, within the very nature [of reality], that which possesses the meaning of awakening is called the Buddha; that which possesses the meaning of maintaining the path is the Dharma;

and that which possesses the meaning of being free from conflict and contention is the Saṃgha. Thus, the Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra states: "All sentient beings are suchness (tathatā); all phenomena are also suchness;
and all noble sages are also suchness. It further states: "The Buddha is the Dharma, and the Dharma is the Saṃgha. This is explained according to their respective meanings.
There are three [aspects]. Because their essence is the single suchness, they are called "one body. Second, regarding their distinct characteristics:

the three bodies—the svābhāvika-kāya (self-nature), sambhoga-kāya (enjoyment), and nirmāṇa-kāya (emanation)—constitute the Jewel of the Buddha. The Mahāyāna principles, teachings, practices, and fruits constitute the Jewel of the Dharma. Samantabhadra and Mañjuśrī...

This constitutes the Saṃgha Jewel. This refers to the distinct characteristics of the essential natures (*svabhāva*) of the three bodies (*trikāya*). Regarding the determination of their essential natures, there is a distinction between the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.
In the Mahāyāna, they are of one essence, as previously stated: *tathatā* (suchness) is their essence. Therefore, the Tripitaka Master of the Tang Dynasty said:

"The nature of the Three Jewels does not depart from *tathatā*. As for the essential natures of the distinct characteristics, these refer to the three bodies, such as the *svābhāvika-kāya* (self-nature body). Regarding the *svābhāvika-kāya*:
Alternatively, its essence is *tathatā* (suchness). The *saṃbhogakāya* has the four wisdoms, such as the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom, as its essence.

If it is the *nirmāṇakāya*, it takes all the untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas of the Buddha-body as its essence. "Dharma" refers here to the dharmas of the Mahāyāna teachings, principles, practices, and fruits.
The essence [of the Sangha] consists of the various untainted dharmas within the bodies of Bodhisattvas and others.

If one wishes to clarify the essence of the Hīnayāna, it is as previously explained regarding the determination of essence based on characteristics. As for the establishment of the three [refuges] and their sequence: first, the reason for establishing the three is set forth.
Next, the sequence of priority is explained. The *Chubian* (Initial Auxiliary Section) asks: "Why are only three jewels established, neither more nor less? The answer states:
"By the nature of things (*dharmatā*), three are required. Why? Just as in the world for treating illness, one first requires a physician, next a good medicine, and a caregiver;
only when these three are present can the diseases of the four great elements of sentient beings be cured. [End of excerpt]

It would then be useless; moreover, it would be insufficient. Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle four, states: "The Buddha is like a king of physicians, the Dharma is like excellent medicine, and the Saṃgha is like a nurse.
It requires these three to be able to cure the disease of afflictions in sentient beings. This is a sound proof.

Regarding the sequence of priority and posteriority, the *Fazheng lun* (Treatise on the Correct Dharma) says: "If one speaks of their single essence, that essence has no priority or posteriority; they are all [present] according to how they are described."

It is obtained. Now, following the sequence of meaning, this supplementary section distinguishes the precedence and succession of the Three Jewels, summarizing them into three points of analysis. First, the precedence and succession are clarified according to their relative superiority and inferiority.

"Buddha" refers to the one who is awakened, which comes first; only then is there the Dharma that is to be awakened to. Those who practice in accordance with that awakening are the Saṃgha; the sequence is thus.

This constitutes the distinct characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the Mahāyāna, as well as the three aspects—the principle-body (*dharmatā-kāya*), the transformative aspect (*nirmāṇa-lakṣaṇa*), and [the other two]—of the Hīnayāna.
The same applies to the relative superiority or inferiority of the Jewels and so forth; in all cases, the Buddha comes first, followed by the Dharma, and finally the Sangha.

Therefore, in the *Pravrajyā-vastu* (Chapter on Ordination) of the Vinaya, it is stated that after the Tathāgata left home and attained enlightenment, he was called the Buddha; immediately thereafter, he taught the Dharma, and subsequently ordained the five disciples, including Ājñātakauṇḍinya.

This refers precisely to the sequence of the transformative manifestation (*saṃdarśana-vinaya*); it must not be contravened. Second, regarding the clarification of priority based on teacher and disciple:
the Dharma takes precedence. As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "That which all Buddhas take as their teacher is the Dharma.
Because the Dharma is eternal, the Buddhas are also eternal. The *Prajñāpāramitā* also says: "All Buddhas, up to and including the Dharma of Bodhi, all emerge from this sūtra. Thus it is established.

In the preceding scriptural passage, the Dharma comes first, the Buddha second, and the Sangha last. Regarding the sequence of these three as it clarifies the generation of faith in sentient beings, the Sangha occupies the initial position.
For example, Śāriputra first beheld the tranquil and composed deportment of the bhikṣu Aśvajit and subsequently requested him to preach the Dharma.
Having heard the Dharma and entered the Way, he then returned with Maudgalyāyana and two hundred and fifty disciples to take refuge in the Buddha and leave the household life.
