"It is always excellent throughout the three periods of time. Haiyun said: "The Sage is the 'old,' while ordinary beings are the 'young. Those on the seven stages of expedient means are the 'middle.
Regarding the manifestation of the image of non-self, the *Śāstra* says: 'Precepts (*śīla*) are like a mirror. If the mirror is bright and pure, images appear within it;

if the precepts are pure, then concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) manifest. Concentration is empty stillness, and wisdom is non-arising. When there is empty stillness and non-arising, who [is there]?"*
To say "there is a self" is the semblance of non-self. Because the mirror of the precepts is pure, this semblance of non-self can be manifested.
Therefore, the Sūtra on the Precepts says: "When the precepts are pure, there is wisdom. Furthermore, regarding what is called "majestic power" (*vibhūti*), this passage has two parts:
first, it cites the Buddha as the superior person; second, it cites the disciples as also being superior persons. The Śāstra states: *Śīla* (precepts) is an increase...
The Superior Meaning: Regarding the Buddha’s great power throughout the trichiliocosm, it is entirely due to the force of his *śīla* (ethical discipline).

As for the matter of driving away the nāgas, the treatise states: Formerly, in the kingdom of Kaśmīra, there was a venomous nāga named Abhaya (Fearless), who was by nature violent and malevolent, causing much harm. A certain Vihāra was frequently harassed and tormented by that nāga. The monastery had...

Five hundred arhats deliberated together, intending to enter meditative absorption (*samādhi*) to drive away that nāga; yet, although they exhausted their supernatural powers (*ṛddhibala*), they were unable to expel him.
There was one arhat named Bhagadatta who arrived from outside. At that time, the original inhabitants related the aforementioned matter in detail.
When the newcomer reached the nāga’s location, he snapped his fingers and spoke, saying: "O Noble-faced One, go far away! Upon hearing his voice, the nāga immediately—

The dragon then departed to a distant place. At that time, the arhats, finding it strange, questioned him: "By what power of concentration did you dispatch this dragon? What kind of supernormal power (*abhijñā*) did you employ? He replied:
"I did not rely on the power of concentration, nor did I exercise supernormal powers. It was simply through the protection of the *śīla* (precepts) that such power arose.
Because I guarded even the minor precepts as if preventing a grave transgression, the evil dragon was struck with terror and fled. It was by virtue of this *śīla*..."

*Śīla*. This means "sovereign power" (*adhipati*). Furthermore, regarding why precepts (*śīla*) are called the "head," the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (Xin pōshā) also states that this is the meaning of *śīla*.
Here, both a dharma and a simile are presented together; in the present commentary, the simile is omitted to clarify the dharma.
First, the simile is set forth, followed by its application to the dharma. The simile says: "Just as a person who has a head is able to see forms."
Hearing sounds, smelling fragrances, tasting flavors, feeling tangibles, and cognizing mental objects—the analogy is complete. The Dharma is likewise.

A practitioner who possesses the head of ethical discipline (*śīla*) is able to see the forms of the Four Noble Truths, such as suffering and its origin; hear the unprecedented sounds and the meanings of names, phrases, and syllables;
smell the fragrance of the flowers of the mind; taste the flavor of renunciation, the state of non-action, and the tranquility of *sambodhi*; and perceive...

Regarding "contact with dhyāna, liberation, and so forth," the *Chao* [Commentary] states that this refers only to the initial vision of the various forms within the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), as well as those dharmas such as the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) that have not yet been fully realized;

by the term "and so forth" (*ādi*), it includes feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness (*vedanā-saṃjñā-saṃskāra-vijñāna*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), and the five contemplations for settling the mind (*pañca-nīvaraṇa-pratipakṣa*).

The general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) and the specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*) of mindfulness, as well as the various intermediate meanings, are omitted here for brevity; hence the phrase "up to and including" (*yāvat*).
Second, regarding the explanation of "keeping one's word" (*śraddhā-vākya-ārakṣaṇa*), it says "one who can arrive [at the goal]":

The third [section] explains the meaning of "practice" (*caryā*). Regarding the phrase "reaching what is to be reached," the *Śāstra* states:
"Just as a person with feet travels to other regions, if one possesses the feet of ethical discipline (*śīla*), one travels to *nirvāṇa*."
The fourth meaning of "vessel" (*bhājana*) refers to its being the ultimate destination of merit. The treatise states: "Because it is the locus upon which all merits depend, it is called a vessel.

Regarding the second layered explanation of the meaning of *śīla*, the phrase "reaching the honored state of Nirvana" refers to the name *Ghoṣa*. This is found in the fifth [chapter] of that treatise.
Outside the group of one hundred teachers, there was a venerable master whose understanding was most profound; five hundred people took him as their teacher.
According to the *Sarvāstivāda Masters and Disciples Biography*, from Kāśyapa to Dharmatrāta there were twelve individuals, and the Venerable Ghoṣa was one of them.
The biography states that this great master was named Ghoṣaprabha; he was extensively learned, possessed a powerful memory, and was highly skilled.
He made a solemn vow to move the hearts of the assembly. At that time, there was a gathering of more than five hundred people.

He instructed each person to contribute a vessel, after which he preached the Dharma. The members of the assembly were moved to realization; their tears flowed freely, and they used the vessels to catch them, collecting them in one place.
There was a prince who was blind in both eyes. The Venerable Ghoṣa then made a firm and earnest vow: "If I am certain [to attain this goal]..."
"When he attains the Unsurpassed Way and benefits those who are blind and ignorant, lacking the eye of wisdom, I shall now use these tears to wash the eyes of this person;
his eyes shall immediately open. Once washed with tears, both his eyes became clear. Thereupon, the fourfold assembly all held him in high esteem.
The third section, the Mahāyāna Sūtra Texts, has two parts: first, the headings; second, the explanations. The headings are as in the text.
Within the explanations, there are six sections: 1. *Avataṃsaka*; 2. *Mahāsaṃnipāta*; 3. *Satyasiddhi*; 4. *Candrapradīpa*; 5. *Nirvāṇa*; 6. A further citation of the *Avataṃsaka*.
Regarding the phrase "from the *Avataṃsaka* to the *Vihāra*," Yanke stated: "Translated by Buddhabhadra during the Jin dynasty, the old version consisted of fifty fascicles; this [version] has two."
[Commentary] First, three types of the Sangha Jewel are cited to demonstrate that the Sangha consists of those who uphold the precepts.

Second, from "the past and future" onwards, it is established that the Sangha does not violate the Dharma and thus abides for a long time. In the eighth chapter of the *Śīlapāramitā-sūtra*, there are three successive expositions. In the first exposition, it says:
"To teach and transform sentient beings, to cause them to resolve upon Bodhicitta, and to ensure that the Buddha Jewel is never interrupted; to reveal and instruct those capable of the profound..."

The treasury of the wondrous Dharma ensures that the Jewel of the Dharma is never interrupted. By being fully endowed with the three types of feeling and upholding the teachings on dignified conduct (*īryāpatha*), it ensures that the Jewel of the Sangha is never interrupted.
Furthermore, in the second instance, it is said: by praising all great vows, it ensures that the Jewel of the Buddha is never interrupted;

by analytically explaining the twelve links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), it ensures that the Jewel of the Dharma is never interrupted; and by practicing the six points of harmonious respect, it ensures that the Jewel of the Sangha is never interrupted.

Third, it further says: "Planting the seeds of the Buddha in the field of sentient beings, one causes the sprouts of perfect enlightenment to grow, ensuring that the Jewel of the Buddha is never severed.

Protecting and upholding the treasury of the Dharma while not begrudging body or life, one ensures that the Jewel of the Dharma is never severed. Skillfully guiding the great assembly with a mind free from anxiety or regret, one ensures that the Jewel of the Sangha is never severed.
The commentary explains: regarding the Jewel of the Buddha, first is the initial arousal of the vow to seek Buddhahood; second is the praise [of the Buddha].
They give rise to practice so that one may cultivate and accumulate it. Third is the cultivation of the seeds of practice. Next, regarding the three types of Dharma:

first is the Dharma of teaching; second is the Dharma of principle; third is the Dharma of practice. Next, regarding the Sangha: first is the Sangha that practices the means; second is the Sangha whose practice is accomplished without discord.

Regarding which of the Three Jewels encompasses others: the reason for now excerpting the passages concerning the Sangha Jewel specifically is that the non-decline of the two preceding Jewels depends entirely upon the Sangha.

If the Sangha maintains dignified deportment, practices the six points of harmonious respect (*ṣaḍ-abhikṣṇa-pratyaya*), and governs the great assembly, and if the Sangha is able to uphold the precepts—[then the other Jewels are preserved].
Thus, the Dharma of the precepts flourishes, and the Jewel of the Buddha naturally remains undiminished; for this reason, the Saṃgha is specifically singled out.
The meaning of the "Sixfold Harmony" shall not be elaborated here, but will be clarified later. All that has been stated above is the True Dharma taught by the Buddhas of the three periods of time.

Those who do not contravene these teachings—the Saṃgha—can fully receive and uphold the majestic deportment and govern themselves through the Sixfold Harmony. By not contravening these teachings, the Three [Jewels]...
The jewels shall not be interrupted; the Dharma shall abide for a long time. Regarding the statement that the *Mahāsaṃnipāta* extends up to the section on precepts (*śīla*), Kō says:
"The Beijing edition translated by Dharmakṣema consists of thirty fascicles. In its nineteenth chapter, the 'Chapter on Protecting the Dharma' (*Dharmapālana-parivarta*), it is said:

'When this sutra was being preached, at that time there were great bodhisattvas from the worlds of the ten directions who came from other regions to discuss the Way and expound the meaning. Thus it speaks of the various bodhisattvas."
He addressed the Buddha, saying: "The Tathāgatas have established prohibitions and precepts for the sake of sentient beings in the five turbidities.

We only pray that the Tathāgata, so that the Dharma may endure for a long time, will further establish prohibitions and precepts—namely, the precepts of body, speech, and mind—and that one shall not receive or store any evil things, just as the pure precepts are established in other buddha-fields.
The Buddha said: "Stop, stop! The Buddha knows the proper time himself; do not request that he establish them."

The intent of the precepts is merely for the long endurance of the Dharma. Regarding the statement that "Saccaka reached his physical [end]," Yu'ke says it is found in either the seventh or eighth fascicle, translated by Bodhiruci of the Later Wei dynasty.

The sutra states: There was Saccaka Nirgrantha-putra, who traveled through various kingdoms with eighty million *nirgranthas*, teaching and transforming sentient beings. He subsequently arrived at the city of Ujjayinī. At that time, the king...
His name was Yaṅ-chi (Ugra). The king held him in high esteem and studied under him. This man extensively expounded various Dharma-gates for the king;
subsequently, he spoke to the king of the fame and merits of the śramaṇa Gautama. The king asked: "What is this Dharma-body like?"
"From what is this obtained? The Nirgrantha replied, "It begins with the precepts. Great King, you should know that because the precepts are pure, the lineage of the Three Jewels is not severed.
Because the precepts are pure, one's merit is immeasurable. If one does not uphold the precepts, one may not even obtain the body of a dog or a jackal;
how much less could one obtain a body of merit? When the King heard these words, he resolved upon Bodhi.

This refers to the "Exertion of Mind. Regarding the term "Moon-Lamp Sage" (Candrapradīpa-māṇava), Yuán Ěr says it appears in either the eleventh or twelfth fascicle, translated during the Northern Qi dynasty by Narendrayaśas.

There is also a single fascicle of ten sheets translated by the "Former Lord" (Xian Gong) of the Song dynasty. Lì says: "Though one may possess a handsome appearance, noble lineage, and so forth, the Sūtra states:
'It is like a corpse adorned with golden necklaces. [Even] extensive learning [is no avail if... [The text here is incomplete].

The precepts are likewise so. That which is called "the superior person who upholds the precepts" refers to one who maintains the moral discipline. As for what is called "the Sūtra on Reaching Nirvāṇa," it means that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature;
however, it is only through the practice of upholding the precepts that this nature is subsequently seen. Once Buddha-nature is seen, one spontaneously realizes Great Nirvāṇa.
As for what is called "the Flower Garland reaching the Head," it first manifests the Threefold Jewel of the Saṃgha, which is capable of...
This ensures that the Three Jewels are not interrupted and that the Dharma may endure for a long time. It benefits those who maintain it in the present;

thus, this verse is now cited to clarify that the precepts are the root of Bodhi and to encourage their observance. The Buddha praises the future benefit, stating that because the precepts are pure, one shall attain Bodhi.

Since this refers back to what was previously mentioned, it is called a "repeated citation. To encourage constant mindfulness and retention, it says: "cause them to recite [the precepts] as the foremost in the heart."

The fourth section of the *Mahāyāna-śāstra* has two parts: the heading and the explanation. The first is as the text states. Within the explanation, there are three sections: first, the *Jñānaprasthāna*; second, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*;
and third, the *Daśabhūmika*. Regarding the phrase "from wisdom to fear," Kuo (K’o) says: The *Jñānaprasthāna* consists of one hundred fascicles, translated by Kumārajīva of the Qin dynasty.

To explain the treatise, it is divided into two parts: first, from the beginning up to "the essentials of leaving home," which is the heading; second, from "as if cherishing oneself" onwards, which is the explanation. The first [section] has three parts.

[The commentary on] the *Śikṣāsamuccaya* states: "First, from 'desire' up to 'precepts,' it clarifies that precepts have the meaning of benefit (*artha*). Second, from 'all' up to 'roots,' precepts have the meaning of being roots (*mūla*).

Third, from 'leaving home' downwards, precepts have the meaning of being essential (*sāra*). Within the headings there are three parts; the explanations likewise have three. First, from 'as if cherishing' up to 'dwelling place,' it explains the meaning of roots.
Second, from 'again as' up to 'that which is obtained,' it explains the meaning of essentials. Third, from 'although people are poor' downwards, it explains [the meaning of benefit]."
Regarding the meaning of benefit: the fruit of Buddhahood, Bodhi, is called the "great benefit. Because one’s life is sustained by these jewels, they must be cherished.

Protecting the body that sustains life leads to longevity; this is the meaning of the "root. The phrase "having no desire for further travel" serves as a counter-illustration of the essential meaning. As for the explanation of the body and so forth:
According to the *Abhidharmahṛdaya-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, it is asked: How is it that the fire element (*tejo-dhātu*) can dissolve the joints and limbs? It is answered:

When the fire element dissolves them, the fire element increases and pervades, burning the tendons and joints; once the tendons and joints have been dissolved, death occurs before long. As for the dissolution by the water element (*ab-dhātu*), it first causes the tendons to rot.
As for the dissolution by the wind element (*vāyu-dhātu*), it causes the tendons to be shattered and destroyed. Once the joints and limbs have been dissolved, death occurs within a day or night.

End. Regarding "the earth element being greatly unfavorable," it means one cannot [attain] liberation. As for "the mind having no fear," the *Śāstra* says: "Either one sees auspicious signs, or one knows for oneself that one’s observance of the precepts is pure;
thus the mind has no dread. It is by virtue of observing the precepts that one obtains this benefit of fearlessness.

Regarding the statement "the *Dìchí* [Śāstra] up to its retribution," Yuè Ē said: "The *Śāstra* consists of ten fascicles, or eight fascicles. It was translated by Paramārtha at the Northern Court. *Bō*.
Śāriputra asked: "What is the meaning of 'marks' (*lakṣaṇa*)? It means 'excellence' or 'auspiciousness'; thus they are called marks. As for the thirty-two [major marks]:
first, the soles of the feet are level and full; second, the wheels with a thousand spokes; third, the fingers and toes are slender and long;

fourth, the heels are rounded and long; fifth, the hands and feet are delicate and soft; sixth, the hands and feet have webbed membranes; seventh, the insteps are prominent and thick; eighth, the *ūrṇā* hair-tuft."
10. The private parts are concealed within a sheath; 11. the ten parts of the body are perfectly rounded; 12. the body hairs point upward; 13. each pore has a single hair growing from it;
14. the body hairs curl to the right; 15. the body is golden in color; 16. a constant light extends one arm’s length; 17. the skin is fine and smooth; 18.
the seven parts of the body are well-filled; 19. the body is broad, majestic, and straight; 20. [the legs are] like those of a lion.
19. His body is well-proportioned. 20. His shoulders and collarbones are perfectly rounded. 21. Standing upright, his hands reach his knees. 22. He has a jaw like that of a lion.
23. He possesses forty teeth. 24. His teeth are even and closely set.
25. His teeth are brilliant white. 26. He possesses the supreme sense of taste. 27. His tongue is broad and long. 28. His eyes are deep blue.
29. Blue eyes; 30. Eyelashes like those of a bull king; 31. A white tuft of hair between the eyebrows; 32. The mark of possessing the Brahma-voice.
Regarding the non-differentiating causes, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Treatise on the Great Perfection of Wisdom), fascicle 29, states:
"Throughout his successive lifetimes, the Buddha maintained the precepts with single-minded firmness and did not allow others to violate them. By virtue of these karmic causes and conditions..."
Therefore, one attains this first mark, namely the mark of the soles of the feet being well-placed and level like the bottom of a cosmetic box.
Up to the attainment of the mark of having forty teeth, all of which are obtained through the observance of the precept against double-tongued speech;

thus it is said that the thirty-two marks have no difference in their causes. Regarding the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā*, Kuò says: it consists of fourteen fascicles and was translated by Kumārajīva of the Qin dynasty.
Treatise, Chapter Fourteen. This chapter consists of two sections. The first, "An Exposition Praising the Precepts," states: I shall briefly praise a small portion of the *śīla*.
*Śīla* is the very foundation of the holy life (*brahmacarya*). *Śīla* is a heap of jewels of merit; it is also the dwelling place of merit.
*Śīla* enables people to cross over birth and death, just as a sturdy ship can carry one across the great ocean. Just as...

Just as excellent medicine can eliminate various illnesses and so forth, the subsequent "Chapter on the Retribution of Precepts" explains that the Bodhisattva is able to purify the *śīla* (precepts) and attain the Stainless Stage (*vimalā-bhūmi*), which is the second stage.
He constantly acts as a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*), transforming people through the ten wholesome paths of action and enjoying the seven treasures at will;
he obtains such retribution, as described in detail therein.

Regarding the second [section], there are two parts within the exposition of the precepts (*śikṣāpada*). First, the citation of the heading and the enumeration of the items; second, the detailed explanation according to that enumeration. The phrase "The second...
to the two" constitutes the citation of the heading and the enumeration of the items.

The Chinese text is divided into two parts: first, an exposition of the Vinaya texts; second, an exposition based on the Vinaya commentaries (*vinayavibhāṣā*). The first part has two sections: first, the heading; second, the explanation.

The first [section] follows the text as it stands. The explanation of the text has three parts: first, the *Mahāsāṃghika*; second, the *Dharmaguptaka*; third, the *Sarvāstivāda*. Regarding the phrase "from the *Saṃgha* to the *Śīla*":

this establishes the three types of practice, thereby manifesting the upholding of the Dharma through the administration of the rules. Third, regarding those who do not wish to harbor doubts and thus seek instruction: the *Avataṃsaka* states:

"Once one upholds the precepts and possesses a thorough understanding of the sacred teachings, there is no need to consult others. Regarding "wandering through the five directions to transform [beings]" and so forth, Li states:
"The Dharma and its principles throughout the ten directions are without distinction. If one does not understand the sacred teachings, there will be much fear wherever one goes;

if one acts in accordance with the teachings, one will have no timidity when traveling abroad. Regarding the phrase "reaching the four [directions]" and so forth, Li states: "Although there are five phrases,"
The meaning is summarized into three parts. The first concerns one's own practice; the next three concern the conduct for governing the assembly.

If these two types of conduct are perfected, one is then able to uphold the Dharma so that it does not fall into ruin for a thousand years. Therefore, the final section establishes the practice for upholding the True Dharma. The commentary states:

mindfulness, wisdom, equanimity, and so forth, cause the precepts to be pure and prevent them from being destroyed by external conditions; thus they are called "firm. Second, regarding those who break the precepts:
Contrary to those who uphold [the precepts] merely outwardly, its meaning is like that of an enemy; yet with a pure inner mind, it excels them.

Third, being free from any blemish, one may sit among the assembly to adjudicate matters without any fear or hesitation. Fourth, by clearly understanding what constitutes upholding and violating [the precepts], one is able to resolve the doubts and obstructions of others.

Therefore, one is well able to open up and explain [the meaning]. Fifth, if one does not uphold the precepts, the Dharma will not abide for long; this is distinguished in the "Ten Benefits" section of the lower fascicle.

Regarding the statement that the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* says "until then," the forty-seventh fascicle of the Vinaya asks: "How long will the Buddha-dharma of the past remain in the world? The Buddha replied:

"It remains as long as pure bhikṣus do not allow the method of reciting the precepts (*prātimokṣa*) to be destroyed; this is called the 'abiding of the Dharma. This applies to the present and the future as well."
The Buddha also spoke in this way; therefore, it is said that the three periods of time are likewise so.

Second, regarding the two parts of the Vinaya-śāstra: the heading and the explanation. The first is as the text states. Within the explanation, there are five sections: first, the *Mingliao-lun* (Luminous Treatise); second, the *Shan-chi-bahulaka-vinaya-śāstra* (Saṃghabhadra’s Vinaya-śāstra);

third, the *Jian-lun* (Vision Treatise); fourth, the *Pañcaśata-praśna* (Five Hundred Questions); and fifth, the *Shan-chi-bahulaka-vinaya-śāstra* again. Regarding the phrase "from 'clear' to 'matter,'" the *Liaoshu* (Commentary on the Essentials) says: "This is a citation..."
There are two kinds of arising: first, it can induce the forty-two thousand merits of the True Dharma;
second, it can induce a mind free from regret, leading even to liberation. The *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* states: "If one attains the fruits of humans or devas, it is mundane goodness;

if one attains the fruits of the Three Vehicles, it is supramundane goodness. Regarding the phrase "second, it can teach [others] equally," the commentary explains: "It can restrain the body and speech..."

Causing [afflictions] to arise is the meaning of "teaching. Because one is not defiled by the turbidity of delusion (*kleśa-kāṣāya*) or the turbidity of karma (*karma-kāṣāya*), it is called "purity of body and speech.

Because one is not defiled by the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kāṣāya*), it is called "uprightness. Because of purity, one proceeds toward the good realms; because of uprightness, one proceeds toward *nirvāṇa*.
Regarding the phrase "the three can extinguish," the commentary explains: there are two kinds of extinction. The first is the extinction of the means (*upāya-nirodha*).

Second, the extinction of actual transgressions. This refers to attaining *pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha* (nirvāṇa). Because ethical discipline (*śīla*) can obstruct all obstacles of transgression, it is called the "means of extinction.
Because obstacles do not arise, the extinction of transgressions is attained. The attainment of both of these is termed *vinaya*.

Regarding the fourth point, "that which can lead," the commentary states: "It can lead householders to leave the home life; it leads those who have not yet abandoned desire to attain the Brahma-abodes (*brahmavihāra*). From...

Through the Brahma-abodes (brahmavihāra), one attains the noble abodes (āryavihāra). From the noble abodes, one attains nirvāṇa with remainder (sopadhiśeṣanirvāṇa); from that with remainder, one enters that without remainder (nirupadhiśeṣa).

Because these subsequently become increasingly superior, they are said to "induce the ultimate meaning" (paramārtha). As for the statement in the treatise that there are eight kinds of abodes, this refers generally to the eight types of dwellings occupied by the Tathāgata.
The first is the abode of the objective field (viṣayavihāra), which means that the Tathāgata relies upon the ten [powers].
He dwells in six ways: first, he dwells by relying on the six great kingdoms; second, he dwells by relying on the mind, specifically by relying on the Jetavana Monastery;

third, he dwells in the four modes of deportment, namely walking, standing, sitting, and lying down; fourth, he dwells without relinquishing his life-span, meaning that for eighty years prior, he dwelt in the fivefold Dharma-body (*pañca-dharmakāya*).

The five *brahmavihāras* (abodes of Brahma) refer to the Buddha’s constant dwelling in the four *dhyānas*. The six *brahmavihāras* refer to the cultivation of the four immeasurable concentrations (*apramāṇa-samādhi*) that open the path to the Brahma realm.
The seven *āryavihāras* (noble abodes) refer to dwelling in the three *samādhis*, namely the *śūnyatā*, *animitta*, and *apraṇihita* samādhis.

The eighth is the "dwelling in non-dwelling," which refers to attaining *nirvāṇa* within the realm of *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇadhātu*. Because the preceding five [categories] are omitted in the *Chao*, it says “up to” (*zhì*).

Regarding the "five superior persons," the *Liaoshu* (Commentary on Understanding) states: "The most superior person" refers to the Buddha and others. As for the phrase "all beings reaching that [state]," it means all sentient beings.

Regarding the statement "they exist by virtue of precepts," *E* says: "Superior retributions as humans or devas arise from upholding the precepts; inferior retributions in the three miserable realms are obtained through violating the precepts.
Therefore, everything exists by virtue of the precepts. If one were to follow those who violate the precepts, they would properly be situated below."
Since this is clarified within the section on the extinction [of offenses] that violate the precepts, we know that it does not refer to all instances of breaking the precepts.

According to the tenth fascicle of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, when the Buddha spoke a verse stating that "giving everything" is solely worthy of praise, Cunda questioned the Buddha as to the meaning of this.
The Buddha replied to Cunda that "everything" refers to a partial entirety; thus, we know that this refers specifically to the three types of wholesome [giving].
The Way is for the sake of all beings; this refers only to a small portion [of its scope]. Possessing these four meanings, its efficacy is superior to that of other sutras.

The *Avataṃsaka* states that it specifically designates wisdom. Regarding the phrase "excellent until one's years," it refers to the five types of persons who uphold the Vinaya, speaking in terms of those who maintain the Sangha according to the sutras.

The *Mahāsannipāta Sūtra* also states: "In a single grove or a single village, if five Dharma masters strike the gong to assemble the Sangha from the four quarters, this is called the Sangha acting according to the Dharma, creating a great ocean of merit.

Even if immeasurable monks are breaking the precepts, provided that five persons are pure and act according to the Dharma—whether they be four or up to twenty persons—to protect and uphold [the community] and to bring about the purification of transgressions, one begins with repentance before a single person. Up until...

It reaches until the twentieth [year] when the offenses are removed; hence it says "up to. Once the body is purified, one is able to uphold the Dharma through the administration of its rites, thereby causing the Dharma to abide for a long time.
Regarding the statement that it abides in the world for five thousand years, the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 18, states there are two periods of five thousand years.

During the first five thousand years, during the first millennium, one attains the three types of supernormal knowledge (*trividyā*). Furthermore, during the next millennium, one attains the state of an Arhat, though they do not possess the three [supernormal knowledges].
He attained realization of wisdom. For another thousand years, he attained the stage of Anāgāmin; for another thousand years, he attained the stage of Sakṛdāgāmin;

and for another thousand years, he attained the stage of Srotāpanna. After five thousand years, his studies no longer yielded penetration. At ten thousand years, the scriptures and written characters were completely extinguished.

It merely mentions shaving the head and donning the *kāṣāya*. If one follows the period when [the Buddha] dwelt in the world and attained the fruits [of the path], it refers to the first five thousand years.
If one discusses the period when the Buddha-dharma remains in the world but the fruits are not attained, it refers to the subsequent five thousand years.

Regarding the phrase "up to five," it should have included the intermediate period, stating such words as "if the Buddha were still in the world, take the Buddha as your teacher. Since these words are now missing, it says "even" (*nai*).

[It] arrives. If one who upholds the five precepts immediately perceives the Dharma-body, then upholding the precepts is the purity of morality (*śīla-viśuddhi*). Because of morality, concentration (*samādhi*) arises, and from concentration, wisdom (*prajñā*) arises;
thus, one immediately attains liberation (*vimukti*) and the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimukti-jñāna-darśana*). Therefore, by relying on the five precepts, one perceives the Dharma-body.

Regarding "if one protects the Dharma" and below: both the principle and the metaphor are clarified. This means that apart from the Dharma there is no Buddha, and apart from water there are no insects. If one protects the Dharma, then...
This is the protection of the Buddha. To protect water is to protect the insects within it; to drink water is to kill those insects. To damage the precepts is to damage the Buddha.
This analogy of drinking water and killing insects serves as a proof for the realization of the Dharma-body through upholding the precepts.

Although the *Naiyāya*, the *Mahāsāṃghika*, and the *Sarvāstivāda* Vinayas differ in their specific teachings, the general meaning regarding the two cases involving bhikṣus is the same. Now, following the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*:

The commentary explains: At that time, the World-Honored One was staying in Śrāvastī. There were then two bhikṣus who, having completed their summer retreat, came from the kingdom of Kośala wishing to pay their respects to the World-Honored One.
On the road, it was parched and there was no water; they saw only a single well containing insects.
One of the bhikṣus, desiring to see the Buddha, drank the water containing the insects. The other bhikṣu died of thirst rather than do so.

Regarding those who drank water containing insects and those who did not drink it: at the end of their lives, they were reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, endowed with celestial bodies and wearing crowns of a hundred jewels.
They first descended to the place where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and after the Buddha had preached the Dharma for them, they attained the purity of the Dharma-eye.
Having received the three refuges and the five precepts, he immediately returned to his celestial palace. Later, the one who had drunk water containing insects arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling.
Knowing the reason, the Buddha questioned him, and he related the preceding events in detail. Thereupon, the World-Honored One rebuked him and removed his upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*).
He manifested a body of golden hue. "You deluded person, what is the use of seeing my physical body? It is better than this for one who upholds the precepts to first see my Dharma-body.
(From the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, Chapter Five, Part Three. First, the *Mahāvibhāṣā* correctly explains [the point]; second, from "Furthermore, distinguishing" onwards, it provides an interpretation.
Because the former was secret, it must be within the Saṃgha; third, from "The three great adornments" onwards, it explains that laypeople are incapable [of such realization].
The first proclamation of the practice of righteousness states: "As for the term 'Sa-zhi' (薩至), the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra* cited previously distinguished its powerful efficacy;

here it is cited again to clarify the secret of the initial assembly. Thus, the time and place are specified to elucidate its supreme meaning. This is from the *Pinfen gongde lun* (Treatise on the Analysis of Merit).

Kē states: Four fascicles, or five fascicles; translator lost. Its first fascicle clarifies the two communities of monks and nuns, explaining the matters of the two hundred and fifty and five hundred precepts.
By citing the Dharma to prevent wrongdoing, it is kept secret; thus, it is not for the practice of lay officials or commoners, nor is it for śrāmaṇeras or śrāmaṇerīs to hear or see.
Regarding the *Mahāvyūha* (Great Adornment): Kē states it consists of fifteen fascicles; [translated during the] Qin dynasty.
Translated by Kumārajīva. This is a Mahāyāna treatise; it should have been included previously, but as its textual flow here is distinct from that context, it is cited in succession.
Regarding "the foolish and inferior": Ling Shan says that the sages of the Three Vehicles are superior because they possess wisdom and all revere the precepts, thereby attaining *triyāna-bodhi*.
As for those of the lowest and most ignorant sort, they are deluded and their aspirations are base; they hold the dharma of the precepts in light esteem and thus fall into [lower realms].
This refers to the three miserable realms (*tridurgati*). The preceding section concludes the explanation that the Three Jewels are sustained by compliance with the precepts.

The second part concerns the destruction of the True Dharma through the violation of the precepts; it consists of two sections: first, stating the intent of what is being explained; second, from "The twenty recitations" onwards.

First, citing external obstacles and various explanations to clarify the characteristics of the assembly; the seven groups of followers may all collectively perform this duty. Second, "If according to... and below; in our own school, it is not stated that a *bhikṣu* may perform it.
Regarding the first of these [two], the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* explains both the agent and the object. Regarding the second, "The Twenty Recitations" and below, it speaks only in terms of the agent.

The *Daming* (Clarification) states that the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* extends [the rule] to include striking. It says in the twenty-second [chapter]: At the time of the *poṣadha*, [a monk] refused to assemble, neglecting seated meditation and the practice of the Path.
He reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said: "One should announce that the time has arrived; one may do so by striking a *ghanṭā* (gong) or similar instrument."
Not knowing who should strike [the gong], they informed the Buddha. The Buddha said, "Let the novice monks and the gardeners strike it. They then struck it too many times.
They informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "It should be struck three times. The visiting novice monks did not know the location and missed the proper timing.
They informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "The resident monks should strike it. The bhikṣus did not know what kind of wood to use for making it. They informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
Regarding the rule concerning trees: one may strike other trees that produce sound, provided they are not "stained" (*rakta*) or "poisonous" (*viṣa*). As for the "three strikes":

after the sound has ceased following the sequence from *zhēng* (the second note) to *xī* (the seventh note), one adds three more blows; this constitutes the "three strikes. A "stained tree" causes sores when bitten by people, while a "poisonous tree" merely harms them.
Both types are restricted to the two periods, namely the times for the major and minor meals. The subsequent citation of various reasons for striking is intended to... [text ends].
It is proven that both the monastic and lay sevenfold assemblies may strike [the drum].
The second section has two parts: first, concerning men and women; second, concerning only the monastics. Regarding the statement "In the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* it says... and so forth:
Haiyun says this refers to the case in the Bhikṣuṇī-prātimokṣa where a bhikṣu is in an araṇya and a woman sends him food. The second part concerns only...

Regarding the two instances within the Saṃgha: first, Ānanda goes to strike [the gong]; second, the *karmadāna* (ritual master) is appointed to strike it. As for the phrase "increasing by one" (*zēng yī zhì yě*), Kē says:
