He ordered Ānanda to strike the gong to assemble the Saṃgha. Ānanda went to the lecture hall and took the *gandi* (wooden gong) in his hand."
Thus it is said: "I now beat this drum of faith of the Tathāgata; all disciples shall assemble from every quarter. The *Zhongzhong* (Commentary on the Bell) states:

"The purpose of summoning by the sound of this bell is to move the hearts of sentient beings. Regarding the phrase "the arrival of the *Daśabhāṇavāra*," there are two meanings here: first, the direct clarification;
second, the further explanation following the oral tradition of the masters of phonology (*śabdavidyā*). [This refers to] Vimalakīrti.
[This is] the meaning. It cites the original intent of the text to instruct the *karmadāna* to announce that the time has arrived and to strike the *gandī*.
Regarding "sweeping and plastering," Ling Shan says: "In the Western Heavens, they sit cross-legged while eating; they prepare a *maṇḍala*, spread grass upon it, and eat on top of that."

Thereafter, one should sit in the squatting posture (*utkuṭukāsana*). One sits in this manner to prevent contact with unwholesome things; therefore, even when doing so, one must sweep and clean the area.

Regarding the instruction to have someone cleanse fruits, vegetables, and the like, according to the original text: "If there is no one to cleanse the fruits and vegetables. As for "no one": [it refers to the absence of such a person].
It is an insect found in fermented grain wine (*kaṣāya*). According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 11, it is translated as "Temple Guardian" (*sīhù*).
Some say its Sanskrit name is *karmadāna*. *Dāna* means "bestowal," and *karman* means "matter"; thus, it is translated as "Bestower of Affairs" (*shòushì*).

This is based on the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, fascicle 34, regarding the formal motion (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*) for the appointment. Fǎ Chángfáng’s catalogue states that it was translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Saṅghabhadra. This is [the same text].

It is one of the five fields of knowledge (*pañcavidyāsthāna*). Regarding the "five fields of knowledge": first is the field of grammar (*śabdavidyā*), which refers to phonetics; second is the field of medicine (*cikitsāvidyā*);

third is the field of arts and crafts (*śilpakarmasthānavidyā*); fourth is the field of logic (*hetuvidyā*); and fifth is the field of incantations and seals (*adhyātmavidyā*). "Joy" (*yuè*) means delight.
Having attained the proper sequence of affairs, one causes the multitude to rejoice; hence it is called "joy. As for the phrase "according to the arrival," Mount Ling says:

This corresponds to the third [category], which is the sound of striking the ground; it is omitted in the present text. The *Karmavācanā-vyākhyā* states: "The seven signs for summoning the Saṃgha do not depart from form and sound.
That is to say, measuring shadows and observing smoke belong to form; the rest all belong to sound. Regarding "measuring shadows," Master Liang says:
"Take a one-foot wooden stick and use its shadow at midday as the standard. Regarding "making smoke," it refers to the beacon fires used by military forces today.
This refers to the ritual procedure (*vidhi*) performed with one who is already acquainted with the Saṃgha. Regarding "breaking bamboo":

it means taking a bamboo stalk about one *zhang* long, splitting one end while leaving the other end intact, grasping the intact end with the hand, and shaking it to produce a sound. Regarding the "conch" (*śaṅkha*): the *Shuowen Jiezi* states: [it is a shell used for sounding].
The "sea-shell insect" (hǎi jiè chóng) refers to the sea snail (*lǐ*) found in the ocean, which can produce sound when blown upon.

When chanting, "Venerable sirs, the time for the *poṣadha* recitation of the precepts has arrived," this [insect] is not originally included among the seven [categories]. The *Chao* (Excerpts) excludes the sign of striking the ground because it is considered a corrupt practice that causes confusion;

thus, this [insect] is added to complete the number of seven. Furthermore, it does not specify that a *bhikṣu* performs this act, as it is intended for the various sections of the Sūtras and Vinaya mentioned above.
In these and other instances, it is stated that a bhikṣu may also strike; for example, Ānanda struck [the Buddha], and in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, the *karmadāna* strikes, and so forth.

This Vinaya likewise does not explicitly state that a bhikṣu performs this act. The intent is to show that by drawing from various Vinayas, Sūtras, and other texts, it is permissible for a bhikṣu to strike as well.
Thus, the *Karmasūtra* states: "As the Vinaya ordains that a resident *kappiya-kāraka* (lay attendant) of lower status shall strike—this is a regulation established by the Saṃgha, and is not..."

This is the practice of those who possess the Way; there must never be two [masters] acting together. Only when they assist one another may they be permitted to do so. By citing that [text] as evidence for this, it is sufficient to understand the *Chao* (Excerpts).
The preceding citation of various schools and the subsequent reliance on the specific Vinaya serve to clarify that striking a person does not apply solely to the *xiang* (gong).

Regarding the statement "the words emerge and reach the bell," the *Jie-mo-su* (Commentary on the Karmavācanā) states: "The term *gāndī* is a Sanskrit sound. The following phonological analysis is as found in the *Chao*.

The second section on the formal establishment (*vidhi*) has two parts: first, connecting the preceding to the following; second, from "Generally, regarding the dharma of giving" onwards, the actual explanation of the formal establishment.

Regarding the phrase "the aforementioned complete [procedures] up to the formal establishment": a question is raised—since the preceding citations from the Vinaya and Śāstras are sufficient to clarify the compilation of the dharma, why is it necessary to establish it through a formal procedure?

The *Karmavācanā-vyākhyā* states: "For now, following the Western Indic manuscripts, there are no formal headings (*kośa*). Regarding the miscellaneous textual fragments, matters that follow one another in sequence for explanation must have their practical procedures established according to the meaning, so as to provide a detailed order of events."

The second section consists of two parts. First, a general explanation of the rules for convening the assembly (*saṃgha*). Second, from "Various Persons" onwards, the specific protocols for striking the bell are established.

Regarding the phrase "all who reach the midday [meal]," the instruction on ringing the bell follows the previously cited teachings, which specify three strikes according to the fivefold characteristics (*pañca-lakṣaṇa*), and seven strikes according to our own Vinaya.
As for other schools, with the exception of those that exclude the "poisonous tree," there are others who ring it.

It is permitted to strike [the bell]. Regarding the persons involved: for the seven assemblies of other schools, according to their own Vinaya, this applies to śrāmaṇeras and pure attendants (kappiyakāraka). This is based on the aforementioned principles concerning the characteristics, the persons, and the striking.
Therefore, it says "according to the text, ring the bell," as detailed in the *Sangha-saṃnipāta-vidhi* (The Method for Assembling the Sangha). Yuan’er states:

The author of the *Chao* (the *Zhiyi Chao*) separately compiled a diagram of the procedures for assembling the Sangha spanning over three pages, in which the rules for striking the bell are clearly explained. It says therein: "Recite the names of the Three Jewels."

The five aggregates are maintained. Each aggregate is distinguished by eight classes; thus, forty is established as the differential. The three paths ride upon these, resulting in one hundred and twenty as the divisions.
According to the rule, when measuring time and delimiting the assembly, the minimum number is taken as twenty-seven.

There are three classes for each of the eight groups; three times eight is twenty-four. To these are added the remaining three lower ones, totaling the three vehicles; hence, twenty-seven. As for the middle [measure]...
Forty [days]; at most, one hundred and twenty. That source lists the three dharmas in full; thus it says "fully as.

Now, we take the minimum as our standard for the second [section]. The text has three parts: first, a general overview comparing ancient and modern practices to establish the overall standard; second, from "If one follows the ordinary...

onwards, the invocation according to common practice, which correctly reveals the ritual procedure; third, from "In the world there are... onwards, the exclusion of the excesses of past practitioners.

Regarding the statement "those who have reached [the limit]": Ē (Kē) says that the *Mahābhikṣu-sāhasra-vaipulya-vinaya-sūtra* (The Sutra on the Three Thousand Dignified Manners of a Great Bhikṣu) consists of two fascicles and its translator is lost.
As for the "Essential Sections" (*kēyào*), because the matters involved are of many kinds, it contains highly structured divisions and essential summaries.

As for the "Segmented Explanations" (*jiéjiě*), they are so named because they differ according to the number of beats. It says therein: "If a bhikṣu is assembled, he receives four beats; if a śrāmaṇera is assembled, he receives..."

Three times for the *xià* (lower); twice for the *yōubāsè* (upāsaka); once for calling out "Sīmī. According to the lower fascicle, there are further five matters: first, the time of the regular assembly;
second, the time of the provisional meal; third, the time of the daytime meal; fourth, the time of submitting a petition—Master Shìzhōng says this refers to placing it in a bowl or vessel;
fifth, the time of non-regular [occasions]. There are further seven matters: first, government officials; second, great floods; third, great fires.
1. The four types of thieves; 2. The assembly of śrāmaṇeras; 3. The upāsakas; 4. The "hu-sōng-ér" (literally, "calling for the pine-child").
Regarding the term *sōng-ér*, Shìzōng says it refers to the small children of the *jìngrén* (lay attendants). Regarding the "great standard": when there are many monks, slowness is the standard;

when there are few monks, urgency is the standard. For the two regular meals, slowness is the standard; for sudden matters such as official business, fire, water, and so forth, urgency is the standard. This applies universally.
Regarding the urgency [of the situation], this text comprehensively clarifies the ritual procedures;

therefore, it is titled "The Great Standard" (*Dà Zhǔn*). Section Two consists of two parts: first, the formal explanation of the striking method; second, from the words "Now, at the beginning... onwards, establishing the mind as the marker for the dharma.

The first part consists of two sections: first, explaining the method of the three downward strikes; second, from the words "Subsequently, because of... onwards, distinguishing the long-striking method. As for the phrase "If one reaches...", it refers to the third [section].

Regarding the "three strikes": Zhongyang says that the first strike generally assembles the assembly of *śrāvakas*, the second strike generally assembles the assembly of *pratyekabuddhas*, and the third strike generally assembles the assembly of Mahāyāna bodhisattvas.
Thus, one knows that the three strikes assemble the monks. The long striking is for saving those in suffering.
In current practice, the three strikes signify the cessation of duties, while the long striking signals proceeding to the hall; used according to the occasion, both methods are effective.
The *Jie-mo shu* (Commentary on the Karmavācanā) states that after the three sounds have ceased, another three strikes are added;

hence it is called "three rounds" (*san-tong*), which refers to the "three downward strokes" mentioned in the text of the *Chao*. Regarding the phrase "later, due to [the arrival of] others," this refers to the invitation made by others when the thousand-headed fish was summoned by King [Mao].
The character *gai* (pronounced *ju* with the *chi* tone) is defined in the *Shuowen Jiezi* as "dense. This long striking method consists of three sections; first, before...
The two times of striking with four blows each are the same as the three [blows] mentioned above. The intermediate four strikes, continuing down to the very end, constitute a separate section.
Regarding these four strikes, according to the model of the bell: the first sound, which completes one full cycle, is for the sake of saving those in the hells.

Once again, another round is struck to rescue the hungry ghosts (*preta*). Once again, another round is struck to rescue the animals (*tiryagyoni*). Continuing, another round is struck to rescue the asuras.
Finally, two strikes are delivered with a grip; this is called "stopping the blows" (*xi-chui*).

According to the *Sānqiānwēiyí jīng* (Sūtra on the Three Thousand Dignified Manners), one should assemble the community of bhikṣus and strike four times. Since the bhikṣu is the head of the fivefold assembly (*pañcavarga*), if a bhikṣu arrives...

The remaining assembly gathered accordingly; this did not hinder the salvation of suffering beings while simultaneously serving to assemble the Saṃgha. These two purposes were mutually compatible, which was considered successful.

Regarding the phrase "the Sūtras and Vinayas, etc. used by the ancient masters: the first and last sections are both texts from the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*. The middle four sections are explained in the *Trīṃśad-ācāra-sūtra*.
Since the Vinaya is at the end and the Sūtra is situated in the middle, it is said that they "intermingle" (*saṃkara*). As for the Vinaya...
Regarding the *Tongming jifa* (The Collection of Methods for Universal Clarity), the number of strikes in the sutra differs from the intermediate four downward strokes.

If the four sounds were to cease and the striking were to begin immediately, it would resemble the manner of striking a new bell, which is improper; therefore, a gradual sequence was established. This continued until the time of Weiming, who stated that they collectively established this method.
As for the phrase "at the place where the bell patterns are exhausted," at that time there was a temple abbot who followed the ancient masters.
Regarding the Dharma: the manner of striking the bell to signal its end is as follows; it is located at the place where the bell stands.
The second section has two parts: first, the establishment of the meaning; second, from "Therefore, entrusting the Dharma" onwards, citing the teachings to establish the proof.
The statement from "Thus" to "ceases" is easy to understand.
The second section has two parts: first, citing scriptural evidence; second, from "Furthermore, my relatives... onwards, citing actual events to provide an explanation.

Regarding the statement that "the Dharma was entrusted until it reached the deceased," there are three intentions: first, citing the tradition; second, citing the sutra; third, from "These together...

onwards, concluding with the meaning of how [the Dharma] was obtained. Ke said: It consists of six fascicles, or perhaps four fascicles, translated by Ji Jiaye and Tanyao during the Northern Wei dynasty at...

The Chinese translation states that tradition records: more than one hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, Kaniṣka of Jibin fought with the King of Parthia and achieved victory, killing nine hundred million people.
Finally, he killed two virtuous men. Because their faith was so profound, their sin was heavy.
As one man was about to be executed, he invoked "Namo Buddha"; the other invoked "Namo," though it was not known whether this referred to the Buddha or to Pūraṇa.
To kill is called "half a person. Because the sin of killing two virtuous and faithful persons is the most grave, there was once a horse-neighing sound.
An Arhat saw it and took pity on him; fearing he would fall into the evil paths, the Arhat manifested a hell and preached the Dharma there.

Upon feeling fear, the man immediately gave rise to a mind of repentance, and his heavy karmic offenses were thereby extinguished. He then arrayed his fourfold army and punished the three naval forces, and punished the two [naval forces].

The first military expedition concluded. Upon reaching the third military expedition, the hoof of the horse upon which the king was riding buckled. The king said to the horse, "I have completed my campaign against the three seas; I shall no longer ride you.
The ministers, seeing that the king constantly delighted in military expeditions, desired to eliminate him.

The king soon fell ill with a malignant plague. The men sat upon his head, and he subsequently passed away. This was because of the previous discourse on the Dharma given by the Arhat. It did not [happen otherwise].
Having experienced the hells, he was reborn in the great ocean as a thousand-headed fish. A wheel of swords revolved around him, cutting him;

as soon as one head was severed, another grew back in the interval of a mere moment, until his heads filled the entire ocean. At that time, there was an Arhat serving as the *karmadāna* (steward) for the Saṃgha. The king immediately addressed him, saying:
Now, when this wheel of swords heard the sound of the wooden gong, it immediately ceased, and their suffering was briefly relieved. "We only pray that the Venerable One will show us compassion;
when you strike the gong, please strike it for a long duration. Out of pity for them, the Arhat then struck the gong for a long time.
After seven days had passed, they were released from these bodies of suffering. Because of this event, to this day [the gong is struck] for a long duration.
[The Buddha] struck him. This refers to that which is ultimately indestructible. The *Jie-mo-su* (Karmavācanā-vyākhyā) states: "In general, karma is either determinate or indeterminate;
therefore, the experience of suffering is either terminal or non-terminal. If the karma created is determinate, even a Sage cannot avoid its consequences.

Indeterminate karma, however, results in suffering only when conditions are met; if the conditions are absent, it ceases. In the present case, the transgressor’s past merit serves as the cause, while the striker’s vow serves as the condition."

Having attained the transmission of the sound, suffering was extinguished through spontaneous resonance; thus it is said that causes and conditions summon one another, and the principle of spontaneity does not perish.
"Perish" means "to cease. Regarding the passage beginning with "I arrived at... and so forth, the *Xu gaoseng zhuan* (Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks) states:

At Dong Chan-ting Temple in the Western Capital—this is the present-day Zhuangyan Temple—there was the Vinaya Master Zhi-xing. His secular surname was Song, and he was a native of Luoyang. He followed the Vinaya Master Shou...

He received his training. In the second month of winter in the fifth year of the Daye era of the Sui dynasty, he served as the *karmadāna* (venerable of affairs) and regularly struck the bell himself.

There was a monk in the same monastery named Sanguo; his elder brother had followed Emperor Yang on his southern journey to Jiangdu but had already passed away along the way. Initially, there were no signs of either misfortune or good fortune.
Suddenly, he had a dream in which he said to his wife: "I followed the imperial carriage as far as Pengcheng, where I unfortunately died and was reborn in hell.
I have undergone all five types of suffering, the bitterness of which is beyond words. Who would have known of me?

Fortunately, today I have received the grace of the Vinaya Master Zhixing of Chanding Monastery, who rang the bell; when its sound resounded through hell, those suffering together with me were [all liberated]."
"Regarding the one who attained liberation in his time and is now born in a place of bliss, you should offer ten bolts of silk to repay his kindness and convey my intentions.
His wife was startled awake and recounted the origin of her dream, but at first no one believed her.

Soon thereafter, she dreamed again, and various shamans and diviners all gave accounts identical to her previous one. Within ten or so days, the tragic news arrived suddenly, exactly as in the dream. Indeed, [he] then offered [the gift].
He gave the silk to him, but Xing himself stated that he possessed no merit, and thus distributed it all to the great assembly. The assembly all asked, "By what cause was this inspired?
He replied, "I have read the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* concerning the story of King Nanda’s sword being halted, as well as the *Ekottarika-āgama* regarding the merit of the bell's sound.
I have frequently followed these precedents and practiced them with diligent effort. Whenever I ascended the tower, the cold wind was piercing."
His bones were exposed and his hands gripped the pestle; his flesh was torn and his blood congealed. With a mind fixed in reverence, he exerted himself without slackening.

Furthermore, at the beginning, he vowed that all worthy sages and saints would enter the maṇḍala together, and later, that all those in the evil realms would simultaneously be freed from suffering. Unexpectedly—

His sincere sincerity was thus able to evoke a distant resonance, and the multitude were humbled by his words. He passed away in the third month of the sixth year of the Zhenguan era at Zangyan Monastery, at the age of forty-five.

The third section distinguishes this from the excessive interpretations of past scholars regarding the "middle three. First, it refutes what is not the word of the Sage. Second, from "In various sūtras and śāstras...

onwards, it cites scriptural authority to clarify the basis. Third, from "Knowing purity... onwards, it establishes the formal thesis and provides the correct refutation. Regarding the statement "The world... to abandoning": however, within this third section there are three parts.
First, the heading that marks the phrase "knowing purity. Second, from "Not applicable... onwards, it distinguishes those cases where [the rule] does not apply to monastics or laypeople.

Regarding matters to be performed together, there are three exhortations to abandon [them] early. The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Sifen lü) and the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* (Wufen lü) state "striking the *gandī*";

the *Āgama-sūtras* state "beating the *gandī*"; and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states "striking. Therefore, they are referred to as "striking," "beating," "striking," and so forth. Ci [Zhiyi] says: This refers to when laypeople and monastics perform an action together;
since one does not employ the "pure speech" (*jìngyǔ*) of those who know [the rules], it is said that this does not apply to laypeople, nor to oneself.
It is so. If it is permissible for the laity to perform [a certain action] but not for the Saṃgha, then one must understand "pure speech" (jìngyǔ). Thus, the *Jīemó sū* states:
"Nowadays, there are those who say that for one who knows the bell, saying 'it is the bell' constitutes pure speech, whereas striking the bell constitutes impure speech."
Originally, this "knowing purity" (zhī jìng) cannot be performed by oneself; one must cause another to perform it, which is why it is called "knowing purity. A bell is not like this;

it is used universally by both self and others and possesses no specific characteristics. How could one avoid it? One must abandon it as soon as possible. The *Jie mo shu* (Commentary on the Karmavācanā) states:

"Although the term 'knowing the bell' is not a major vessel [of transgression], it is nonetheless a great taboo for those who know the Dharma. Therefore, it is urged that one should [abandon it] early.
[This is] the relinquishment. Above, the assembly has been gathered and the ordination completed.

From here, the second major section clarifies the accessibility or restriction of the "place of arrival" (*āgama-sthāna*). This is divided into two parts: first, the restatement of the chapter heading;

second, the explanation beginning with the phrase "First, clarifying the place. Regarding the expression "Second, clarifying the arrival": this restates the chapter heading. "Arrival" (*āgama*) refers to coming or proceeding; "place" (*sthāna*) refers to...
"Location" refers to both constructed (kṛtaka) and natural (svabhāva) sites. There are three types of constructed sites and four types of natural sites.
Regarding the assembly of the Saṃgha at these seven locations, each has its own general and specific characteristics; hence it is so called.

The commentary on the text has two parts. First, the initial section lists the chapter headings. Second, within that first part, the "boundaries" (*dhātu*) are explained according to the topical outline.
Regarding the phrase "First, explaining... as to the universal and the specific": this refers to the chapter headings. "The demarcation of locations" means the boundaries of the various *dhātus*;

specifically, there are four types of boundary demarcations for a great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) with a ritual site (*sīmā-kṣetra*), and two types of boundary demarcations for a great boundary without a ritual site. Third, the small [boundary].
The boundaries for the designated sitting places can naturally be distinguished as village areas;
these are defined by the limits of a village. Where village areas cannot be distinguished, the boundary is sixty-three paces. For an araṇya (wilderness), the boundary is five li.

For those traveling on the road, it is one small krośa, which is six hundred paces. Regarding the water boundary, it is the area reached by the spray of water. When these are employed, they are used by the Saṃgha.

Regarding the extent of the general and the specific: the ability of four persons to perform all *karmas* is called "general"; the division into four or seven according to the specific matter is called "specific.
These two sections differ. First, I shall explain the boundaries of the first section, which is divided into two parts; the first of these excludes those who have arrived.

[This is] the intention. Second, "Now, directly below," correctly clarifies the boundaries. Regarding the phrase "from the beginning up to the explanation": as for "within the boundary-establishment," it says there:
the original intent of establishing a boundary was simply to perform the ritual (*dharmakriyā*); however, because Jambudvīpa is so vast, it is difficult to assemble the *saṃgha*.

The Great Sage, out of compassion for this extreme difficulty, opened the allowance to perform the ritual by demarcating sections according to their respective locations. This is the general meaning; such is the purpose [of this section].

Regarding "the differences between what is permitted (*kai*) and what is prohibited (*sei*)," this refers to clarifying the differences between what is naturally permitted and what is prohibited based on the formal rules (*sahajadharma*).

That is to say, prior to the formulation of the formal rules, everything was universally and naturally governed by the principle of prohibition (*niyama*). Later, due to difficulties in assembling the community, it was permitted to adapt to specific circumstances and encompass various situations.

Regarding the locations, there are four different types; regarding the fixed measurements, there are six distinct characteristics. This is the difference between what is naturally permitted and what is prohibited.

Furthermore, there may be cases where one attempts to establish a great Dharma ground (dharmabhūmi) but it is weak and cannot sustain it; this is a prohibition (*niyama*). Conversely, the Tathāgata, in accordance with the dispositions of sentient beings, permits the establishment [of such grounds] wherever appropriate;

this is an allowance (*anujñā*). Thus, these ritual procedures differ in their prohibitions and allowances. Moreover, this is discussed in terms of both the two textual traditions concerning natural [grounds] and ritually established grounds.
The opening and the exposition differ.

The main explanation of the boundaries consists of two parts: first, the general heading that enumerates the numbers; second, from "If one performs the ritual... onwards, the specific explanation according to the headings.
Regarding the phrase "Now, up to the specific," this is the general heading for the enumeration of the two types of differences between the ritual procedure (*vidhi*) and spontaneity (*svabhāva*).

The commentary on the text has two parts. First, up to the point "separate from the ground," it clarifies the boundaries of the two realms. Second, from "Now further" onwards, it generally distinguishes the differences between the two realms.
This first part has two sub-sections: first, it clarifies the ritual procedure; second, from "If one discusses" onwards, it distinguishes the natural [state].

The former of these two has two parts: first, a general heading; second, from "Where there is a *śīmaṇḍala*" onwards, a detailed explanation. The phrase "If one reaches the third distinction" is the general heading.
In the commentary, there are three distinctions. First, the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) with a ritual ground (*sīmaṇḍala*). Second, the great boundary without a ritual ground.
Third, the small boundary (*kṣudra-sīmā*) established in difficult circumstances. Regarding the phrase "extending to the exterior," the *Karmavācanā-vyākhyā* states:

"If other *karmavācanā* rites are performed, they are restricted by the specific divisions of the boundary, and the assembly does not need to gather together; this is as in the present text, where the monks assemble at four locations and each may perform the rite."

Regarding the statement "if there is no *sīmā* (boundary), they assemble [within the *kṣetra*]," this refers to the two locations, namely inside and outside the great boundary (*mahāsīmā*). The *Karmavācanā-vyākhyā* states:

"If one discusses a *kṣetra* that lacks a designated site (*maṇḍala*), the two locations are assembled separately; because both the interior and exterior of the boundary are subject to regulation, it is permissible to follow the assembly.
This excludes the previously mentioned *śikṣāpada-maṇḍala* and open ground. Regarding the statement "if it is small, they assemble [at the site]," the *Karmavācanā-vyākhyā* states: "Because..."
The boundary (*sīmā*) is restricted to the body; outside the assembly, there is no dharma. It is established according to the gathering of persons; therefore, there is nothing external.

If one were to allow for an external boundary, it would contradict the person who rebukes (*nāha*). In the *Jie-mo-su* (Karmavācanā-vyākhyā), regarding the distinction between the universal and the restricted among the three aforementioned positions:

if one performs other *karmas*, the boundary is divided according to the location, and persons do not gather together—this is "restricted. If one performs the *pravāraṇā* (invitation to admonish), then [the boundary includes] both the internal and external.
[The text] generally includes [both]. Question: It is said that for the *pravāraṇā* (invitation ceremony), the assembly of monks at the site is required, whereas for other dharmas it is not.

Answer: These two are methods of inclusion because they concern those who dwell in purity of conduct; therefore, within the boundaries (*sīmā*), both those inside and outside must follow them equally. As for the remaining *karmavācanā* (formal acts) and other dharmas...

The methods employed were manifold and not restricted to a specific time; as many were occupied with various other duties, if a general assembly had been mandated, it would have resulted only in mutual exhaustion.

Although there was the aforementioned provision for exemption, it ultimately yielded no subsequent benefit. Therefore, within the text, there is no mention of reciting the precepts together within the *sīmā* (boundary).

There are also two types of assemblies. According to the regulations, these are restricted; however, when explaining matters such as the *pravāraṇā* (invitation for criticism), they are opened up in accordance with difficult circumstances, which constitutes a general rule.

If one discusses the small boundary (*kṣudrasīmā*), it is exclusively restricted and lacks generality. The *Jie-mo-shu* (Commentary on the Karmavācanā) states: "The original regulation restricts those who are excluded, even if there are instances where they do not assemble."

The second [section], Naturalness (*svabhāva*), is divided into two parts. First, the heading, enumeration, and explanation of the names; second, the detailed explanation based on the headings, beginning from the section on "the initial gathering.
Regarding the statement, "As for discussing its application," there are four points herein: first, the general heading; second, the specific enumeration, beginning with "That is to say" (*yad uta*);

third, the explanation of the names, beginning with "All"; fourth, the indication of other sections for application, beginning with "In this regard. Ling-shan says: "This refers to the place where a bhikṣu arrives."
They exist spontaneously, like a halo following the moon; they do not require construction or fabrication. Generally, all things possessing form are created and brought into being by human effort.

These four [elements] are natural and are not created by anything. Regarding those who study them in detail across various schools, this refers to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, and so forth, as cited below.

This is divided into four sections according to their headings: first, the village (*grāma*); second, the forest hermitage (*aranyaka*); third, the path; and fourth, the water boundary (*udakakṣetra*). Regarding the first two, there is both a heading and an explanation.

As for the statement, "Within the first, the village, there are two," this is the heading. Bianchang says: "A cluster of households is called a *grāma*; neighboring villages are called a *pallī*. The *Karmavācanā-vyākhyā* states:
"That which can be distinguished [as a boundary] is due to three conditions: first, the physical characteristics of the enclosure (*sīmā*) can be distinguished."

Secondly, as for the Sangha being present, there is no ambiguity. There are also two cases where it is impossible to distinguish them: first, when villages and settlements are dispersed and lack enclosing walls;
second, when the Sangha is intermingled with market folk, making it difficult to investigate their comings and goings.
In the commentary, there are two divisions based on the headings. First, that which is "discernible" (*vibhajya*); second, "if it is a village," which is "indiscernible. Regarding the former two:

first, the scriptural authority is cited to determine the measure of what is discernible; second, from the question-and-answer section below, the meaning is explained by analogy with the *ārāmika* (monastery attendants), as their gathering is similar to that of a village.
As for the statement, "if it is discernible up to the assembly," this accords with the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, Chapter 22, which says: [text follows].
"O monks, when a monastery is first constructed within a village that previously had no monastery, and the boundary has not yet been established—at that time, how large should the boundary be?

(This is the question. The Buddha said: "It shall be according to the boundary of the village; this is the boundary of the monastery. (This is the answer. It does not matter whether the monastery grounds are fully enclosed or not;
it depends solely upon the village. If the villages are the same, one gathers according to the village; that is, the characteristics of the village are predominant.

"Regardless of whether the monastery precincts are complete or not. The commentary states: "The term 'etcetera' refers to a passage in the seventh fascicle of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*. Upāli asked the Buddha:

'In a village, when first constructing a monastery, to what extent should the boundary (*sīmā*) be established? The Buddha replied: 'It shall follow the boundaries of the village, extending as far as the area where people come and go.
This establishes the limits; that is to say, the monastic boundary according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* possesses a sphere of influence (*prabhāva-bhūmi*)."
The range of an arrow’s flight; the range of a cock’s flight; the place where a person of modesty performs the functions of nature—ancients say this should be one hundred paces.

Regarding the determination of the boundaries of a monastery (*ārāma*) according to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*: while a robe-boundary (*cīvara-sīmā*) possesses a zone of influence (*prabhāva*), a monastic boundary (*saṃgha-sīmā*) does not.
One simply assembles within the limits of the marked area. Thus the Vinaya says: whether it be a village, a city, a field boundary, a garden, a grove, or a pond.
Regarding trees, stones, walls, or shrines for deities, there are no words concerning their hierarchical status; all follow the characteristics described above.
The second section consists of two parts: first, the question, and second, the answer. As for the phrase "the question reaches the Sangha," this intended meaning follows the doctrine of Nanshan.
[The text] stands. There is no scriptural authority for this in the various schools. If it is a remote *araṇya* (forest hermitage), one relies on a distance of five *li*.

Now, there are monasteries (*saṃghārāma*) that possess the characteristics of an *araṇya*, yet they have lost these four characteristics and are no different from the characteristics of a village (*grāma*). It is not known whether they still rely on the five *li* [limit] or whether the monks should assemble as if they were in a village.
The answer has three parts: first, citing the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* (Shisong lü) to provide the correct answer; second, under the heading "Therefore, the text says," citing...

Regarding the text and evidence concerning the *araṇya* (wilderness) in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, it is inferior to the three [other] Vinayas. This clarifies that the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the *saṃgha* and the village are not distinct, thereby establishing them as having the same characteristic of being a single settlement (*grāma*).
As for the statement "the answer reaches the gathering of people," there are two parts: first, the direct answer from the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*;

second, the establishment of principles below this to explain and substantiate the intent of this answer. Since the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states, "In accordance with the settlement, this is the boundary of the *saṃgha*," now, regarding the *araṇya*...

If a location already possesses the four characteristics of a *saṃghārāma* that completely surround it, such that they are no different from the surrounding boundaries of a village, what need is there for a five-li radius?

If this monastery complex lacks these characteristics, it is defined as an *araṇya* and thus relies on the five-li limit; however, as soon as the characteristics of a monastery complex are present, it is no longer within the boundary of an *araṇya*.
These characteristics of a monastery complex are no different from the characteristics of a village; the purpose of the monastery complex is to encompass the Saṃgha.

Strong. Regarding the meaning, it cannot be based on the *araṇya* (wilderness). This means that what we now call the surrounding boundaries of a monastery (*vihāra*) are the four marks of a *saṃghārāma* (monastery);
what is called a "village" (*grāma*) consists of the four marks of a village. That is to say, within the precept against stealing, there are the four marks of a village;

when reaching the section on being separated from one's robes, the four marks of a *saṃghārāma* are pointed out as being identical to the village marks mentioned in the context of stealing, with no further distinction. Therefore, it is said they are "not divided. Thus, up to... [text ends].
Regarding the "boundary" (*sīmā*), there are also two points of interpretation. First, the passage from the *Āraṇyaka* is cited to provide an indirect clarification.
Second, the section beginning with "Therefore we know" establishes the meaning of the "village" (*grāma*) by citing the text from the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, chapter fifty-three. It states:

"If a bhikṣu begins to construct a monastery in a forest hermitage (*āraṇyaka*) where no village exists, and the boundary has not yet been demarcated, within what distance is it designated as a 'boundary'? The answer is: "One *krośa* on each side."

And so forth. If it is said that there is no village or *araṇya* (wilderness) and one first establishes a monastic dwelling (*saṃghārāma*), then we know that the characteristics of a courtyard have not yet existed;
thus, one returns to the wilderness empty-handed. If one intends to establish a monastic dwelling here for the first time, one must first demarcate the boundary (*sīmā*).

This clearly shows that if a monastic dwelling already exists, it is identical to the boundary of a village and is not an *araṇya*. Regarding the statement "the Vinaya says 'assemble the Saṃgha'," there are also two [points].

My intention is as follows: First, I have distinguished that the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the two types [of boundaries] are not different; second, I must necessarily conclude by returning to the *araṇya*.

According to this Vinaya, within the precept against stealing, the four characteristics of a village boundary (*grāma-sīmā*) are explained: first, a perimeter enclosed by a wall; second, a perimeter enclosed by a fence or hedge;

third, a perimeter where the fence or wall is incomplete; and fourth, a perimeter surrounded by buildings. Later, in the section on the precept regarding being separated from one's robes, the four characteristics of a monastery (*saṃghārāma*) are explained.

This refers to what was previously stated in the section on the precept against stealing. Since the village of Nalanda is cited here, one should know that the two boundaries are not distinct. This passage is cited as proof:
provided that the four boundary markers (*catur-lakṣaṇa*) completely surround the *araṇya*, it is identical to the characteristics of a village (*grāma*).

If they can be clearly distinguished, the assembly must be convened based on these four markers; there is no need for a distance of five *li*. If the characteristics of the *araṇya* are destroyed, one must instead convene the Saṃgha based on the [village] boundary.
[The subject] incurs the fault of ignorance on their own part; the meaning is as explained in the preceding introduction.

Regarding the second section, "That Which Cannot Be Discerned," there are two parts: first, establishing the definitive measure; second, calculating and refuting errors by analogy with the common characteristics below.
First recitation: Regarding the phrase "if it reaches the *āmra* tree," according to the eighth section of the *Cīvara-vastu*, this is called the boundary of the *āmra* tree.
When the Buddha was in Śrāvastī, there was a brāhmaṇa who asked the Buddha about the method for planting the *āmra* tree.
The Buddha answered him; having shown it, he departed. At that time, Upāli asked: "If there is a location, such as a city, town, or village..."

Regarding the "indefinable boundary": if one wishes to perform a formal act (*karmavācanā*), to what extent must it be measured so that it is called a properly performed act, such that the members of the community see one another and the act is accomplished without the fault of performing it separately from the assembly? The Buddha said:
"The measure of a bow is five cubits; seven bows make the distance for planting one *āmra* tree. At a distance of seven trees apart, one may perform the formal act."
This is called a properly performed *karmavācanā*. Although the members of the assembly see one another from different positions, there is no offense of a separate assembly (*pṛthag-saṃgha*).

This differs from the previous interpretation. Regarding the "seven intervals of sixty-three and a half paces," the author of the *Chao* (the *Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā-ṭīkā*) calculates this as seven trees, six intervals, and sixty-three paces;
it does not agree with the interpretations of former scholars. For instance, Master Ruoyuan, in his commentary on the *Qishijinglü*, also provides [an interpretation of] six...

Calculating the intervals, the *Sifen shu* (Commentary on the Four-Part Vinaya) cites the text of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* and erroneously marks seven intervals, stating they are seventy-three paces and a half.
If one refers to the rules for the four-part robe (*catur-amśa-cīvara*), it says there are eight trees and seven intervals, which likewise amounts to seventy-three paces and a half.

Thus, we know this is the *Shouyong chao* (Manual of Practice). Therefore, the *Jiemoluoshi* (Commentary on the Karmavācanā) states: "The former calculation of seventy-three paces and a half was an error in counting the seven intervals. The *Seng* [text]...

In the *Jishu* (Commentary on the *Shisong*), it states that there are seven trees and six intervals, just as in the case of the four-part robe boundary (*caturbhāga-sīmā*) which has eight trees but is calculated as having only seven intervals.
How can it be that in the monastic boundary (*saṃgha-sīmā*), there are seven trees rather than six intervals? Some who cling to the old view say:

"The trees mark both ends, each having its own sphere of influence (*prabhāva*). Therefore, each is divided in half, and thus there are still seven intervals. Furthermore, another master says: "It is like planting trees in a circle..."

The moon has a halo; thus there are seven intervals. Furthermore, changing the *Saṃghāṭī* robe from "seven trees" (*sapta-vṛkṣa*) to "eight trees" (*aṣṭa-vṛkṣa*)—this self-indulgence of mine involves excessive and forced interpretation.
Where is there actually a tree? One simply uses the measurement of a tree as a convention. The Vinaya accords with worldly circumstances, employing such metaphors to manifest the meaning.

The second section on *araṇya* (forest hermitages) has two parts: first, a general indication of its distinctions; second, "Now, to clarify... and below, which restricts it to the specific school’s tenet.
Regarding the phrase "second, clarifying the actual matter," Mount Ling says: the sound of the Sanskrit original is *āraṇya*, also called *lianruo*.
*Ā* means "non-" and *raṇya* means "matter. This refers to a place that is secluded and free from affairs. As for "even of many kinds": [text follows].

Fazheng says: This Vinaya has six kinds. First, regarding *dhūta* (ascetic practice): it refers to the slander of precepts and the refinement [of conduct]; "refinement" is shared with the others. Second, regarding "storing robes":
among the thirty rules, there is no fixed limit for days when storing robes; other circumstances allow for six nights, which is the *araṇya* (wilderness) storage of robes.
Third, regarding the rule against stealing: the text says "in a secluded place," which is the *araṇya* of the stealing rule. Fourth, the monastic boundary (*sīmā*). That is—

Regarding the establishment of the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*): it is for the purpose of assembling the Saṃgha within a radius of five *li*. As for the "five-clothing boundary" (*pañca-cīvara-sīmā*), this refers to the following:

the *araṇya* (forest) protection, the seven intervals, and so forth. Regarding the "six difficult circumstances," these refer to those mentioned in the *Pratideśanīya* [offenses], such as remote locations, places of terror, and places of fear or difficulty.
This refers to the precept regarding receiving food in an araṇya (forest hermitage).

The detailed analysis of the text has two parts: first, the absence of difficulties; second, the presence of difficulties. Regarding the phrase "provisionally reaching the [section on] concentration," this means that the current discussion primarily analyzes the *saṃgha-sīmā* (monastic boundary), while other matters will be explained subsequently as they arise.
Huayan states: "It is like the dhūta [practices]; it follows the section on theft within the Dhūta-piṭaka."

Regarding the "explanation according to the characteristics" (*suxiang*), matters such as the robe-boundary (*cīvarasīmā*) and difficult circumstances are explained according to the thirty characteristics; hence it is called "according to.

As for the single boundary of the *araṇya* (forest hermitage) being indefinite across various schools, this means that while all clarify it is one *krośa*, its size is not fixed; most say the monastic boundary (*saṃghasīmā*) is one *krośa*.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations Vinaya), fascicle 22, states: "When the bhikṣus were in a secluded place without a village, they first established [the boundary]."
Regarding the monastic quarters (*saṃghārāma*) before the boundary has been formally established: at that time, how large should the boundary be? The Buddha said: "One *krośa* square.
Within this area, one must not perform separate *poṣadha* ceremonies or separate *karman* (formal acts). The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* also states: "The monastic boundary is one *krośa*.
The *Karman-sūtra* commentary says: "All schools state it is a *krośa*. 'Indeterminate' means that its small or large dimensions are not fixed."
The *Karmavācanā-vyākhyā* states: "Large [distances] are like those in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, which is two thousand bow-lengths; one bow-length is five cubits (*hasta*).

Small [distances] are like those in the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*, which is five hundred bow-lengths; one bow-length is four cubits. Thus, the *Mahāsāṃghika* distance is too far, while the *Sarvāstivāda* distance is too near.
If one follows the 'hearing the sound of a drum' [criterion], then since drums come in various sizes, the distance at which the sound is heard would vary accordingly."
In the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, one *krośa* is [equivalent to] □□ *li* □□; this is simply ten *li*.
Because the various schools hold differing views, we now take the first fascicle of the *Ratnakaraṇḍa-sūtra*, which states: "One *krośa* is, in the language of Qin (Chinese), five *li*."
It is traditionally said that this was used for *samādhi*. Ke said: "The eighth fascicle [of the *Sifen lü*], translated by Ji Jiaye and Tanyao during the Later Wei dynasty.
In the second [section], there are two difficult passages. First, the determination of the measure; second, the calculation of the number below. The first chant states:
'If it reaches eight inches, it is because there is someone who does not agree, so one should gather seven *pāṇḍa*s as an agreement. As for the time of the formal act (*karmavācanā*):"

However, regarding the area occupied by the Sangha’s seating, when performing the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*), one must not establish a boundary (*sīmā*) where the ritual cannot be performed; this is because the water is shallow and its boundaries are difficult to discern.

Now, it is possible to establish the meaning by demarcating the boundary according to the shore, as in the case of the five locations on an island mentioned in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*. Based upon...
The two sides are marked and bound; within the water, one may take a distance of three *yojanas*, as one desires to cross over and emerge from the boundary.

This is clearly evidenced by the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Sifen lü), which states that if rivers merge, they may be bound together. Thus, the *Five Hundred Questions* (*Wubai wen*) says: "One may perform the binding while staying on a boat in the water."

The second section, the general discussion of the two realms, consists of two parts: first, the heading; second, from "If there are three... onwards, the explanation. Regarding the phrase "Now, as for the essence":

above, the three types of ritual procedures (*karmavācanā*) and the four types of natural occurrences were each explained individually; now, these ritual procedures are gathered together to discuss their essence in terms of their squareness or roundness—this constitutes the first point.
The four types of natural occurrences are likewise treated in this manner—this constitutes the second point. Therefore, it is so stated.

The commentary consists of two parts: first, establishing the fixed characteristics of the ritual; second, from "If one discusses... onwards, distinguishing the characteristics of the natural and the indeterminate.

Regarding the phrase "if it reaches a corner," there are three types of ritual procedures: those with a *śīma-kuṭi* (precept enclosure) and a *mahā-sīmā* (great boundary), those without a *śīma-kuṭi* and a *mahā-sīmā*, and the three small boundaries (*kṣudra-sīmā*).
These refer to boundaries established according to the specific location, which are indeterminate as to whether their substance is square or circular.

Regarding the two types within "natural" (*svabhāva*), the first is a general enumeration; the second, beginning with "If in a village," is a detailed explanation. The phrase "if it reaches a fixed [boundary]" generally enumerates what is not fixed.
If it is something that can be distinguished, it takes the characteristics of a village as its natural substance.

Therefore, it is not fixed as either square or round; it cannot be defined as the four cardinal directions or the four intermediate points. If there were a distinct boundary, it would then be pointed.

Since this is so, all other cases are likewise; they are explained extensively in measureless detail. Next, [the distinctions] are analyzed according to the realms of rebirth (*gati*). This involves both specific and general oppositions.

That is to say, "specific" refers to distinguishing from other realms, while "general" applies to the human realm. Because it specifically distinguishes from others, one may form a mistaken perception or doubt regarding the object as being different.

These instances of mistaken perception regarding the object and so forth are narrower in scope than the preceding state. Since this is so for the human realm, all others are likewise. Next, [the analysis] is applied to non-sentient things (*asattva*), following the same principle.

It is as explained previously; however, the objects differ and so forth, being even more restricted than before. This is explained by analogy according to the breadth or narrowness among the five [factors].

Regarding the statement that "the two *maṇḍala* [intentions] both possess four," this refers to cases where there is no difference in the object (*viṣaya-viśeṣa*) but there is either a mistaken perception (*saṃjñā*) or doubt (*vicikitsā*).

Because the mind is broad and inclusive, and the intention is without limitation, whatever the quality of the object—superior or inferior—it is all part of the original intent. Even if, at the time of the act, one encounters a different condition, it does not constitute a difference in the object or the like; rather, it is a subsequent error.

Section on Errors. Generally speaking, what is termed "erroneous application" (*cāsa*) refers to a state of mind characterized by confusion and error. When explained in general terms according to the specific circumstances, the distinctions between them are difficult to discern.

However, when defined by their names, the respective cases differ. For example, if two objects are clearly distinct and one has no intention to harm the other, yet the action nonetheless results in an error, this is termed "error" (*cāsa*).

Conversely, if there is only a single object, and one easily shifts focus toward it while intending to act upon another, yet commits an offense due to that mental state, this is termed [an intentional transgression].

This constitutes an error. Once one understands the distinctions between errors, they are distinguished in relation to the seven [types of] discerners. However, regarding the seven preparatory stages (*prayoga*), there is no error whatsoever.

Even if an error occurs while accomplishing a task in relation to the object, it still does not constitute a fault; how much less so could an error exist within the stage of preparation? Alternatively, even if an error were possible, although it would not be a fault in terms of its difference [from the intended], it would nonetheless be a discrepancy regarding the primary object.

Therefore, [the first of the four... (Note: The text appears to be a commentary on the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* or a related treatise concerning the nature of error (*viparyāsa*) in the context of meditative practice and the distinction between objects.)
There are twelve types. Regarding the locations, they apply to two realms; the ritual procedures are either formal or spontaneous.
In one location there are twelve types, and in two locations there are twenty-four. Regarding the persons, they apply to the five assemblies, from bhikṣus down to śrāmaṇerīs.

In one assembly there are twenty-four types, and thus the five assemblies constitute one hundred and twenty types of *an-guo* (rainy-season retreat). This is merely according to traditional transmission; however, if one follows [the Vinaya]...

The *Karmavācanā-vyākhyā* (Commentary on the Ritual Procedures) consists of two hundred and ten types. The commentary states: "Regarding the *pratideśanīya* (confession before another), the *manasikāra* (mental recitation), the *smṛti-lupta-siddhi* (accomplishment through forgetting), and the *sīmā* (boundary), these are further divided into seven.

The first three are not subdivided; regarding the boundaries, there are four, because the *ārāma-sīmā* (monastery boundary) and the *grāma-sīmā* (village boundary) each have both double and single [applications].
Using these seven methods, when applied to the three times, they become twenty-one; multiplying this by the two boundaries results in...

Forty-two. By multiplying these five groups by this [number], one arrives at two hundred and ten types of *an-gio* (rainy-season retreat). These two sections of text are both the core intent of the *Chao* (the *Shibunritsu Shō*).
Regarding the passage "The Buddha ordained the five groups, etc. in the *Shibunritsu* (Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya), a question is raised: "The Buddha ordained the *an-gio* for the five groups;

while this may apply to *śrāmaṇeras* who possess the precepts, what of the two groups of *śrāmaṇeras* who lack the precepts? Should they also observe the retreat? The answer is: "Those who have left the household life..."
Their status is identical. To incur public censure and equal blame would obstruct the cultivation of the Path; therefore, remaining settled [in one place] is without fault.

Thus, the Vinaya prescribes three periods for wandering and establishes the rules for the non-observance of the summer retreat (*varṣā*) as offenses for the five groups of practitioners. Question: Why is it that the five groups count the years of their full ordination (*upasaṃpadā*), whereas the three groups do not? Answer:

Because the Great Precepts (*mahāśīla*) involve a distinction in rank between teacher and disciple, and because they require a defined period of dependence (*niśraya*) and formal instruction (*avavāda*).

The Bhikṣuṇīs and the other three lower assemblies do not [calculate] it; therefore, they do not count the years. Thus, in the *Vastu* on Dwellings (*Śayanāsana-vastu*), for the three lower assemblies and others, the sequence is determined by the year of birth, rather than taking the reception of the ten precepts as the basis for seniority.
The second section has two parts. First, it generally demonstrates that the intent of the two dharmas regarding ancient and modern times, or earlier and later periods, is the same.
Second, "forgetting and establishing" and below, it specifically distinguishes how the two dharmas differed in terms of their opening and closing dates in ancient times.

Regarding the phrase "approximating the day," it begins from the sixteenth day of the fourth month and ends on the sixteenth day of the fifth month; the presence of an intercalary month is easy to discern. These two dharmas are [observed] in both ancient and modern times.

Second, regarding the difficulty of moving during the summer retreat: since this is a fixed restriction, from the day one first departs to seek a secure location elsewhere, if one has not yet found such a place and returns, even if they have spent the night away, it is not termed negligence;
it does not constitute a breach of the *anvaya* (summer retreat), nor does it invalidate a prior breach. However, if a dwelling place is obtained, [the retreat is maintained].
The summer retreat rules (varṣā-dharma) follow one wherever one goes; there is no need to formally extend the retreat. Once the preceding period is completed, one may not depart arbitrarily.

According to this principle, even if one moves the summer retreat due to two kinds of difficult circumstances, it is established based on the original boundary. Regarding that which requires both the circumstance and the formal procedure (dharma):

the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* states, "Since I am unable to return, if there is now a circumstance for generating goodness and extinguishing evil, one should immediately perform the formal procedure for receiving [an extension of] the days. Therefore, it is said: "and the dharma."

Furthermore, the second section has two parts. First, it cites three Vinayas and two treatises to prove that [the monk] may depart, though it does not explicitly state that he may remain for the summer retreat (*varṣā*).

Second, from "The *Māyī*" onwards, it cites three Vinayas and one treatise to verify that the acceptance of robes is permitted; logically, this also applies to remaining for the summer retreat. As for the statement in the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* regarding "attaining... [it refers to this].

Regarding "one who departs," the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: A bhikṣu, having insufficient coarse food, thought to himself, "I am observing the rains retreat here, yet the coarse food is insufficient.

He informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "In view of these circumstances, I permit you to break [the retreat]; there is no offense. Subsequently, in the text concerning frequent coming and going, it says:
"If one sees a king, a person of noble rank, or even parents and relatives, whether they are in distress or joy, one should fear that the resolve for the Path will be lost."
It is also like this. To grant permission to break the *anvaya* (the summer retreat) is equivalent to shifting the summer retreat. Regarding "suffering and joy":

Master Li says that gathering with one's kin, seeing them off, celebrating auspicious occasions, or receiving official appointments are called the "joy of relatives. If one is suddenly beset by the calamity of bandits and must lodge a complaint, this is the "suffering of relatives.
Hearing that permission to break the *anvaya* is granted, there is no offense. As for the detailed explanation of the eight difficulties (*aṣṭāvaraṇa*): if a king seizes [one’s property]...

The dwelling place; or being driven into service by those who have left the household life—these are called "difficulties from kings. As for "thieves," they are those who plunder and steal one's robes and bowl.
As for "people," they are relatives and acquaintances who entice and lead one away from the path, or entice and lead one toward evil—these are called "difficulties from people.
Ghosts, spirits, celestial demons, and the hosts of dragons—all of whom are capable of creating obstacles—are called "difficulties from non-humans. The earth...
Within it there is a hidden treasure. Knowing that such an object exists, one will inevitably give rise to a covetous mind; if one takes it, it constitutes a grave offense.
Or, if one dwells near a place where there is much buying, selling, and trade, seeing this may give rise to greed and lead to the commission of a major transgression;

this is called a "difficulty regarding the holy life" (*brahmacarya-vighna*). As for the term *mātṛka-śrāmaṇera*, the Master says: *mātṛkā* refers to the *Vinaya-mātṛkā* and so forth; this is translated as "mother."
This is because it can give rise to wisdom. *Lì* states: "The *mātṛkā* (matrix) principles constitute the foundation of the teaching;

that is to say, all treatises (*śāstra*) are able to generate the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), and since the treatise is the foundation of meaning, it is so called. There was a disciple of a non-Buddhist sect who had gone forth into the Buddha’s Dharma.
His kinsmen among the non-Buddhists said, "Why have you abandoned the path of an Arhat to go forth among the Śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas? You must return and take it up again.
They further said, "If he hears of this, he might perhaps flee; for the Śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas, do not break their *anvāsa* (rainy-season retreat) until the summer has passed."

"Go and fetch it; you will certainly obtain it, have no doubt. Upon hearing this, he did not know what to do and informed the Buddha. The Buddha permitted him to break his *anvāya* (the summer retreat).
That bhikṣu then traveled from one residence to another, not knowing where he should receive his share of the offerings for the *anvāya*.
He informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said: "If you have stayed for more days at a particular place, you should receive your share there. If, however, [the time spent] at both..."
Regarding the phrase "at the place of residence on the day [of the *pravāraṇā*]," etc., this means that each person takes half of the portion of the robe-cloth.

Below the section on those who have broken the *anvaya* (the retreat), the author of the *Chao* establishes a logical argument to prove that one who has shifted their summer retreat is permitted to receive robe-cloth at two locations, even taking the cloth at the place of the *pravāraṇā*.

This is because, according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, one who has broken the *anvaya* is not entitled to a share of the cloth; yet, since it is now clearly permitted for them to take it, we know for certain that they have successfully completed the summer retreat.

This section explains the meaning of the gains and losses regarding the formal acts (*karmas*). There are four points: 1. The first point concerns being restricted to the *mahā-sīmā* (great boundary). If one enters another [area] while remaining within it, the act is broken. 2.

The second point concerns if one relies on the area below the *mahā-sīmā*, such as a monastery (*ārāma*) outside the boundary; traveling there does not break the act. 3. The third point concerns if one relies on the area below, such as a monastery within the boundary; upon leaving the monastery and entering the boundary, the act is lost. 4.

The fourth point concerns the fundamental rule that, provided one remains within the boundary throughout the course of action, the act is not broken. The passage states: "If one relies on the *mahā-sīmā*... up to "...it is broken."

Regarding "summer" (*grīṣma*): Fazheng states that this refers to the essential mind of relying on a great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) for the rains retreat (*varṣa*). If one enters the ordination platform (*sīmā-maṇḍala*), it acts as an internal partition.
Regarding "natural" and other small boundaries (*kṣudra-sīmā*), Cizong states that these are still part of the great boundary used for gathering the Sangha;
they are called "small" only in relation to the encompassing great boundary because they lie within its perimeter. This, then, constitutes a loss [of the retreat] from the outside toward the inside.
As for the statement, "If one relies on [the monastery] until later," this means that the *ārāma* (monastery) is broad while the boundary (*sīmā*) is narrow.
Having originally completed the summer retreat (*varṣa*) based on the *ārāma*, one subsequently establishes a *dharmasīmā* (Dharma-boundary) that is smaller than the *ārāma*.

Because it is still called the original essential site, one may travel between this *ārāma* and that boundary without violating the rules of the summer retreat. The commentary states: "The establishment of the summer retreat comes first, and the establishment of the boundary comes later."—Lín.

The *Yun-chao* states the essential meaning: "If there is a *sīmā* (monastic boundary), one must rely upon that *sīmā*; relying on the monastery (*ārāma*) is not established. Therefore, the subsequent text says:
"Because the Buddha prescribed reliance upon the *sīmā*. In the *Jie-mo-su* (Karmavācanā-vyākhyā), it is permitted to take either the monastery or the *sīmā*, depending solely on one's intention.
Regarding the phrase "if one relies on [the monastery], it is also thus," the *Zhong-zhong* states: "This means that while the *dharmadhātu* is vast, the monastery is small. If the original..."
