At this time, [the text] distinguishes the different procedures for monks and nuns regarding the method for nuns to come and request absolution (*pravāraṇā*). There are four parts: first, the arrangement of the location and the measurement of the time;
second, the formal procedure for the nuns to face the Sangha and perform *pravāraṇā*; third, the announcement to the nuns regarding the rules and ritual forms;
fourth, the method for returning to the temple and transmitting the notification. Regarding the phrase "one chant" and "three times to the dharma," it does not [apply].

The *Poṣadha* must be recited together. Regarding the inquiry as to whether there are any *bhikṣuṇīs* present, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "At the time of reciting the *Poṣadha*, one asks, 'Who has sent the *bhikṣuṇīs*?
This regulation requires that one inquire [beforehand] so as to appoint someone to go and instruct them; thus, the assembly of lay *bhikṣuṇīs* remains pure, and both parties benefit.

As for the current *Pravāraṇā*, it simply involves the *bhikṣuṇīs* coming to request that the *saṃgha* point out their transgressions. The Sage did not establish a rule requiring an inquiry as to whether they will come or not.
Therefore, there is no need to inquire further. As for the case of separate procedures, this is clarified in the *Bie xing pian* (Chapter on Separate Conduct) for the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha.

Regarding the timing of the *pravāraṇā* previously explained, when discussing the ritual procedure (*vidhi*), it is generally applicable over three days; it is not strictly required that the monks perform it on the fourteenth day and the nuns on the fifteenth.
Rather, one may simply fix the date as the sixteenth, suspend the monks’ *pravāraṇā*, and wait for the nuns to offer their confession of faults; this is also permissible.
Subsequently, according to the Vinaya text, it is further set forth on another day.

The second section has two parts: first, the formal clarification of the nun coming before the Saṃgha to request absolution for her offense; second, from "The Question" onwards, the general resolution of objections.

Regarding the statement "Now, as for the demonstration," the remainder is the same as previously demonstrated; that is to say, just as the great assembly remained silent for a long time, [the Buddha] then commanded the nuns and so forth.

...Furthermore, within the question-and-answer section there are two parts: first, the question; second, the answer. The first is as in the text. The answer-text has three sections: first, answering by establishing the principle; second, "Therefore, in the Vinaya...

and below, proving it through the authority of this specific school (*nikāya*); third, "The *Mahāsāṃghika*... and below, citing it as a standard. Regarding the statement "The answer reaches the point of doubt": [it refers to] the single proclamation.

It follows the *Śrāmaṇerakārikā*. Tomorrow, when the nuns arrive, the monks shall request an instructor to deliver the teaching from among the senior monks (*sthavira*) of the great assembly, which is then to be proclaimed back to the community of nuns.
If there are nuns who do not come, their *chanda* (consent) must be declared; this monastic rule should be applied accordingly without doubt. Regarding the phrase "because of the five [categories]":

as for "grave offenses," the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states that these refer to the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (formal meetings) offenses; they are considered grave in comparison to the lower categories, but this does not mean...

This is the *yī* (the *yī* [monk]). However, regarding the appointment of a *bhikṣuṇī*, one may only appoint a single *bhikṣuṇī* through formal ritual (*karmavācanā*), while the remaining *bhikṣuṇīs* are appointed as companions by verbal designation.

Regarding the fourth section, which clarifies the abbreviated explanations, there are two parts: first, the actual clarification of the abbreviated explanation; second, from "The above... onwards, the general conclusion.

As for the preceding four sections, according to the underlying principle, it would also not be appropriate to divide them here; however, this was done for the sake of the second gate within the *Chao* (the *Nanhai Jigui Neifa Zhuan*).
This is divided into two sections to prevent confusion among readers; however, following the fourth gate, the preceding section is concluded and the subsequent one is introduced.

For now, the division follows the text itself. The first part has two sub-sections: first, explaining the method for the *pravāraṇā* (self-examination) within the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) during times of the eight difficulties or other circumstances;

second, explaining the method for establishing a small boundary (*khuḍḍaka-sīmā*) for the *pravāraṇā* when hindered by inferior or wicked bhikṣus. Within the former of these two, the eight difficulties are first raised; "time" and "heat" are treated briefly.

The conditions for this are as follows. Second, "In the present day" and below correctly clarifies the abbreviated method. Regarding the phrase "the four... etc.," the remaining conditions for the eight difficulties are all as previously explained in the section on the precepts.
The second section has two parts. First, a brief explanation of the method regarding those possessing the five virtues. Second, from "If there are thieves...

onwards, a brief explanation of the method not regarding those possessing the five virtues. Regarding the first of these two: first, the actual clarification of the method for the abbreviated recitation; second, from "Now, perhaps...

onwards, the classification and discernment of what is correct and incorrect. As for the phrase "one should proceed to the *pravāraṇā*," Ke said: according to the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, when performing the abbreviated recitation in relation to those possessing the five virtues, there is...

To speak again is to speak twice. The current commentary does not clarify this "speaking again. Regarding the *vinaya* rule on "whispering": this clarifies the aforementioned "speaking once," which was intended for the great assembly to hear and know.
Because the group of six monks whispered rapidly during the *pravāraṇā*, the Buddha declared it to be contrary to the Dharma.

Regarding the phrase "now, as for 'arriving,' etc.," there are three points of intent. First, it describes what constitutes an improper form. Second, under the section on the *Vinaya*, it cites the *Vinaya* to demonstrate what is improper.

Third, under the section on the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, other schools clarify what is proper. The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* states this; the *Shu-chao* (Commentary) cites the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* to provide realization.

This refers to *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* 27, which says: "One should follow the sequence from the *sthavira* (senior elder), down to the general proclamation, and must not create a sequence in reverse order."

"First" refers to proceeding from the bottom upward, which constitutes the reverse order. Regarding "the manner of serving food": suppose there are ten practitioners seated in a single row, each wearing their robe;
they perform the *paṭimokkha* (self-examination) according to the five virtues, following the method of serving food. Regarding "transcending" in the manner of serving food:
this means not following the sequential order, but passing over the first elder, then passing over the second elder, and taking up the third.
The *Sēngqì* (Four-Part Vinaya) also contains [this], identical to the *Zhì* (Mahīśāsaka). It is not clearly explained. Regarding the "general proclamation," it says:

"All virtuous monks, please grant me the *pravāraṇā* regarding offenses seen, heard, or suspected. This refers to the fact that the text of that Vinaya uses the term "and so forth" (*děng*) to include other matters that are contrary to the Dharma.
The second section, concerning the five virtues, is briefly divided into three parts in the text. First, it clarifies the three methods of preaching.

Second, from "difficult matters approach closer" onwards, it distinguishes the single method of preaching performed twice. Third, from "the fourfold division" onwards, it explains the method of proceeding directly.

Regarding the statement "from the fourfold division to the Dharma," as for the phrase "each respectively facing [another]," it is, for example, like a hundred people forming fifty pairs; each individual person [faces] three [others].

Regarding the statement, "The text is the same as the preceding rule," this refers to the phrasing and sentences. As for the phrase "because the objection has arrived": when the objection is imminent, one performs a formal announcement (*jñapti*) and speaks twice;

if it becomes more urgent, one performs a formal announcement and speaks once. These constitute three types of single announcements (*ekajñapti*), namely: those involving three recitations, two recitations, and one recitation.
This refers to the three *śuddha-śrāvaṇas* (formal announcements). These do not correspond to the five virtues (*pañca-guṇa*). Regarding the statement "from four to departing":
this means that for the sake of the five virtues, one [announcement] is doubled to become two; then, within the assembly, there are three; now, with the single *śuddha-śrāvaṇa*, they total five.

When a sixth difficulty arises, one startslely departs immediately—this constitutes the six types of abbreviations (*saṃkṣepa*). Regarding the statement "from two to -ing," the Vinaya says: "For a monk facing difficulties..."
Having finished bathing, matters such as quickly exiting the boundary together with one's teacher and fellow practitioners are rarely encountered; therefore, they are omitted here.
As for the statement "from above to above," this refers to a division within the second section, intended to prevent later readers from becoming confused by establishing a distinction between them.
The second section clarifies the *pañcavargika-dharma* (the rules concerning groups of five). This is divided according to the second passage of the *Vinayavibhaṅga-vṛtti*;

the lecturer has combined the first division [with this]. Regarding the statement "Next, as for the *dharma*," there are four points: first, a general heading that distinguishes [this case] from others; second, the distinction between the presence and absence of the *dharma* of desire (*chanda*);

third, from the question downward, the distinction between the general and specific differences in appointing persons; fourth, from the taking of the *pravāraṇā* downward, the distinction between the dual and single reception of the *pravāraṇā*. Question: The above...

Question: Six people and five people are both subject to the same monastic rules (*saṃghadharma*). How then can they differ? Answer: The proceedings for five people are not the same as those for six people;

they are distinguished because one fears that [the quorum] might be improperly applied. Below, three points of difference are set forth. If there are six people within the boundary (*sīmā*), one person may convey the *chanda* (consent).
The remaining five constitute a *saṃgha* for the purpose of obtaining the formal act (*karmavācanā*) and appointing the five virtuous ones (*pañca-guṇa*).

If there are five people, one person expresses their consent (*chanda*), while the other four, though they constitute a *saṃgha*, are merely those capable of presiding over the rite. If one were appointed as a virtuous one from among them, the [remaining] three would not constitute a *saṃgha*, and thus they could not provide consent.

Regarding the prohibition against appointing two people and so forth, the author of the *Chao* (the *Nanhai Jigui Neifa Zhuan*) correctly takes this to mean that at the time of the appointment, there must be a *saṃgha* of five.
The essence is simply this: one person may not be appointed; two people cannot be appointed simultaneously because the individuals being appointed do not constitute a quorum.

Since three is not a *saṃgha*, how could they be dispatched? As for "the rest is the same as the previous method," this refers to the fact that prior to the formal accusation, it was already clarified that five persons are required to announce the suspension of the accusation.
Furthermore, regarding the abbreviated procedure when a *bhikṣuṇī* arrives due to difficult circumstances, these are all the same as before.

The second major section, "The Text on the Majority of *Pratimokṣa* Confessions," has two parts. First, explaining the gathering of the saṃgha and the addition of the ritual procedure; second, from "If one commits...

onwards, distinguishing whether there is an offense and whether there is progression toward punishment. Regarding the first part, there are two sub-sections: first, a general explanation that when gathering the saṃgha, one may not receive a proxy consent (*chanda*);

second, from "four persons" onwards, the formal explanation of the characteristics of the ritual procedure for four persons. The first [sub-section] consists of the proclamation and the words "going before [the assembly]," as in the text.

The second section, "Discriminating the Text on the Treatment of Offenses," has two parts: first, for those who have committed a light offense, one confesses and performs the *pravāraṇā* (self-examination) oneself;

second, for those who have committed a grave offense, such as the four [parājika] offenses and below, one discloses the offense and performs the *pravāraṇā*. Regarding the phrase "if one reaches the *pravāraṇā*," it is as stated in the text.

The second section has two parts. First, it briefly presents the principle that there is no disciplinary penalty for the offense committed. Second, "If one follows what comes below," it cites the text to establish the principle that one may still perform the *pravāraṇā* (invitation to admonish).
Regarding the phrase "if it reaches the meaning," Lingshan says: "If one commits a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense) involving four or more [monks]..."
Regarding the prohibition against confession: if one person has committed an offense and there are only three others present, confession cannot be performed.

This is based on the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, which states that a "small group" consists of four people; thus, for offenses of the middle grade of *sthūlātyaya* and above, there is no provision for disciplinary punishment.

However, according to the section on "settling disputes" in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, a small group may consist of two or three people; in this case, confession by a small group for a middle-grade *sthūlātyaya* offense is also permissible. Now, as for what is said here...

Regarding those involving four or more persons, this constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* of the highest grade. As for what it means to "enter into the discourse on *sthūlātyaya*," the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:

"This refers to having committed a *sthūlātyaya* offense and brought it before the Saṃgha; before the formal disciplinary action can be carried out, one is startled by an emergency and rises up. This is called 'entering into the discourse on *sthūlātyaya*.
It means that the offense has already become manifest and is thus described as a transgression within the Teachings; hence it is said to 'enter into the discourse.'"

"Up to and including" (*nai-ji*) means "beyond this" (*yue-yi*). The same applies to the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses; thus, if the assembly is incomplete, there is no principle for administering disciplinary measures.

The second section of the text has two parts: first, according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, one makes a formal announcement (*jñapti*) to suspend [the ceremony] and then performs the *pravāraṇā* later; second, from the *Caturvargika-vinaya* below, it cites an example.
Confessing [one's offenses] makes it appropriate to perform the *pravāraṇā*. Regarding the statement "if one reaches the *pravāraṇā*," Fuyang says:

this refers to cases where, during the *pravāraṇā*, one is accused of having committed grave offenses such as *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. If the assembly is incomplete, the confession cannot be finalized, and the *pravāraṇā* cannot proceed.

Therefore, the matter of confessing the offense is temporarily set aside; because the offense has been brought to light and the assembly has reached a consensus on it, it is similar to a formal confession (*viśuddhi*), whereby the *pravāraṇā* may be performed.
In the second section, citing examples, there are three parts: first, presenting the example; second, from "The principle requires... onwards, demonstrating the method of confession (*pratikarma*);

and third, from "In this context... onwards, distinguishing the offense for non-truthfulness. Regarding the first part, there are two intentions. First, citing the example. Second, from "Since both...

onwards, reconciling and explaining the single proclamation. As for the statement "From four [points] up to the hindrance," the *Fǔpiān* states: "The *Chāo* cites this text to use it as an analogy for the *Pravāraṇā* ceremony. Fuyang..."
It is said: Once the *poṣadha* (recitation of the precepts) has been completed by means of confession, one may hear the precepts even if the offense has not yet been expiated.

During the *pravāraṇā* (invitation for criticism), one may participate in the *pravāraṇā* even if the offense has not yet been expiated after having been formally charged. Since both are pure practices, the *poṣadha* prevents non-virtues that have not yet arisen, while the *pravāraṇā* prevents faults already committed;
because their function in preventing transgressions is identical, both are pure practices. Furthermore, both the *poṣadha* and the *pravāraṇā* are [pure].
Regarding the various dharmas: the merit of gathering the Saṃgha is equal; regarding the delimitation of the boundary, all must assemble; the merit of the disciplinary punishment is equal;

those who have committed an offense may not hear the *śīla* (precepts), and those who have committed an offense may not perform the *pravāraṇā* (self-examination). Since the *pravāraṇā* may be applied by analogy to the recitation of the *śīla*, what harm would there be in using it?

As for the statement "the principle is ultimately pure," this refers to the one who has committed the offense, indicating the wording of the recitation. The *Fǔpiān* says: "Two or three people [perform the rite] themselves..."

Regarding those who, during the *pravāraṇā*, incur a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense: they should say, "May the two virtuous ones attend to me with one mind," or simply say, "Virtuous one, please attend to me with one mind.
I, bhikṣu [Name], have committed such-and-such a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense. Because the assembly was incomplete, I have not yet received its formal treatment;
the rest of the community is pure. This follows the procedure for the *poṣadha*. Furthermore, at the time of the *pravāraṇā*, if each individual has an offense...
Each [monk] shall state the name of the offense. Once the disclosure is complete, one may also perform the *pravāraṇā*. Regarding the phrase "this has arrived," there are two meanings:

first, it clarifies that if the offense is not truthful, the transgression is grave; second, it distinguishes this from the following cases, where silent falsehood incurs a light offense. As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:

In reality it is impure, yet one claims it is pure in the presence of others; therefore, this is a deliberate falsehood (*mṛṣāvāda*). There are three types of objects [of such speech], and for each, three *thullaccaya* offenses are incurred.
This differs from the case of silent deception during the *poṣadha* ceremony, where one merely incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.

The third [section] concerns the mental recitation (*manasikāra*) by a single person; it has two parts. First, the presentation of the procedure for acting at will (*yathāsukham*). Second, "If one commits... and below, regarding whether the confession and treatment should be performed.

Regarding the first of these two, there is first the origin story (*nidāna*) concerning the gathering of the Saṃgha. Second, "If there is no... and below, the addition of the ritual formula for mental recitation. One recites once. As for the statement "If it reaches the point of being explained," it is according to the text.

The second section has two parts. First, it clarifies that one may perform the *pravāraṇā* after having completed the repentance for light offenses. Second, regarding the phrase "if one commits [an offense] below" and so forth:
if one has committed a grave offense, should one undergo treatment and repentance? One response states: "If it reaches the former [category]," the *Fǔpiān* says:

"For offenses from *sthūlātyaya* upward, if there is no one to face, there is no sense of repentance; furthermore, one cannot disclose them alone. Therefore, one should not perform the *pravāraṇā*. This is based on the underlying principle.

Thus it is. Regarding the phrase "the remainder follows the former," the intent of the *Chao* (Excerpts) is as follows: according to the section on the formal announcement of the *Poṣadha* (*śīla-saṃghāta*) by mental recitation, that text states:
"Some say 'to confess' (*praticchādana*), others say 'to wait for others'. The *Lingshan* commentary explains: "As for 'waiting for others,' this refers to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* text, which says:
'If no guests arrive, one should form a thought: "If I obtain a pure bhikṣu, this offense shall be removed in accordance with the Dharma. Having formed this thought, [one's] mind..."

One should recite this mentally. Second, regarding the two ways of proclaiming the *poṣadha*: that [text] further cites the *Pañcaśata-praśna-śāstra*, which states that one should confess before the Saṃgha of the four directions with palms joined, and subsequently recite the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* in detail.
Both of these methods are dharmas for the purification of conduct; their efficacy in subduing and regulating [the practitioner] is equal.

Furthermore, one must first state the offenses committed, while declaring the remainder to be pure. Only then does one perform the *pravāraṇā* (self-invitation) by means of mental recollection and verbal expression, repeating it three times.
Question: How is it known that the remainder depends on what precedes it? Is it because one simply adopts the preceding text for the mental recollection of the *poṣadha* (confession of precepts)?
Answer: In the *Jīemoluosū* (Karmavācanā-vyākhyā), within the section on the method of mental recollection, it is largely the same as the procedure for the *poṣadha*.

The third major section: Miscellaneous Clarifications on Characteristics. This text contains eleven segments. First, it clarifies the differences between the formulas for communal (*saṃgha*) and individual (*pṛthak*) [recitations].

Second, following the question regarding whether one may recite the precepts after the *pravāraṇā* has concluded, it distinguishes whether the recitation of precepts is permitted once the *pravāraṇā* is finished.

Third, following the question regarding whether one may hear the *pravāraṇā*, it addresses whether those who have not yet received full ordination may listen to the *pravāraṇā*. Fourth, following the passage in the Vinaya stating that after the communal and individual recitations are completed, there are further arrivals...

1. Regarding the re-explanation of whether one may enter [the boundary] again; 2. Below the question regarding the fifteenth day, distinguishing whether one may leave the boundary after the *pravāraṇā* on the fifteenth day of the seventh month;
3. Below the question regarding the earlier retreat (*pūrvavarṣā*), clarifying whether those who observe the later retreat (*paścimavarṣā*) receive their share of robes;
4. Below the question regarding the single recitation, explaining the absence of difficult circumstances (*an-āpatti*).
Is it briefly explained as being accomplished? Ninth, "The Four Parts Below" concerns the methods for instructing the ignorant, whether young or old.

Tenth, "The Question on the Boundary Below" distinguishes between the sequence of installation and the practice of acting according to the majority. Eleventh, "The Question on the Rains Retreat Below" explains whether one may depart from the location once the summer retreat is completed.
Regarding the phrase "reaching the Sangha," it refers to those who possess the authority to discipline and reprove; this clarifies the *pravāraṇā* (self-examination) procedure of the Sangha.

If one is accused of a *pārājika* offense, they shall be immediately entombed and abandoned; those who have committed residual offenses (*śeṣa*) may undergo the six-night *parivāsa* (probation) and other procedures for the expiation of offenses, extending even to *sthūlātyaya* and *duṣkṛta*.
All such cases may be subject to disciplinary treatment. Regarding the requirement that a quorum be met by visiting monks, as stated in the preceding text:

if the number reaches twenty, all may be treated accordingly; this refers to cases where the quorum is strictly required. However, if there are only six or seven people present, they may still carry out the procedure for the expiation of residual offenses.

Regarding the confession of heavy *thullaccaya* offenses: according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, eight people are required; this [number] is insufficient. Therefore, it is said that while it is possible, it is not necessarily certain that one will attain [the purification].

Although there may be individuals who have undergone disciplinary measures (*kamma*) or formal acts of censure (*tajjanīya-kamma*), if the governance and treatment are not yet complete—for instance, if it concerns a *pācittiya* or *dukkaṭa* offense—one may receive disciplinary punishment.

However, if it concerns a *pārājika*, *saṅghādisesa*, or a heavy *thullaccaya*, the number of people is too small to perform the confession and treatment; since the matter cannot be fully resolved, it is simply stated as follows:

It is purity. Regarding the statement "inquiring into the ultimate precepts," according to the *Viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī* (or *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*), if five persons perform the *pravāraṇā*, they first recite the *Prātimokṣa* precepts in their entirety.
Next, the first person rises, kneels with palms joined, and requests someone to act as the master for confessing offenses (*āpatti-vinodaka*).

This person is asked to speak of offenses seen, heard, or suspected, and to seek out those same offenses. This so-called "master for confessing offenses" is another name for the one endowed with the five virtues (*pañca-guṇa*) who presides over the *pravāraṇā*.

This refers to the prior recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*). The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Sifen lü), fascicle 37, states: "After the invitation for criticism (*pravāraṇā*), the recitation of the precepts caused exhaustion.
The Buddha said: 'One should not recite the precepts again after the invitation for criticism. The invitation for criticism itself is the recitation of the precepts. Question:

The recitation of the precepts is for the purpose of knowing the characteristics of the precepts (*śīla-lakṣaṇa*) and preventing unarisen transgressions. The invitation for criticism is for purifying body and speech and removing transgressions that have already arisen. Since their respective remedies (*pratipakṣa*) differ, [how can they be the same?]
"What does 'it is the same' mean? Answer: Although there are differences between the "already" and the "not yet," the intent is to bring about purity without distinction;

therefore, it is said that *pravāraṇā* (self-indulgence) is itself the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*). Regarding the phrase "the inquiry has arrived," it is as stated in the text. Regarding the phrase "the Vinaya has reached clarity":

when three more persons arrive, the *saṃgha* performs the *pravāraṇā* according to the Dharma, as previously explained in the section on the procedure for five persons. When two persons arrive, it is likewise the same as the face-to-face method.

[The] Head [of the assembly]. As with the ritual for the four types of persons mentioned above: "Venerable sirs, attend to me with one mind," and so forth, up to the threefold recitation of purity, as well as the formal announcement of the offense and so on, are all as previously described.

Regarding the phrase "from the inquiry until the return": because the night-watch of the fifteenth day has not yet ended, one may only leave the boundary after the appearance of the dawn light (*aruṇa*).
As for "being separated from one's robe," this refers to those who have entered the *pūrvavāsa* (the earlier retreat) and have obtained the *kārttika* [robe].
He enumerates five benefits. Since the summer retreat is not yet over, if one leaves the boundary with one's robes, one has not yet entered the *kārttika* [autumnal] period;

would this not constitute being separated from one's robes? The rest is as stated in the text. Regarding the phrase "asking until one incurs an offense," *Shen* says: The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states that if one is in residence here for the summer retreat, one may receive a formal extension of time (*ādiṣṭa*) to go elsewhere and still perform the *pravāraṇā*.
The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* does not allow this; it states that if one is in residence here for the summer retreat, to perform the *pravāraṇā* elsewhere constitutes a transgression.
Regarding the *Vinaya*: if one receives [an invitation] for a day or a month, one must return by the time of the subsequent *pravāraṇā*. If one does not return, it constitutes an offense.

However, if there are difficulties on the road or if one fears for one's life, it is no offense to perform the *pravāraṇā* there. As for the statement "from inquiry until receiving," the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:

"This is the proper time during which the Saṃgha may accept offerings, without distinguishing between those who have already entered the rainy season retreat (*varṣā*) and those who have not. This applies to both parties.

These boundaries all apply to the universal community of monks (*ekavyavahārika-saṃgha*). As for property present before the assembly (*pratyakṣa-vastu*), it is by no means appropriate to distribute it according to the time [of the season].
Property present before the assembly possesses four characteristics: first, the determination of time; that is, it must have been received on the same day, the sixteenth of the seventh month.

Second is the determination of place (*sthāna-niyama*), which restricts it to those who observe the rains retreat within this specific boundary. Third is the determination of persons (*pudgala-niyama*), which restricts it to those currently residing together as part of the preceding rains retreat.

Fourth is the determination of the rule (*dharma-niyama*), meaning that there is no need to perform a formal ritual (*karmavācanā*); rather, the distribution is made by simply counting the number of people present.
Therefore, it is known that those who enter the later retreat (*paścimā varṣā*) do not receive these items. It is for the sake of the future [monks]. Regarding the recipient, the *Yang* states:

According to the Vinaya text, when those who entered the earlier retreat (*pūrvā varṣā*) travel after the summer is complete, they divide the lodgings at the time of the invitation ceremony (*pravāraṇā*).

May those who entered the later retreat, though their term is not yet full, also receive a share? The Buddha said: "It is permitted; they may receive it for the sake of the future. This expectation remains the same.

One who has completed the summer retreat (*varṣā*) must not accept [an invitation] immediately. Now, regarding the winter quarters (*hemantika-śālā*), those who have entered the later retreat (*paścimikā*) may also receive it, as they are receiving it during the winter season.
Looking from the present toward winter, this is termed "the future. As for the statement "asking until one reaches the appropriate [time]," these words do not leave the lips;
such private, whispered speech is improper. Even if the speech is rapid and others cannot understand it, both are contrary to the Dharma. This concludes the fourth section.
Regarding the phrase "those who have reached [this state]," the text consists of three sections: First, a direct description of how those of young age do not know the Dharma;

second, from "the young" downwards, an explanation based on the fact that even the elderly do not know the Dharma; third, from "therefore, according to the Vinaya" onwards, citing specific cases to prove that although they are old, they may still be subject to the same rules as the young, and that if they remain forgetful and fail to remember, one must have someone else grant them instruction—specifically, having a person of the five virtues (*pañcavarga*) provide the instruction during the *pravāraṇā* ceremony.

This refers to the person who receives the *pravāraṇā* (invitation to point out faults); therefore, they are called those who perform the *pravāraṇā*. Why is this? Is it fitting for an elder to follow the manner of a junior?

Quoting the Vinaya, Ānanda said: "It is because he did not examine [the matter] well; Kāśyapa addressed him as a 'junior. Now, the foolish conduct of an elder—how does it differ from that of a junior?
Thus, he distinguishes them by way of analogy. As for the phrase "inquiring about [the boundaries] and so forth," it refers to within the boundary (*sīmā*).
There are those who observe the earlier and later *varṣā* retreats. They do not understand the principle that the former person follows the latter, and the latter person follows the former;
rather, they argue based on the majority. As stated in the Vinaya: once the Saṃgha has completed the *pravāraṇā*, if more guests arrive, if they are numerous, another *pravāraṇā* must be performed.
To follow the many by means of the few; this case is likewise so. The eleventh section consists of two parts: first, the question; second, the answer.

The first is as stated in the text. Within the answer, there are two parts: first, a direct response that one must depart; second, an expanded explanation [starting from "one less"] regarding the permanent cessation of departure.

There are five types of non-Dharma; the first three concern the initial point: first, citing the offense incurred for not departing according to our own school's tenets; second, [the section starting with] "Vinaya," which examines the presence or absence of conditions.

Thus, one is freed from fault. Regarding the invitation and the location, there are five or three divisions for distinguishing right from wrong. Once the proclamation has been made, the response reaches those who remain.

According to the *Mātṛkā-vinaya*, when a donor invites monks to observe the rains retreat (*varṣā*), and the retreat is concluded, the bhikṣuṇīs do not depart because of their attachment to food and drink.

The donors become weary and dissatisfied. The bhikṣus inform the Buddha, and the Buddha says: "Once the retreat is finished, after one night has passed, the bhikṣuṇīs must leave. This is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.

*Saṃghāvaśeṣa*. In the *Pañcavargika Vinaya*, among the *Naiḥsargika-pāyattika* rules: if one accepts an invitation for a meal and, having finished eating, does not depart, the nun incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. This does not apply to only one summer retreat;

rather, there is no offense if the invitation was made with a general intention (*mānasa-citta*) and was not a formal acceptance of an invitation. "Non-acceptance of an invitation" refers to locations such as within a monastery, mountain caves, and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "increasing by one up to the single virtue," it is as stated in the text.

Second, the *Kathina* robe procedure consists of two parts: first, clarifying the purpose of its introduction; second, citing the name and providing an explanation. First, regarding the purpose of its introduction, the *Avataṃsaka* states:

"Because of the preceding *anvārambhaṇa* (pre-monsoon) retreat, one advances in practice; because of the summer rains retreat (*varṣā*), one has merit; and because of the *pravāraṇā* (invitation to criticism), one is free from fault—this is excellent."

Its resonance spreads far and wide; both internally and externally it is pure and clean, moving the hearts of sentient beings. At such a time, one should accordingly receive the bestowal of blessings.
The Sage opened up five benefits to reward virtue and support merit. Is it not said in the secular world that "those who have merit are rewarded"?
Therefore, this robe should be received once the *pravāraṇā* ceremony is concluded; thus, it has been appended here within this section.
The second section contains two parts: first, the citation of the title; second, the commentary explaining it. Regarding the phrase "From *kā* to *dharma*," this is the citation of the title.

The explanation of the text has two parts: first, the commentary sequentially explains the meaning of the names; second, from "In the midst" onwards, the chapters are opened for detailed explanation. The former consists of two [sub-sections].
First, the explanation based on the treatise; second, the ancient translations below, translated according to ancient meanings.

Of the former four: first is named "Solid" (Kathina); second is "Difficult to Sustain"; third is called "Firm"; and fourth is titled "Shelter. Regarding the first chant, from "Manifesting" to "Covering":
as for "Solid," the *Liaolun shu* (Commentary on the Vinaya-vibhāṣā) states: "The *kathina* robe is that which can move the robes. If one receives the *kathina* robe..."
When there are donors who offer robes, they all belong to this person. This person is able to attract many robes, and the robes do not become worn or ruined;
therefore, he is called "solid and firm" (*kaṭhina*). Furthermore, all solid and firm objects are termed *kaṇa*.

Even when one sees that a person’s afflictions—such as greed, hatred, and delusion—are so powerful that they are stubbornly held and difficult to relinquish, such a person is also called a "person with a *kaṭhina* mind."

Huayan said: "The robes do not suffer decay because one receives the five benefits; consequently, one may possess many extra robes (*cīvara*) without incurring the offense of failing to perform the ritual of *śuddhi* (purification), which is termed 'robes not suffering decay.
Had one not received these robes previously, possessing them beyond the limit would constitute the offense of forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*), which is precisely what is meant by 'decay.
Regarding 'difficulty of livelihood,' the *Lüeshu* (Commentary on the Vinaya-mātṛkā) states: 'A poor person’s means of subsistence...'"
It is short and incomplete. For those who find it difficult to sustain their livelihood, being able to set aside even a small amount to contribute to this robe brings superior merit.

For those who live easily, even if they gather robes as vast as Mount Sumeru to offer as a great gift, [the former is more meritorious]. This is because when the Buddha ordered the making of this robe, he specifically directed that alms be sought from the poor;
thus, it derives its name from the source of the objects recommended for giving. As for "firm," it is not...
Regarding the refutation of this meaning, Huayan asked: "How does this differ from the previous 'solidity'? Lingshan replied:
"The former refers solely to the ability to procure many robes such that the robes do not become damaged; this, however, concerns the absence of transgressions regarding the robes themselves.

The present 'firmness' refers to the absence of transgressions regarding the precepts; because one receives benefits through the robes yet does not violate the five kinds of precepts, the precepts attain firmness."
The *Zhi shu* states: "Because one receives this robe without violating the five precepts, it is called 'firm and solid' (*kaṭhina*). Regarding 'sheltering' (*chādana*'), Master Li says:
because this robe can shelter and cover the five benefits, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* designates it as the 'sheltering robe' (*chādana-cīvara*)."
The second passage has two parts. First, the meanings are reversed. The two meanings of "rewarding the good and punishing the evil" are translated as the *guṇa-cīvara* (robe of merit).

Regarding the statement that it is "ancient" (*gǔ*) and "arrived at" (*zhì*): one who observes the *pūrvavāsa* (early retreat) obtains it, hence it is called a "reward"; one who observes the *paścādvāsa* (late retreat) does not obtain it, hence it is a "punishment. Huayan says:
"It thus brings forth the five benefits of merit" refers to the designation being manifested through its functional efficacy. However, among these five benefits, [one] attains freedom from...

Regarding the "three robes": this does not mean that one may be entirely separated from all three. In the original account of the origin (nidāna), it was only permitted to be separated from the outer robe (saṃghāṭī) because of its weight;
there is no textual allowance for being separated from the other two.

The second section, the opening chapter explaining the text, has two parts: first, stating the number and listing the names; second, from "First, clarifying... onwards, citing the gates and providing the explanation.
Regarding the phrase "concerning the ultimate characteristics," it is as the text states.
Within the commentary, there are five distinct sections. Now, we shall address the first: the timing for receiving the robes (*cīvara*). This section contains two parts: first, clarifying the timing;

second, from "twenty recitations" onwards, distinguishing whether or not the intercalary month (*adhika-māsa*) is included. Within the first part, there are two sub-sections: first, citing textual passages to establish the specific time;

second, from "on the sixteenth day of the seventh month," determining the exact number of days based on whether the reception occurs before or after that date. Within the first of these two sub-sections, there is the initial [point].

The establishment of the rules according to our own school is as follows. From "In this way" below, the establishment of receiving robes over a period of thirty days is based on the doctrine of other schools.

Regarding the statement "from the beginning until the relinquishment": in the *Vinaya-nidāna*, after the *pravāraṇā* ceremony was completed on the fifteenth day, on the sixteenth day one took up a *pāṃsukūla* (rag-robe) and a new robe and went to see the World-Honored One.
On the way, they encountered rain; the robes were heavy and they were utterly exhausted, so they informed the Buddha.
For these reasons, the Buddha assembled the community of bhikṣus. At the conclusion of the rainy season retreat (*varṣā*), there are four matters that should be performed by oneself:
the invitation for criticism (*pravāraṇā*), the dissolution of the boundary (*sīmā-bandha*), the establishment of the boundary, and the acceptance of the *kaṭhina* robe.

Regarding those who enter the "early" retreat (*pūrvavarṣā*) and accept [the robes] on the sixteenth day of the seventh month, Mount Lingyun says this is to avoid confusion. The text states: "At the conclusion of the retreat, one accepts the robe. However, there are both early and late retreats.
Regarding the phrase "later... later": after the later *anvāroka* (rainy-season retreat) has concluded, it is not permitted. The original sound for this month is *kārttika-māsa*;
here in this region, the characters are abbreviated, dropping *ti* and *na* from *kārttika*, thus it is called the *kātti-māsa*. As for the phrase "reaching the twelfth month," the Buddha said:
"The robe is not received for one month; it is received for five months. It is discarded at the end of the four winter months, which is the fifteenth day of the twelfth month."
The second [section] concerns the textual passage on receiving robes within thirty days as established by other schools; it has two parts. First, establishing the doctrine based on scripture.

Second, from "Therefore, according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*," etc., citing evidence from other schools to establish the proof. Regarding the first of these two: first, establishing the principle based on other schools;

second, from "Therefore, the text says," etc., citing the scriptural passage regarding the "immediate day" to prove that one may receive [the robe] every day. One recitation: the words "As for... and so forth.
Regarding this, Fazheng says: "The *Mahīśāsaka*, *Dharmaguptaka*, and other three Vinayas generally permit the acceptance of robes for a period of one month.

The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, however, restricts it specifically to the sixteenth day of the seventh month. Based on the passage concerning the acceptance of the robe and bowl, it is said that "one may accept them daily," meaning that from the sixteenth day of the seventh month until the fifteenth day of the eighth month, throughout that intervening month, one may accept them every day.

Regarding "not remaining overnight on that very day," the prohibition against staying overnight is established because if one stays overnight with others, there is a fear of defilement through contact, whereby the ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*) will not be valid.
It is just as if one were to stay overnight on pure ground (*śuddhasthāna*); one may not perform the formal act of assignment (*vibhaṅga-karma*). Ling-shan says:

"This refers to cases where the gift has already been bestowed upon the Sangha. When the Tathāgata bestows [a gift] upon the Sangha, although it may have stayed overnight, there is no offense. The *Ji-lü* (Dharmaguptaka Vinaya) below states: "Not yet..."
If one uses the three robes as a mere pretext for making [a robe], is this not within the boundary? It is like the purification of another's property;
if it was originally intended as a gift for the purpose of making something, then [the act] is not accomplished.

Regarding the second section, which cites proofs from other schools, there are three parts. First, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations) proves that one may receive [the precepts] every day within a single month.

Second, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* (Five-Section Vinaya) proves that while the reception is the same, it distinguishes the abandonment as being different. Third, the *Mātṛkā-vibhaṅga* (Matrix Analysis) proves that the two texts concerning both reception and abandonment are not distinct.
One recitation states: "Therefore, until the point of abandonment," which is as written in the *Daśabhāṇavāra*. Ling-shan says: "Five."
[The period] is divided. The observance lasts for thirty days, and the relinquishment likewise lasts for thirty days.
If one undertakes [the vow] on the sixteenth day of the seventh month, it is relinquished on the fifteenth day of the eleventh month.

If one undertakes it on the seventeenth day of the seventh month, and so on, up until undertaking it on the fifteenth day of the eighth month and relinquishing it on the fifteenth day of the twelfth month—each instance of undertaking lasts for exactly thirty days. If, subsequently...
The summer retreat (*varṣā*) was entered on the sixteenth day of the eighth month and relinquished on the fifteenth day of the twelfth month.

This entering and relinquishing each lasts for one day; the two periods of the summer retreat both provide four months of benefit. The latter retreat provides benefit, which differs from the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*.

According to the *Vinayamātṛkā*, one may not enter the retreat after the fifteenth day of the eighth month; thus it says that "beyond this, it is not permitted. The intention of the *Śāstra* (the *Shishi yaolü yixiang*) is to take [the retreat] for thirty days.

Regarding "receiving robes daily" and "the old reception and the abandonment of the pair," these clarify that the text of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Sifen lü) is incomplete. As for the statement "from seven until knowing," it is as the text says.

Regarding the statement "in the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* (Shisong lü), until the intercalary month": if there is an intercalary month and one receives [robes] on the sixteenth day of the seventh month, the count reaches one hundred and fifty days;
one must not include the intercalary month in the calculation.

The second section, clarifying the substance of the robe (*cīvara*), has two parts. First, it sets forth the substance of the robe; second, from "twenty recitations" (*viṃśati-saṃghāṭī*) onwards, it distinguishes the characteristics of its completion or non-completion.

Regarding the first part, there are two sub-sections: first, it clarifies that the substance of the robe must accord with the Dharma; second, from "four sides" (*catur-aṅgula*) onwards, it distinguishes the correctness or incorrectness of the robe’s color and appearance.
One recitation states: "From 'two' up to 'color,' there are two kinds within rag-robes (*pāṃśukūla*). According to the Vinaya text, if it is a new robe..."

If it is old clothing, or if one takes old clothing and new items, folds them together to perform the purification (*śodhana*), and then uses them as a patched robe to purify wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*), this is obtained through the four or five types of wrong livelihood mentioned previously.
To obtain wealth and profit out of greed, to speak deceptively of having few desires, and to curry favor with people's sentiments to acquire goods—this is unrighteous (*adharma*).

Wearing summer clothing in winter, or acting out of fear and expectation to receive alms from others, is called "obtaining by signs" (*nimitta-lābha*). To praise the gifts given by royal families in order to incite [others to give] is likewise improper.

"Moving the person to spread" means causing the person to relinquish [the robe] as an act of giving (*tyāga*). Having obtained the material, one performs the ritual of purification (*viśuddhi*); this is not a relinquishment that follows the movement of the wealth itself.

Apart from the aforementioned conditions, if it arrives on the same day, it is called "in accordance with the Dharma. If it exceeds these numerical limits, Ling Shan says: "This clarifies the characteristics of the robes.
As previously stated, there are five strips and ten intervals; referring to the 'lower' category, one obtains the middle and upper two types of robes. The seven-strip [robe] is large..."

All [these] robes may be accepted and made into [monastic garments]. As for *chan* (pronounced with the initial *n* as in *ni-zhan*), it also has the pronunciation *zhan*. Furthermore, the group of six [monks] used five primary colors (*pañca-varṇa*).
The Buddha said, "I permit the use of the color of the *kāṣāya*. This color is appropriate. The five directions—blue, yellow, and so forth—are called the "correct colors" (*maula-varṇa*).
Since it is apart from the five directions, this is established; conversely, it is called "improper color. The second section has two parts:

first, various schools' miscellaneous views on whether the substance of the robe is formed; second, from "The Four-Part [Vinaya]" onwards, specifically clarifying the arrangement of the borders and the folding to complete the formal acceptance (*pratigraha*).
First, regarding the statement "from ten [robes] to the recipient": it refers to a shroud used for covering a corpse, which was taken from a cemetery and brought back.
Regarding this, Jì says: it refers to changing the upper garments on a corpse during a reburial and taking them to offer to the Sangha;

this is what is meant. The commentary states: "The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* and others... Línshān says: however, the term "refuse" (*pāṃśukūla*) also applies here, but fearing confusion with current practices, we distinguish them.

That which is picked up from a public road or exposed place constitutes a valid substance. If it has been used to cover a dead person, it does not qualify as such. As for "folding leaves," it refers to the aforementioned...

It is said that if one does not cut and piece it together, it will not be formed. Fearing that those who merely fold the leaves [of the cloth] would not achieve this, it is thus distinguished and set forth.

This robe is continuous with its strips; one simply folds the leaves to create the partitions. Regarding the case where an old robe is not formed: Ling-shan says that even down to having been worn for but a single trial, it is called an "old robe.
For example, if a sitting mat has not been folded, it is so; if it has not been folded, even down to having been used for but a single [trial], it is the same.

One sits. When it is time for the urgent offering of robes (*ātyayika-cīvara*), if the robe has been completed and accepted, one stands and says: "I have received this urgent offering of robes during a non-seasonal period.
If, at the time of the original acceptance, it was intended to be made into a merit-robe (*kaṭhina-cīvara*), then this is not permissible.
What is meant here by "obtaining" refers to when one obtains a robe without having originally intended to make it into a merit-robe; this occurs at the end of the summer retreat.
These are the robes for a monk who has completed the summer retreat (*varṣā*). According to the *Upāli-śāstra*, it is not permitted to receive the three robes from a deceased bhikṣu;

however, according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, those that have never been used may be made into them. According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, if a bhikṣu, out of greed for gain, discards his three robes to make a *kaṭhina* robe, five matters will all fail to be accomplished.
Conversely, if one acts as prescribed above, they are accomplished. This clarifies that even when a bhikṣu receives robes as a gift, he is likewise permitted to make a *kaṭhina* robe.

Regarding the *guṇa-cīvara* (merit robe): according to the *Yinjian lun* (Treatise on Citing and Seeing), members of all seven assemblies may accept and consecrate it together. This clarifies the person who is able to bestow the robe.

Even if a bhikṣu’s robe remains within the same boundary and has not yet been relinquished, there is no fault in staying overnight together while making the *guṇa-cīvara*. Whichever one or two [of the seven assemblies] receive it, they obtain it accordingly.

Regarding the three robes (*tricīvara*), as for those who receive one or two robes [as the *kaṭhina* cloth], the intended meaning is that all three robes may be received and made into a *guṇakaṭhina* robe;
it is not necessary, as in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, that it must be the *saṃghāṭī*. Receiving the two lower robes does not constitute a valid reception.
Some explain that one may receive a single robe and make it, or receive two robes together and make them, and both are permissible. This is not the case. This...
This clearly explains the substance of the robe, though its dimensions have not yet been determined; these will be clarified below by citing the *Vinaya-vibhaṅga*.

Therefore, the latter interpretation is not adopted here. Regarding the term "four-part" (*sifen*), the compiler [of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*] used thread to weave it in successive order around the edges.

The third [section], "Distinguishing Persons," has two parts: first, the heading that introduces the individual listings; second, from "dividing into four" onwards, the explanation according to the text.

The first part is as in the text. Within the explanation, there are two sections. Now, for the first, it is divided into three: first, the division into four; second, the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*; third, the *Daśādhyāya-śāstra*. Regarding the phrase "the four":
Regarding "accomplishment" (*siddha*): it refers to one who has offered their consent (*chanda*). The *Lì* (Establishment) states: "If one is inside a room, the acceptance is not accomplished;

one does not obtain the five benefits, nor does one count toward the quorum. Regarding those with obstacles: the *Lì* states: "Those with the thirteen obstacles (*trayodaśa-antarāya*) are not eligible to receive the *kaṭhina* robe, nor do they obtain the five benefits.

In the lower section of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, it is stated that a *śrāmaṇera* undergoing penance for transgression (*śikṣādattaka*) is not accomplished [in receiving the robe]; this should be understood by analogy.

This can be understood. Regarding the absence of the *saṃghāṭī*, the *Huayan* states: "In the context of dependent origination, because the *saṃghāṭī* is originally heavy, one is permitted to receive the *guṇa-cīvara* (robe of merit) so as to grant it five privileges.
Since the *saṃghāṭī* is now lacking, these privileges are also absent; therefore, the reception [of the robe] is not accomplished."

There is no harm in being deficient of the two lower robes. Question: If one was originally deficient of the *saṃghāṭī*, may one now receive the two lower robes in place of the *saṃghāṭī* and thereby complete the formal acceptance (*parigraha*)?
Answer: The Vinaya provides no explicit ruling on this. However, within the texts, robes are categorized as primary or secondary; by principle, it would be permissible.
Nevertheless, while the secondary robe is permitted, there is no offense for being deficient in robes. This is because, according to its nature, that robe is not fundamentally a *saṃghāṭī*. Its...
The matter is very difficult. For now, let us rely on the proper regulation of robes and judge according to the Vinaya; this does not contradict the original conditions.

As for those who were outside the boundary, they were previously inside the boundary when the formal consent (*chanda*) was offered, yet it was not established; then, at the time the Sangha received the robe, they went out to remain outside the boundary.
There is no principle by which this could be obtained. Regarding the statement "the merit reaches the recipient," this clarifies that monks from a different boundary (*sīmā*) cannot receive it;

although it permits inviting persons from a different boundary to complete the quorum and perform the ritual procedure, they still cannot receive the merit. Regarding the statement "according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations), it reaches the recipient," this refers to the fifty-third fascicle of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, which says:
"The Blessed One was away. When the various bhikṣus had finished their summer retreat, many monasteries collectively entered into the rains-retreat (*varṣā*) together."
If one receives a robe within a single boundary (*sīmā*) and then relinquishes it, once that great boundary (*mahāsīmā*) has been dissolved, are all the bhikṣus said to have relinquished the robe?
Answer: It is relinquished by those who relinquish it; it is not relinquished by those who do not relinquish it. The *Fazheng* (Correct Explanation) states:

According to this question, because the World-Honored One, for the benefit of the bhikṣus, had each dissolved their original boundaries after receiving the *kaṭhina* robe, he subsequently dissolved this boundary as well.

Furthermore, when each boundary is re-established according to its original limits, if the monks had previously intended in their hearts to relinquish [the boundary], then it is relinquished at the time of the dissolution of the boundary.

If they had not previously intended in their hearts to relinquish it, then it remains based on the original [boundary]. Regarding the initial mention of one who has committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense but has not yet requested confession from the Saṃgha:
a person in *parivāsa* (probation) is one who has requested *parivāsa* from the Saṃgha; a person practicing penance (*śikṣādattaka*) refers to one who has committed a *pārājika*.

Regarding the granting of *śikṣādattaka* (probation for transgression): this is the disciplinary measure for one who has been expelled (*pārājika*) and refuses to request formal confession from the Saṃgha; thus, they are suppressed and excluded.
As for the aforementioned individuals, because their persons are not pure, it is improper for them to receive the robes.

The second [section], on the person capable of acting as the administrator (*dhāraṇaka*), has three parts: first, distinguishing the qualities required for the person who holds the robe; second, from "seeing the proponent" (*lun*) downward, whether to grant or proceed with it;

third, from "if the *karmavācanā* [is performed] regarding the *kaṭhina*" downward, clarifying the correctness or incorrectness of selecting the person who holds it. Regarding the statement "from two... to clear": the person holding the robe must possess five virtues (*guṇa*).

They must know those who have broken the summer retreat or failed to observe the *anupravrājana*, and those who lack the great outer robe (*saṃghāṭī*) and so forth; such persons may not [be selected].

Regarding "receiving": by doing the opposite of this, one obtains the receipt; hence it is said that "one knows one has obtained it. This does not mean that the receipt is understood with absolute clarity.

As for the statement "goodness reaches the mind," other items are treated as light objects, while heavy objects should be divided. Regarding those belonging to the Saṃgha of the Four Directions, Sengshen says: "This treatise is based on the *guṇavastra* (merit robe).
Since it is obtained by the Saṃgha during the [specific] time, both light and heavy items belong [to them]. If there are many robes, they should all be made into merit robes."
Regarding robes, they must all have four horizontal folds and five seams attached. Nowadays, there are also those who receive items on the fifteenth day of the seventh month;
these are merely termed "out-of-season" (akāla). As for items currently present, regardless of whether they are light or heavy, they must all be divided from among those present.

Furthermore, when giving material goods at the proper time, one must inquire about the donor's intention: is this gift for those who have entered the *pūrvavārṣika* (first) retreat within this boundary, or is it intended as a general offering to the monastic community of monks and nuns throughout the entire region?
If the answer is, "I give this to those in the *pūrvavārṣika* retreat within this boundary," [the distribution proceeds accordingly].
"Regarding 'the gravity of the offense': this clarifies stealing the Dharma through the mind. K'e said: 'A bhikṣu receives the Dharma;
if he obtains it through mental conditions based on his teacher,' this means that having received the Dharma from another teacher, he does not pay the fee or steals it."

The first master says: According to this Vinaya text, stealing livestock is the same as stealing human property; one incurs a *pārājika* offense.

Thus, in the first volume of the *Vinaya*, regarding the theft of a lion’s leftovers down to the weight of five *kārsāpaṇas*, it states that for tigers, elephants, and so forth, the offense is likewise grave. This clearly shows that they are understood to be the same as stealing human property.

"Decidedly. [This refers to] "expecting another," because it is based on that original owner; thus, one incurs a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*) by directing the expectation toward that person. This explanation is divided into two parts: first, clarifying where the incurred offense is attributed;

When the Buddha brought the matter of the rat-stealing to their attention, the group of six was hesitant and could not reach a decision as to whether it constituted an offense.
He reported the matter to the Buddha because he had committed an offense regarding a person, rather than an offense regarding a rat. The Buddha declared it a *pārājika*.

This is because the group of six [monks] knew that the object was human property; since they regarded the person as still being the original owner, the offense was classified as grave based on the person.

If one were to combine the cases of a person perceived as a person and a rat perceived as a rat, the offenses would be distinct—*pārājika* and *duṣkṛta* respectively. Why, then, was it necessary to report this to the Buddha? It was because there was doubt.

Because their desire has been severed, the remnants of a lion may be taken; because their desire has been severed. The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* (Duo lun), fascicle 2, states:
"It is auspicious to take the remnants of all birds and beasts; there is no offense regarding a lion. Thus far, the first category—objects belonging to a master—has been fully explained.

Regarding the case where light or heavy offenses are incurred due to a mutual shift in perception between the preceding and succeeding moments, Dāngyáng says: "First, one forms the perception that it has an owner..."

If one subsequently changes it to the perception that there is no owner, one commits the light offense of *sthūlātyaya*. If one first perceives it as having no owner and subsequently changes it to the perception that there is an owner, one commits the grave offense of *pārājika*.

First recitation: Regarding the statement "However... up to 'demonstrating,'" the *Fazheng* (Correct Teaching) says: "A subtle mind of theft does not depend on whether it was done with a good intention or an evil one."

The mind commits all [offenses]; therefore, it is said that even those of genuine virtue cannot escape them. However, the completion of theft necessarily depends upon the presence of a thieving mind (*caurya-citta*).

This means that when the mind is obscured regarding the characteristics of the teachings and one unjustly damages another's property, this constitutes a thieving mind. This indicates that a thieving mind does not consist solely of the intention to steal a specific object;

rather, theft is bound by the mind itself, regardless of whether the object is right or wrong. As for the phrase "As for the absence of expectation regarding the nature of the object," Ling Shan says: "If there were none..."

thus, we know that [the offense] depends on the mind. It does not matter whether the object or the situation actually belongs to another or not. Regarding the *Mahāsāṃghika* rule concerning "good intention":

this means that when one sees that monastic affairs are not being settled or that matters pertaining to the Buddha and the Dharma are not being resolved, one acts with good intention to accomplish those monastic affairs and the service of the Buddha.

Regarding "Dharma-affairs" (*dharmakārya*): this refers to mutually taking funds or goods belonging to the Buddha for the use of the Saṃgha. Because one hopes to accomplish the aforementioned matters, it is called "good intention.

The author of the *Chao* (the *Shishi Yaolan*), fearing that people might be confused, explains: this refers to an offense of ignorance (*moha*). That is to say, regarding the two types of property—those of the Buddha and those of the Dharma—there is nothing to consult or report.
It is the ignorant mind that misapprehends the characteristics of the teachings, thinking: "Since the Buddha is within the Saṃgha, items belonging to the Buddha may be used [for the Saṃgha]."

"Using it for the Sangha. Although this is a well-intentioned act, it is clearly an offense. Question: If one gives property belonging to the Buddha to the Sangha out of good intentions, there is no intention to steal;
why then does it constitute theft? Answer: Generally speaking, "theft" refers to the unjust deprivation of wealth.

The correct explanation is as follows: Since it is said that [the act was done] with a good intention, it should not constitute theft. However, because the current case violates the prescribed limits of the teaching, it is an offense.

Therefore, the passage is transcribed and shown; "transcribed" refers to copying the text from the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* down to the *Caturvargika-vinaya* to demonstrate it. This gives rise to the underlying intent.

The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, fascicle 51, states: Question: Regarding the six ways of taking another’s property as listed in the *Vinayakośa*, how does one incur a *pārājika* offense?

Answer: With the exception of taking [property] by means of interest (*ucchvāsa*), taking anything else constitutes a *pārājika*. The *Vinayakośa* categorizes these into six types of theft based on intention;

that text refers to them as the "six ways of taking. Regarding "taking through harshness" (*kaṭuka-grahaṇa*), Master Lingshan says it refers to using harsh words and urgent pressure, or insulting and humiliating [the owner] in an improper manner.

The intention is to take the object as a gesture of thanks for having sent it. To take it with such a mind is irrational and constitutes the theft of another's property; this is termed the "thieving mind.

This refers to the third [offense]. "Not giving" means to forcibly seize and take away. "Taking by force" means to take it away by compulsion. Regarding "soft-spoken words," this is identical to the previously mentioned corrupt mind.

even if the other has not yet received it, if one later regrets the gift and refuses to give it, this also constitutes a transgression. This is established.
The correct text says: Question: Does one commit an offense even if unaware, just as one does when acting out of knowledge? Answer: It does not matter whether one knows or does not know.

If that is so, since the thief was unaware [of the ownership], how can the offense of theft be established? Explanation: Although the owner was unaware, at the moment the thief abandoned the object with the intent to sever their connection, it already belonged to another by implication.
Now, having taken it back out of regret, the act constitutes theft. Regarding the phrase "five kinds of sincere mind," this refers to flattery.

Regarding "the mind": Ling Shan says that it involves forming intimate attachments and failing to maintain upright principles; following words and complying with intentions while hoping for others to bestow material goods. Thus, the Abhidharma states:
"To conceal one's true nature and to crookedly comply with the exigencies of the times is called flattery. Regarding "a crooked mind":
it does not follow upright principles, but rather forms bitter alliances and uses a distorted disposition to acquire things. Some say: "All [of these] are not [righteous]."

it refers to harboring even a slight resentment and obtaining wealth under the pretext of being angry. Regarding "fear" (*bhaya*), the *Fǔpiān* states: it is to forcefully speak of portents and omens while the heart covets another's property.
Section four has two parts: first, a general enumeration of the number; second, from "one" onwards, an explanation according to that number. As for the phrase "four... up to the thief-like mind":
These two sets of five are derived from the "Fivefold Texts on the Sangha. Lingshan says: "The first five clarify the mind; the latter five clarify the taking of the precepts. The Commentary states:

"The phrase 'taking with a thieving mind' clarifies that the mind corresponds to the object; it is intended to clarify that the karmic act of stealing is complete when both [mind and object] are present."

One must necessarily combine both conditions to constitute a single act of theft; therefore, they are consolidated into ten sections. In the commentary, these ten segments differ according to their respective increases.
The textual analysis of these increases is divided into two parts: the first five clarify the mental intention (*citta*), and the latter five clarify the act of taking (*ādāna*).

Within these ten, each has its own heading and explanation. Regarding the phrase "first, up to 'appropriating by rule'": the first section contains three headings, namely the three explained below, according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*.

Wealth. This is theft. "Crooked" means not upright; "obstinate" (戾) means resentment or perversity. Regarding "timid and fearful" (*kōkyaku*): the *Ritsu-zō* (律增), fascicle five, section nine, states that this refers to an unwholesome mind.

*Hehe* (pronounced *hāgè*). Lingshan says: this refers to the manifestation of majesty by emitting sounds from the mouth; alternatively, it refers to preaching the Dharma to instill fear in those who grasp [at things].

The *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: it involves preaching with majesty about the evil retributions of the hells, or preaching about the power of kings and officials through which wealth is obtained.

As Mount Lingyan says: "It is taught that stinginess results in the retribution of being reborn as a hungry ghost or suffering poverty; thus, when one says 'I have doubts,' they also fear they will not escape [this fate].

This is a skillful means used to strike at and move the person before them so that wealth may be obtained. To constantly harbor schemes to seize [property] is to always possess a thieving mind. The *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: [as cited above].

To act; that person then gains profit because of these words. To cause another to give alms and thereby obtain wealth—this is the seeking of profit.

This person preaches the Dharma while seated upon his own mind. Furthermore, although he is an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), he is able to maintain the precepts without craving for fame or profit;

This first part has two sub-sections. First, the question is raised by citing the treatise. Second, from the answer beginning with "There are," the three differing interpretations are distinguished.

Regarding the first part, "The answer reaches this point": this refers to the response itself. As for those three masters: the first relies on the currency used in Rājagṛha; the second relies on the currency used wherever one is;

the third further states that death is incurred based on the amount stolen when the value is complete. Regarding the one who relies on the currency used in Rājagṛha, he establishes his position by saying: "The Buddha, based on..."
In Rājagṛha, the Dharma was established and the precepts were formulated. The Buddha asked King Bimbisāra, "Great King, within your realm, for what crime does one deserve death?

The King replied, "For stealing five coins, one deserves death. The Buddha established the precept based on this. Thus, the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* (or *Shan-chi-lü-p'i-po-sha*), fascicle two, states that some say it refers to gold coins or silver coins, while others say it refers to copper coins;
originally, it was not fixed. The second master [states] that wherever the Buddha-dharma exists, and so forth.
