The *Śāriputra-abhidharma-śāstra* (or *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*) commentary refutes itself; thus we know that the "middle" [position] is the later one. An objection is raised:

the two masters—the *Daśabhāṇaka-vinaya* and the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*—are verbose and unclear in their preceding and succeeding sections, so they may simply be set aside. Yet, even the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya’s* rule regarding four coins and three *yong* is more stringent than that of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*.
Since it is said to follow what is "urgent," why discard the rule of four coins and three *yong* and instead take five coins as the definition of "urgency"?

The *Yechao* (Yaoshan’s Commentary) answers by saying: "Even four coins and three *yong*. The *Shanjian lü piposha* (Sāriputra-paripṛcchā-vinaya-śāstra) explains that this is equivalent to five coins (*pañca-kārṣāpaṇa*).
Because it could not be reconciled with the *Sifen lü* (Dharmaguptaka-vinaya), the *Zongyin* (General Seal) takes the five coins as the definitive standard.
According to the eighth fascicle of the *Jian lun* (Vinaya-śāstra): "At that time, twenty *rajasaka* in Rājagṛha made one *kāliṃśapana*; one *kāliṃśapana* was divided into..."
The *kārṣāpaṇa* is divided into four parts; one part is five *māṣakas*. If one steals five [of these], one commits a *pārājika* offense; it is not the same as the present case.
In the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, nineteen coins constitute a *kārṣāpaṇa*. Divided into four parts, if one takes one part, it constitutes a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*), the meaning being the same.
The ancient masters said: "However, in the Western lands, there were originally no coins of the present type; there were only the aforementioned *māṣakas* in form."
It is like a conch-shell horn.

Second, citing the case where a thief follows out of urgency, this is divided into two parts to prove the taking of five coins: first, citing the passage on "merely separating" to prove the urgency of the following;
second, from "furthermore, observe" below, citing the severance of the grave offense to prove it was five coins. One person sang, saying, "Good, it has arrived."
Yun asked: "The *Śāstra* clarifies that five coins constitute a heavy object. Why then is the passage concerning 'leaving the place' (*sthāna-viprakarṣa*) cited here? Answer:

This is to provide scriptural proof for the inclusion of the offense of concealment (*saṃvaraṇa*) based on urgency. That treatise clarifies the meaning of "leaving the place," yet the two masters differ in their views.

According to the first master, one incurs a *pārājika* offense upon leaving the "stiff mouth" (*kaṭhina-mukha*). This is based on the premise that while within the stiff [mouth], it is still considered "the place"; only upon exiting the mouth is it termed "leaving the place. The latter... [text ends]

As for the Master’s statement that "one merely commits an offense by lifting [the object]," this means that the offense is incurred simply by picking it up; it does not require the mouth to utter the word "stiff" (or "hard").

Why is this? Because the precepts ought to be observed with urgency. This proof takes the value of five coins as an example to demonstrate such urgency. Furthermore, other Vinaya treatises observe the five matters, and so forth.
The eighth fascicle of the *Śāstra* states: Regarding "the place," a bhikṣu had a yellow robe which he placed upon his shoulder while walking along.

He subsequently lost it and formed the intention to relinquish it. Later, another bhikṣu came and took it with the intent to steal. Having taken it, he felt remorse and questioned the Vinaya master Cūḍapanthaka.
Cūḍapanthaka searched for the owner of the lost item. When the owner of the lost item arrived at the Vinaya master's location, the master questioned the owner. [He asked: "Long..."

[The owner] says, "Old man, this is your robe. [The monk] replies, "Yes. [The owner] asks, "Where did you lose it? [The monk] replies, "I lost it at that place. [The owner] asks, "Do you have the intention to give it up?

[The monk] replies, "I have already formed the intention to give it up. Again, he asks the monk who stole it, "Where did you take it? [The thief] replies, "At such-and-such a place. The Vinaya Master says:

"If you took it without the intention to steal, there is no offense. Since you acted with a wicked mind, you incur a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing). Afterward, speak to the monk who is the owner of the object."
"You have already relinquished the robe; give the robe to this bhikṣu. He replies, "Very well. When the bhikṣu who was stolen from hears the words of the Vinaya master, his heart is filled with joy.
This is called "observing the location" (*sthāna*). Regarding "time": it refers to the time of taking. This robe is sometimes light and sometimes heavy.
If it is taken when it is light, the offense is determined according to its weight at that light time. If it is taken when it is heavy, it is determined according to its weight at that heavy time.

One incurs an offense according to the value [of the object]. I shall now provide testimony for this: There was a bhikṣu who obtained a coconut-shell bowl and habitually used it to drink water while staying at a monastery on the ocean.
He later went to Mount Cetiya. Subsequently, another bhikṣu went to the ocean monastery and saw the coconut shell;
with a mind of theft, he took it. Later, he went to Mount Cetiya and, upon arriving, used the bowl to eat gruel. [The owner of the bowl...]
Seeing him, he asked, "Venerable sir, where did you obtain this tray? The bhikṣu replied, "I obtained it at a monastery in the ocean.
The owner said, "This is my property; have you stolen it? He immediately seized him and brought him before the Saṃgha, where the matter was fully adjudicated.
There was an Abhidharma master named Ghoṭamukha who questioned the bhikṣu: "Where did you take it? He answered, "I took it from a monastery in the ocean."
Question: What is its value? Answer: In that land, the remaining husks of the coconut are discarded or used as firewood;
they have no value at all. He asked the owner again: "What is the price of this bowl? Answer: "This is a coconut shell; the juice has been drunk and the skin discarded."
The bhikṣu discarded [the previous vessel] and fashioned a new one capable of holding one māṣaka.

Gautama said, "If it is thus, then as long as it does not exceed five māṣakas, there is no grave offense. Having heard this in the midst of the assembly, they joyfully exclaimed, "Excellent! The Dharma Master said:

Thus, one should observe the value according to the circumstances (the *Chao* extracts this passage to prove that the previous interpretation of "five coins" in the *Sifenlü* as the standard for a penalty is correct; the period of calculation ends here).
There are objects that are expensive when new but cheap later, such as a new iron bowl: it is valuable when complete and clean at first, but once broken and old, its value drops accordingly.
When a bhikṣu steals another's property, he should ask the owner: if the object was expensive before use but cheap after being used by him, you should know that this constitutes [the offense].
The Vinaya Master carefully examines these five points before adjudicating a case, sentencing according to the gravity of the offense;
this is all from the *Śāstra*. The *Cíhué* (Compassionate Resolution) states: "There are five headings, but only four in the explanation.

Regarding the word "etc. (*deng*) in the *Chao*: the *Śāstra* does not contain this word. Here, "etc. refers to the light and heavy offenses of the preceding period, thereby completing the five. By means of this period...
The text concerning the grave offense for stealing five *māṣaka* coins serves as proof that taking five *kārsāpaṇa* is appropriate.

Second, regarding the meaning: this explains the characteristics of theft and establishes the boundaries for the formation of offenses. This section is divided into two parts: first, a general heading;

second, from "In the *Daśabhāṇavāra*" onwards, which follows the heading to provide a specific explanation. Regarding the phrase "from two... to the same," Fuyang says: "This distinguishes the first five matters. Now..."
In accordance with various teachings, the textual explanation through these six meanings is now complete.

The commentary is divided into six parts: first, an analysis based on the value of the currency; second, an analysis based on the value of the location; third, an analysis based on the value of the time;

fourth, an analysis of whether the acquisition was shared or not; fifth, an analysis of excess or deficiency; and sixth, an analysis of quantity—whether one or many. Regarding the phrase "one [act] is light": it refers to the minimum degree of gravity.
Huayan says: In the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, Upāli asked the Buddha, "Is there a case where stealing three coins constitutes a *pārājika* offense? The Buddha replied, "There is;
it depends on when the value of money is high. Fuyang says: For example, in this country during the Gān-fēng era, one *qián-yuán* coin [was worth much].
"At that time, one hundred small coins was the standard. He asked again, "Is there a case where one steals five coins and yet does not commit a *pārājika* offense?

The Buddha said, "There is; it is when the value of money is low. Regarding the statement "even if one steals hundreds or thousands, it is a light offense," [the commentator] Daolun says: This refers to iron coins and the like, which were not in common use at the time.

Although one may steal hundreds or thousands of them, one incurs only a *sthūlātyaya* offense; therefore, it is called "light. As for the phrase "from two up to the price," it refers to the point of initiation.
The *Zhengyun* states: "This concerns the determination of the gravity of the offense based on the location. The *Lingshan* quotes the Vinaya:

"At one time, there were many bhikṣus who, through a stratagem, sent one person together to take another's property. That person went to take it; having returned with less than five coins, he reached this place and obtained five coins."

He had this thought: "If we obtain five coins, will we commit a *pārājika* offense? The Buddha said: "One commits a *sthūlātyaya* based on the original location. This is the same in the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* and the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā*;

the meaning is not different. Regarding the phrase "from three up to [five]": Master Li says that among the three ladles mentioned above, these all refer to stealing when [the value of] goods was high and selling them when they were low;
one incurs a heavy offense in view of the original location. If one now reverses this, it constitutes stealing when [the value of] goods was low.
When precious goods are valued highly, they become light; hence it is said "to descend" (*kō*). "To descend" means to lower. If they are light, they are like orchids.

Regarding the phrase "four coins and so forth," as for the "severing of the mind," Ling Shan says: "Because one originally intended to take only four coins and had no further intention to take more, the preceding and following [intentions] do not coincide.
Regarding the category of "five coins and so forth," the *Avataṃsaka* says there are two meanings: first, many people.
If one person is sent to steal, the five share the portion; if two go together to steal, each of the five shares their respective portion. Master Fazheng says:

"Although a single individual may not have obtained five coins, because the act was committed by people at that time such that the full amount of five was stolen and the karma was completed, one incurs a grave offense.

As for stealing the property of many people who have not yet divided it, this refers to cases where the total across the ten directions does not reach five, and therefore one incurs a light offense. Thus it is said.
Regarding the sixth point, "that which should be known," the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: "For example, a teacher says to three disciples, 'He has six coins.

The eldest shall take three; the next two shall each take one; and I myself shall take one. This constitutes the teacher's instruction to the disciples being complete. There are three disciples, and they are likewise instructed.
[The teacher] bypasses the middle two and instructs only the youngest disciple. The *Jieshu* then continues: "And so on, down to the youngest disciple."
He also spoke these words: "There were six coins there. The preceptor took three; each of his fellow students took one; and I myself took one.
We instructed one another so that the three of us together reached five. Because we intended to deprive the owner of one coin, each of us incurs one *pārājika*.

Since each of us individually stole one coin, each also incurs one *thullaccaya*. The *pārājika* is the karma of instructing others; the *thullaccaya* is one's own karma. Thus he both acted himself and instructed others.

These two types of karma do not coincide; therefore, one incurs two offenses for each. Regarding the fifth preparatory stage (*upakrama*), which is not explained in the *Chao* (the *Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā-śāstra*), the *Jieshu* (the *Śīlaskandha-vinaya-śāstra*) states:
"In cases where one does not employ a preparatory means oneself—such as borrowing another's property and failing to return it, or—as stated in the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā*—breaking another's property."
If one does not return the price, one incurs a *pārājika* offense. This does not require further expedient means (*upāya*), for fear of falling into over-extension.

Even if such expedients were present, they would likewise not be clarified here; it is simply understood that everything prior to the point of separation is subsumed under the category of expedient means. Thus, while the conditions are fully established, the specific characteristics are not explicitly detailed, as the *Śastravyākhyāna* (the *Chao*) clarifies them within the section on the point of separation.

The sixth section has two parts: first, citing the names; second, from "dividing into four" onwards, providing the explanation. The first part is as the text states. Within the explanation, there are two sections:

first, citing the teachings to provide a brief clarification; second, providing a detailed explanation by dividing the locations according to their meaning. Regarding the phrase "the four up to the grave":

If one performs a single act and stops through an expedient means, such that the separation from the place is not completed, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense. The following citation from the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* clarifies the boundary between the preparatory effort (*prayoga*) and the completion of the separation from the place.

In the second section, the detailed explanation according to the meaning, there are two parts: first, the general indication of the number of phrases; second, from "First" onwards, the specific explanation according to that number.

Regarding the phrase "departing from the place until [the act is committed]," the *Huayan* states: although it is said that one incurs an offense only upon departing from the place, in principle there are also cases where one is said to have incurred an offense even without departing from the place. For this reason, there is a tenfold classification.

In the second section, the detailed explanation according to number, there are ten items, which constitute ten segments. This is the first of the ten segments. The initial text has three parts: first, the heading;
second, the explanation beginning with "As in the Vinaya..."; third, the corroboration beginning with "The *Sudarsana-śāstra*...". First, the proclamation: from "one" up to "the most serious."
Fazheng said: "It is like a Vinaya master who, when adjudicating heavy offenses, classifies them as light; this is logically correct. Jing said:

"This refers to cases where there is a specific motive and one does not rely on the formal rules. If one were to follow the rules today, even if one were deluded or mistaken, there would be no offense.
Regarding 'using monastic property unlawfully,' Lì said: 'When an administrator disposes of the property of the permanent monastery to act as a matchmaker...'"

The bride is given to a pure person (*śuci-puruṣa*). The marriage implements are provided. The presiding official (*gaṇḍī-vin*) and the judge (*vināyaka*) jointly adjudicate. Once the adjudication is complete, they bind the *nien* (the auspicious day). Citing the intent of the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā*, it is proven that if [the ceremony] is finished, there is no *duṣkṛta*;
if not finished, there is a *sthūlātyaya*. Once the written document is completed, it is considered a grave offense (*guru*). This is discussed as the settlement of the boundary of the land.

The second section has three parts: first, the heading; second, from "In the *Sudarsana*" onwards, the explanation according to the teaching; third, from "That is to say" onwards, the application by analogy.
Regarding the phrase "the second [offense] is most grave": this refers to the issuance of a verbal command. As soon as these words are uttered, the offense is incurred.

According to the treatise: If one with the intent to steal proclaims, "This much land is mine," and the owner of the land conceives doubt as to whether it is his own land or the bhikṣu’s land, at that moment he incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.

If the owner of the land definitively forms the perception that he has lost it, he incurs a *pārājika* offense. If he comes to question the Saṃgha and they all answer identically, it is considered a grave offense;
this refers to when the owner of the land hears the proclamation saying, "This is the Saṃgha’s land," and doubt arises in his mind, leading him to come [and inquire].
Regarding "by the assembly": when the entire assembly collectively replies, "This is monastic land," regardless of the number of monks present, it constitutes a grave offense (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*).
"Judging [the transfer] contrary to principle and granting it": Yang Jing says this clarifies that a *bhikṣu* has made a biased judgment and granted it to others.

"Judging [the acquisition] contrary to principle and obtaining it": This clarifies that one seeks to obtain this object by making a judgment that violates the principles of the Dharma. Ling Shan says: "To contend..."

Regarding those who violate the principles concerning fields: whether they encroach upon an entire plot or encroach upon a portion of its boundaries, the offense is established according to the violation of principle.
However, if the land is recovered through right, there is no offense.
The third section has two parts: first, the heading; second, from "In the *Sudarsana*" onwards, the explanation based on the teachings. First, the proclamation:

regarding the statement "from three up to that," according to the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra*, if there are two designations, mentioning one constitutes a *duṣkṛta* (offense), while mentioning both constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (formal meeting offense).

If there are three designations, mentioning one is a *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing); mentioning two is a *duṣkṛta*; mentioning all three is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. If a sentient being has many designations, one should refer to the final two designations.
To cite one *pārājika* offense; to cite two *pārājika* offenses. In the former case, whether the number is many or few, all are grave. The *Chao* cites the first two as markers, hence it says:

"Even a single hair or a single grain of wheat is grave. This is because the ground is of immeasurable value; that is to say, it reaches down to the Golden Wheel (*kāñcanacakravāḍa*), and thus its depth is of immeasurable value.
If this bhikṣu comes to ask the Saṃgha, "I shall now take this land," and the monks answer in agreement, all [offenses] are grave.

The commentary states: "This refers to measuring the ground by pacing. Ji explains: The meaning of the *Chao* (the *Vinaya-saṃgraha*) is that one holds a bamboo bow level and uses it to measure the ground as a standard.

"The same applies to marking with a cord" means that, according to the *Jian lun* (Treatise on Seeing): if, with a thieving mind, one marks out another's land with a cord—placing one end at the boundary marker (*lāna*) and the other end at the second boundary marker—it constitutes a *pārājika* offense. If both ends are placed [within the marked area], it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
The fourth section has two parts: first, the heading; second, the explanation. First, the proclamation: "Regarding 'the four... arrive,'" it is as the text states.

The fifth section is divided into four parts: first, the heading; second, from "twenty recitations" onwards, the formal explanation; third, "or like... and so forth, which clarifies the borrowing and reduction.

The *Sifenlü* (Four-Part Vinaya) states below [in the section on] "Establishing Proof": "Regarding the phrase 'from five [units] to [the point where it reaches]': this means that with the intent to steal, one pulls an object from beneath the leaves up to the flowers;

this constitutes a different location from its original place of placement. Thus, the meaning of Master Li’s commentary is that when money or goods and a woolen rug have different owners and are separated from their place of storage, an offense is committed;
however, when they have the same owner and are both items belonging to a single household, the condition of separation has not yet been established.
This is the section.
The sixth text has three parts: first, the heading; second, the formal explanation; third, from "The five divisions below" onwards, clarifying what is inappropriate.
Regarding the first chant, the statement from "Six" to "Luo": Ciyun says this refers to double-six dice, counters, chess pieces, and the like, as they were used for the teeth of the assembly.
Because it is made from bone and so forth, it is called a "tooth-turner" (*dantapona*).
Seventh, the heading and explanation: First, the recitation says, "Regarding the offense of seven [coins] up to the crime. The *Cīvara-vastu* states:

"If a bhikṣu steals a horse intending for it to go east, and the horse goes mad and heads toward the south, west, or north—although it has left its original place, because his intention was to go east, yet it instead went elsewhere..."
"Direction" refers to not having departed. If one heads toward the east, that is the point at which one has departed from the place.
If, at the time of the original theft, the direction or location is not specified, then merely lifting all four legs constitutes the point of departure.

If a bhikṣu steals a horse and departs, and the owner later pursues it—if the owner has not yet formed the thought that it is lost, and the bhikṣu has not yet formed the thought that he has acquired it—the offense of *pārājika* is not yet established. If the owner...

If one forms the perception that [the animal] has been lost, while the bhikṣu forms the perception that it has been obtained, he commits a *pārājika* offense. If one uses a mare to lure away another's stallion so that they move beyond the range of sight or hearing, it is immediately a *pārājika*.
Cattle and other animals are to be judged according to this same principle.
The eighth section has three parts: first, the heading; second, the formal explanation based on the text; third, from "like throwing a staff" onwards, citing an analogy to establish the point.
Regarding the statement "the eighth constitutes a grave offense": this refers to a secluded place where there are no people. Since there is no one present, the theft will inevitably succeed;

even if the object has not yet been removed from its location, it is certain to be removed once moved. Thus, the movement itself constitutes a grave offense, regardless of whether the object has been fully carried away.
The ninth text has two parts: the heading and the explanation. Regarding the phrase "the nine," etc., Lingshan says: this refers to fields, houses, and so forth, which cannot be moved;
it simply requires that one strike them with urgency. There is a mention of "five," which constitutes a summary of the grave offenses.

The tenth section has two parts: the heading and the explanation, which are recited together. Regarding the phrase "From 'Ten' to the Commentary," this refers to the citation of the commentary below for explanation.

The *Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra* states: "If a whirlwind blows a garment into the empty sky above, and a bhikṣu, with a thieving mind, reaches out and seizes it, he incurs a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) for each instance.

If the garment moves, it is a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense); if it leaves its original place, it is a *pārājika* (defeat). Therefore, the Vinaya says: 'There was clothing and property blown by the wind...'"

Regarding the property of another, to take it by theft—this clarifies that "separation from its place" means the object becomes empty of its original location; this is what is called "separation from its place. Other cases follow this principle.
As for stealing a bird, the *Abhidharma-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: There was a bhikṣu who wished to steal a peacock.
As the peacock was about to fly into the air, the bhikṣu stood directly in front of it. Seeing the bhikṣu, the peacock was unable to fly and remained there with its wings spread. The bhikṣu...
It is auspicious. It is also auspicious to touch it with the hand. If one shakes a peacock feather, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense. If one pulls the tail away from the head, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
If one pulls the left wing past the right wing, it is also a *pāyattika* offense; the same applies to moving them up and down. Standing [the teacher] said: "If a bird chick is kept in a cage..."

If a bhikṣu steals a bird, he commits an offense as soon as it leaves its cage. If he had no initial intent [to steal], even if he takes it away while it is still inside the cage, the *pārājika* offense is not yet established;
the offense is only committed when the bird has left the cage. Regarding "curved pegs" (*vakra-śaṅku*): the commentary states that this refers to hooks on a wall, such as "dragon-tooth" pegs.

Therefore, the *Jianlun* (Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra) says: "It refers to stealing an object from within a curved hook on a wall; the gravity of the offense is determined by whether the object has been separated from the wall and the peg."

It is as follows: if one has moved away from the wall but not yet from the peg, it is a *duṣkṛta* (light offense); if one has moved away from the peg but not yet from the wall, it is also a *duṣkṛta*.

If one has moved away from both the peg and the wall, it is a *pārājika* (defeat). Furthermore, according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*: if one takes a robe but does not take the rack, and carries the rack away, there is no gravity [of offense];

only when the robe subsequently leaves the rack does one incur the gravity [of the offense]. Regarding "severing the flow," the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: the *Caturvargika-vinaya* merely says, "If by means of a stratagem..."
Regarding the destruction of ponds and the taking of water-related objects, the specific limits of the damage are not clearly defined. As stated in the *Cīvara-vastu*:
"For irrigation flowing water, [the value] may be one *kākaṇī* per night, up to four or five *kākaṇīs*.

If a bhikṣu, for the sake of the Buddha, Dharma, or Saṃgha, steals or destroys their framework, he incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense; if the value reaches five [units], it is a *pārājika* offense. Furthermore, the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "The community..."

A family shares a single pool of water that irrigates their fields. A bhikṣu steals this by cutting off the flow of water for another’s field. If the crops planted have not yet died, it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense;
if the crops have died, one incurs an offense according to the value of the loss. Regarding "the flow of water," the *Jiwei shu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states:

According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, if one uses a bamboo tube to drink until the mouth is full through the opening, it is a grave offense (*duṣkṛta*). If one drinks little at a time, swallowing with each intentional sip, it is a *sthūlātyaya*. If... [text ends]

If the vessel was previously stopped and one pours it into another vessel while pulling out the stopper, it is a *sthūlātyaya* (Thullaccaya). If the pouring has ceased and the vessel is full, it is a heavy offense (*guru*).
If the pouring has not yet ceased and one immediately feels regret or fear, it is a heavy offense. If the water reaches back into its original vessel, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.

Even if the pouring has ceased but the liquid has not yet left the place, or if it has left the place but the pouring has not yet ceased, both cases are *sthūlātyaya*. "And so forth" includes ghee, oil, honey, and the like; these are treated according to the same principle.

In the third section, which summarizes the essential points, there are four intentions. First, it describes how the characteristics of theft are difficult to discern, with the underlying intent being to value the Path while censuring worldly affairs.
Second, from the words "What are they? onwards, it investigates and explains the reasons why the faults of worldly affairs arise. Third, from the words "Therefore, in the *Shanlun*... onwards...

This reveals that while urgent protection is manifest, its realization is difficult to know. The fourth section, "By Comparing with What Follows," concludes by returning to the summarized intent. First, regarding the statement "Now, as for... and so forth:

sentient beings harbor degrees of superiority and inferiority, lacking a mind of equanimity; furthermore, regarding the subsequent distinctions between self and others, or intimacy and estrangement, they have not yet discarded their own biased patterns.
Therefore, it is only those who have attained the first fruit and the state of no-more-learning who may engage in such matters.
Regarding the third section on non-offenses, there are two parts: first, the heading; second, the explanation. The first is as stated in the text.
The commentary has two parts: first, a general explanation of non-offenses; second, a specific explanation of "intimacy" found below in the Vinaya.

Regarding the phrase "four [factors] leading to an offense," "the perception that it is one's own" means, as the *Jieshu* states: "It refers to when an object is actually another's property, yet one intends it to be one's own because there is no perception of it being another's.

"The perception of it being discarded refuse" means: although it actually has an owner, one intends that the owner perceives it as discarded refuse and takes it; this opens up the possibility for the object.

Within the section on "Perception" (*saṃjñā*), the first is the phrase concerning the perception of a master. Regarding "taking temporarily": since this is not for permanent use, one takes it by way of temporary borrowing.
As for the statement "the arrival of the Vinaya": that which is difficult to perform is exemplified by Yang Ang’ai assisting Bo Tao by sharing their provisions.

That which is difficult to bestow is exemplified by Lei Yi nominating himself for the position of "Talent of Eminence" (*maocai*) and yielding it to Chen Ren; when the Provincial Governor would not permit it, Yi then feigned non-compliance.
"Life! This is it. "That which is difficult to endure! This refers to the principle of Guan Zhong and Bao Shu dividing their wealth. "The four or five are easy to understand;
the six do not abandon [the friend]" means that when Xun Chen’s elder brother was ill, and a Hu rebel attacked the commandery, the elder brother could not bear to leave.
When the rebels reached the commandery, [Xun Chen] said, "There is no one else here; how can you dare to stay alone? He replied, "I cannot bear to leave because my friend is ill."

"I would rather die than let my body [be taken]. The bandits knew he was a worthy man and withdrew their troops to return home. As for "not slighting others," those with whom Xi Chao associated were all the most talented and refined of their time;

even if someone blocked his gate before entering, he would still welcome them and form a friendship. The *Jieshu* (Excerpts on Precepts) states: "If one's feelings are like those of zithers and lutes, how can there be any distinction in wealth?
In antiquity, it was said that when eating, one must share with others, and when dressing, one’s garments should be shared as well. Thus, clothing was shared between two people, and food...
The same applies to the characters. The intention of the *Chao* (Excerpts) is that, fearing this may be difficult [to understand], it instructs one to measure it according to this.

Second, the separate explanation of the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, based on the *Zhujieben* (Commentary on the Prātimokṣa), is briefly divided into eight parts: 1. "If a bhikṣu" (referring to the person who commits the offense). 2. "In a village" (there are four types of villages:

first, those with walls on all four sides; second, those with fences; third, those where fences and walls do not completely surround [the area]; fourth, those surrounded on all four sides by buildings). Or, "in a secluded place" (that is, outside the village; a quiet location. Regarding "place," it refers to a single spot within the ground...).
1. The location (referring to the place where the theft is committed). 2. The object taken (referring to the item stolen). 3. The non-giver (the owner who has not relinquished it). 4.

Taking with a thieving mind (taking with a criminal intent). 5. Following the law of taking what is not given (regarding the stolen object; for according to the king’s laws, if one takes five coins or an object worth five coins, the punishment should be death;

the Buddha follows the king’s law and establishes a heavy penalty when the amount of theft is complete). 6. If [the object] belongs to a king (who possesses sovereign authority and does not [belong to others]) or a high minister (various great officials who assist the king).
They may seize him, or bind him, or drive him out of the country, or kill him, saying: "You are a thief! You are deluded! You know nothing [of the dharmas to be cultivated]!"
Regarding "seizing": King Bimbisāra’s distant ancestor governed criminals by merely ordering a Caṇḍāla to strike them on the head and seize them by the hand, after which they were released.

Regarding "binding": although they were seized, they were still treated as the subjects of the ancestral king; he surrounded them with ash. When it came to his father, the king, he implemented the law of banishment.

Upon King Śreṇika ascending the throne, he began the practice of cutting off fingers. It was under Ajātaśatru that the execution of lethal punishment was carried out. The remaining three [punishments] are as follows.

7. This refers to verbal abuse. "This bhikṣu commits a pārājika offense" (this clarifies the formal conclusion of the transgression). 8. "He shall not dwell together [with the Saṃgha]" (this clarifies the rules for the funeral rites).
The reason it is necessary to cite the King’s laws of governance is that, although they are worldly regulations, they serve as a basis for the Path.
Regarding the second [section], the precept against killing: first, the designation of the name of the regulation; second, the conditions for its violation, which follows the text for explanation.
As for the phrase "the third precept," regarding the initial origin story (*nidāna*), the Vinaya states: "The Buddha was at Vaiśālī for the sake of the bhikṣus..."
The Buddha taught the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*). Once that contemplation was accomplished, they came to feel revulsion toward their bodies and lives.

There was a bhikṣu named Mūlapaṇḍita who, for hire, carried out acts of killing. The Buddha, noticing that the assembly was small, questioned Ānanda. Ānanda answered truthfully, and consequently, [the Buddha] requested that the contemplation be changed.

The Buddha spoke of the *ānāpāna-samādhi*. A bhikṣu who cultivates it realizes the fruit of higher realization (*uttaraphala*) within the Saṃgha. The Buddha twice rebuked [the offender] and established this precept.

Regarding the intent behind its establishment, the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: "The reason killing is not permitted is that the human realm possesses a superior retribution, being summoned by wholesome causes;
both body and mind are vessels for receiving the Way. Those who have left the household life ought to harbor the four immeasurables and provide compassionate succor."

Regarding the life of a sentient being: if one now harbors anger and resentment within, severs that continuity, violates compassion by distressing others, and damages the vessel of the Path, this is the most extreme of transgressions.

Therefore, the Sage established the prohibition. As for the three explanations of the name, they are drawn from various sources in the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) and the *Xiangshu* (Commentary on the Characteristics).
In Sanskrit it is called *manuṣya-vadha*, which means "killing a human. The *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra* states: "The five aggregates are not real. Within this—
The provisional designation "sentient being" is established; to sever those five aggregates (skandhas) is called "killing.

This means that karma and afflictions constitute life, while form and mind constitute the substance of life, and continuity constitutes the meaning of life. Now, because one severs this continuity, it is called "killing.
This is what is to be prevented; the precept is that which counteracts it. When both the agent and the object are mentioned together, it is termed the "precept against killing persons."
The second section, the explanation based on the text, has two parts: first, the correct interpretation according to the text; second, the specific explanation of the *Prātimokṣa* (Precept Text).
The first part has two sub-sections: first, the characteristics of an offense; second, the characteristics of no offense.

The first [characteristic]—the object of the offense—is omitted because it is easily understood in relation to persons and thus is not treated separately, but is clarified within the "complete conditions" (*pratyaya*). The first of these [two sub-sections] has three parts: first, the full enumeration of the conditions for an offense.

2. First, regarding the section on persons and below, the explanation follows the specific difficulties. As for the statement "from an offense up to severance," it is as the text says. Next, the deficiencies of conditions are distinguished.

Regarding the first person, there are three cases of error concerning the object (*viṣaya-viparyāsa*), each resulting in three *thullaccaya* offenses: (1) perceiving a non-human as a human; (2) perceiving an animal as a human; (3) perceiving a tree stump as a human.

If the second perception—that it is a human—is lacking, one incurs six *thullaccaya* offenses. There are three propositions regarding perception: (1) a human who is not a [specific] human; [and so forth].

Regarding the three cases of killing with the perception [of the victim]: first, one kills with the perception that it is a human; second, one kills with the perception that it is an animal; third, one kills with the perception that it is a wooden stump. Regarding the three cases of doubt, there are likewise three phrases:

first, one doubts whether it is a non-human; second, one doubts whether it is an animal; third, one doubts whether it is a wooden stump. These are categorized according to the shifting of perception and doubt, which result in the offense of *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) for the preceding mental state;

they do not refer to the original delusion. In the case of the original delusion, there is no offense at all. This excludes the third factor of the murderous intent and opens up the [discussion of the remaining factors].

Regarding the four preparatory efforts (*prayoga*), if two conditions are entirely absent, there is no offense. If the fifth condition—taking life—is missing, one may incur the offense of *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) regarding the preparatory effort;
this refers to cases such as when the object is resistant (*balāt*) and so forth.

The explanation according to the difficulties is divided into two parts: first, the individual explanation of the initial condition; second, from "the fourfold division of killing" onwards, the combined analysis of the fourth and fifth conditions.
Regarding the phrase "from 'the first' to 'describing it,'" the person who is the object of the first condition is defined in the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) as the "object of killing.

As for the term "person" (*rén*), it means "benevolence" (*rén*). Benevolence means "patience" (*rěn*). This refers to a person whose resolve prioritizes the preservation and nurturing [of life]; therefore, they are called "benevolent."

The commentary states: "Initial consciousness in the womb is still merely coagulated mucus. The *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) says: "Initial consciousness entrusting itself to the womb is simply impure coagulated mucus;
this refers to the union of the male and female red and white elements. This is because it is that upon which initial consciousness relies;
thus, it is the stage of the *kalala* according to the *Nirvāṇa* and *Mahāsannipāta* sūtras. As for the phrase "even unto the very last meal before the end of life":
Huayan says: "This is the final consciousness that maintains [existence], namely the eighth consciousness. It refers to the single thought-moment at the time of death when there is still warmth;

this is the 'subsequent consciousness. Regarding 'the end of life,' Lingshan says: it refers to the maintenance of this provisional body-retribution, which is the fundamental cause for the duration of one's physical life;
thus it is called the 'life-faculty' (*jīvitendriya*), because it is upon this consciousness that [the life-force] relies and abides. As it is said:

The *Abhidharmasamuccaya-vyākhyā* states: "Life (*jīvitendriya*) has as its essence neither form nor mind. It is that which is determined by the past karma of sentient beings and abides for a fixed duration;

because it maintains this physical form without interruption, it is called 'life. Thus, although the breath of one who has now died has ceased, as long as there is warmth and consciousness, consciousness abides therein.
This locus of consciousness is subsumed under the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*). However, the retribution of the one who kills [is not yet exhausted]."
Because form exists, by what means could it be killed? Consciousness is fundamentally formless; it likewise cannot be killed.

Now, speaking in accordance with conventional appearances, when its locus is severed and the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) no longer continues, consciousness has nothing upon which to rely; therefore, it is said that "life is cut off."
The second section consists of two parts. The first follows the current Vinaya, directly listing the various modes of taking life committed by oneself or by instructing others;

the second part, following the *Viṃśatikā-bhāṣya*, cites the texts of the *Saṃghabhedavastu* to corroborate and explain the aforementioned modes of taking life. This [second part] has two sub-sections: first, taking life by oneself; second, instructing others.
Regarding the first recitation, from the words "four" up to "chapter," the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: "The characteristics of the act of killing are divided into two parts.
First, there are eight types of self-killing: 1. self-killing; 2. by bodily gesture; 3. by verbal speech; 4. by both body and speech; 5. by a pitfall; 6. by leaning or pushing;
7. by giving medicine; 8. by providing the means for killing. Within the category of instructing others, there are eleven: first, dispatching a messenger; second, going..."
1. Sending a messenger; 2. Sending a messenger in three stages; 3. Sending a messenger in a series; 4. Seeking someone; 5. Teaching someone to seek; 6. Seeking one who carries a blade;

7. Teaching [someone] to seek; 8. Sending a letter; 9. Teaching [someone] to send a letter; 10. Sending a messenger to praise [the act]. The *Chao* (Excerpts) omits items seven and eight. Regarding "killing by oneself":
whether by one's own body or by means of a weapon, resulting in death, all such cases are included. Regarding "manifesting signs with the body": or now...
Fearing a fall into a ditch or ravine; or manifesting the signs of death by displaying such signs with the mouth; or exhorting one toward death through speech;
or causing death by shouting threats in a loud voice; and those involving both body and speech, such as when one in this world grows weary of the body.

Some cast themselves into fire or leap from cliffs; some sever their limbs with knives or hang themselves by ropes. Those who do not know how to instruct them join their palms and chant "well done," or they assist them in climbing the mountain or provide the necessary cords and equipment.
This is precisely what is meant by "instructing toward praise while actually conforming to the commission of a transgression" and "causing others to fall into a pit."
Knowing that a person traveling must take this path, they set a pit so that he would fall to the ground. Regarding "relying on a leaning stick" (*yībó*; *bō* is pronounced *mò*):
having ascertained that the person relies on a leaning stick at a certain spot, they place weapons there; the person leans upon it and dies. This is what is meant by "relying on a leaning stick."

Knowing that others will constantly lean against a certain place or constantly push against a certain place, one constructs a mechanism at that spot so that when they subsequently lean against it or push against it, it is immediately triggered.
As for "installing the lethal apparatus," this is like a place where executions are carried out in the world.

The bhikṣu goes and places a rope around [the victim], causing them to lie prostrate and die. As for those who provide the medicine, they are easy to identify. Regarding those who instruct in killing:

this includes either instructing another person to kill, or merely instructing another on the means for bringing about death; the *Cāo* (Excerpts) states that this refers to following the instructions of a previous agent. As for those who instruct in inciting [others]:
this involves sending someone to speak to another person, causing that person to speak in such a way toward the victim that it generates many offenses; it is not as [simple] as [direct instruction].
Regarding the phrase "premature death": it refers to the teaching that dispatches a messenger to indicate that the person to be killed is in a certain direction, so that they may go and harm them.

The messenger who travels back and forth receives these instructions and goes to that place; before having accomplished the task, he returns. It is this [messenger] who subsequently goes again to kill. As for the "repeated messengers":
once the primary messenger has gone to kill, fearing that the killing might not be achieved, one repeatedly and continuously dispatches further messengers after him. This is what is meant.

When one reaches a hundred or a thousand such deaths, the gravity of the offense is determined by its beginning and end. That is to say, the "beginning" refers to the initiator (the teacher), and the "end" refers to the one who is taught (the recipient);

therefore, these two constitute a grave offense. Those in between receive only the light offense of *duṣkṛta* (āpatti), because they are neither the initiator nor the recipient, as they did not act on their own initiative.
Regarding the term "successive instigation," Master Li explains it as follows: the first person instructs Zhang to go and kill; Zhang then dispatches Wang; and Wang further dispatches Li. Thus...
These continue in succession up to a hundred thousand people, all of whom are culpable. The first person is solely the instructor, while the last person is solely the one instructed;

those in between act as both instructor and instructed interchangeably. Regarding "seeking a man": Ling Shan says that among sentient beings, one seeks someone who is skilled at wielding a blade and free from fear.
"Instructing the seeker" means teaching the person to go and seek [the murderer]. "Sending a letter" refers to when one does not [go oneself].
"Facing one's parents" means either writing a letter oneself or sending someone else to write a letter, thereby causing them to meet their death.

Regarding the term "and so forth" (*ādi*), it includes the seven types of seeking [death] and the eighth, teaching others to seek it. As for the phrase "all according to skillful means," the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states:

"This does not mean that the aforementioned list is exhaustive; rather, it refers to other skillful means beyond those enumerated. Although these are not recorded in the Vinaya, if a person dies by relying upon them, [the offense is incurred]."

All of these are included within the category of "grave offenses" (*gurutara-āpatti*). Thus, the net is cast wide to capture them all in one; yet, if one wishes to apprehend the offender, it truly comes down to a single point.
Among the three natures (*tri-svabhāva*), that which constitutes a grave offense through instruction refers to cases where one commands another to kill, praise [the act], or the like.

Regardless of whether one abides in any of the three natures—wholesome (*kuśala*), unwholesome (*akuśala*), or neutral (*avyākṛta*)—if one merely causes the life of another to be cut off, one is capable of [committing such an offense].

"Both [the *Jiao* and the *Ju*] are weighty. 'The rest is as in the subsequent chapter' refers to the 'Gate of the Place of Accomplishment,' which clarifies the offenses incurred regarding the three natures (*trisvabhāva*).
'The *Avataṃsaka*' refers to the question concerning the object and perception; the meaning is that this is not so, as it is clarified within the fourth 'Gate of Penetration and Obstruction.'"

This is the section on "acting oneself" and "instructing others. All that has preceded is explained according to the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts). If one were to select [passages] from individual schools, this would mark a distinction.

Second, among the six parts of the citation of texts from various schools to prove and explain the various characteristics, the first is the *Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra* of the *Daśabhāṇaka* school, which proves and explains "acting oneself."
1. *Śā* (Killing) and *Upāya* (Expedient Means). 2. *Sarvāstivāda* (Sāpōduō), lower section: evidence and commentary on the dispatching [of another] for the purpose of death. 3.

*Triṃśaka-vinaya* (Sānshìsòng), "In order to cause a person" section, lower part: evidence and commentary on the pitfall. 4. *Sarvāstivāda*, lower section: evidence and commentary on verbal praise of the signs of death. 5. "Furthermore" section, lower part:

evidence and commentary on the placement of lethal instruments. 6. *Pañcavargika-vinaya* (Wǔfēn), lower section: evidence and commentary on the limits of the offense incurred by committing suicide oneself. This entire passage is...
This is the topical outline (*ko*) based on the meaning of the *Śīla-vibhāṣā*. The first two sections: the first distinguishes [the case] of oneself toward oneself;

the second, from "The *Vinaya-ghaṭikā-śāstra* states" onwards, clarifies [the case] of oneself toward another. First, it is stated that from the ten [offenses] down to the *sthūlātyaya*, according to the *Vinaya*, one must not injure the physical form;

this makes it clear that one must not commit suicide. "Stretching" (*shu*) refers to stretching out one's waist and legs; if one forcibly causes another to die while they are sitting in meditation (*kāyotsarga*), even if done with good intentions, [it constitutes an offense]. It is not permitted.
Because there was an intentional motive for killing, one does not incur a grave offense (*ānantarya*). Regarding the phrase "the same as *sājīva*," the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states:

"Sending a letter or manifesting signs through the body, recording them on paper or ink to cause a person to die—such as in the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, where if a lay follower (*upāsaka*) or a monk (*bhikṣu*) knows auspicious or inauspicious signs and causes another to break their integrity or ruin their livelihood, thereby obtaining wealth or life—it is all the same as the grave offenses of killing and stealing."

Furthermore, it is said that although a bhikṣu does not personally kill or steal, if he sends a letter to another person to cause them to break their *saṃvara* (vows) and obtain wealth, and that wealth is obtained, he incurs two *ānantarya* (heinous) offenses.
As for the analogy applied to upāsakas, this refers to the same cases of the two offenses of killing and stealing; it does not refer to *ānantarya* offenses.

Regarding the passage from the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* concerning "light and heavy," the *Zhongzhong lun* (Treatise on Determining the Middle) states: "If one digs a pit for the sake of another, and an animal falls into it, it constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* offense. This concerns the domestic environment of a household.

"Dust" (duṣṭhula) means "stain. Regarding the construction of a pit for livestock that results in death: according to the Vinaya, this constitutes a *thullaccaya* offense. If a human dies, it is a *pārājika*;

if livestock die, it is a *duṣṭhula*, which is auspicious [in the sense of being a lesser offense]. As for the gravity depending on the circumstances: the *Huayan* (Avataṃsaka) states that if a human dies, it is a *pārājika*;

if a non-human (*amanuṣya*), it is a *duṣṭhula*; if livestock, it is a *thullaccaya*. This is because of the underlying mind of arrogance. Regarding the statement that the *sāṃghāvaśeṣa* is most grave: the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) says that as for manifesting signs with the mouth, one may either...
Regarding the statement that praising and encouraging someone to die involves two meanings: first, providing scriptural citations as proof; second, from "Now there are many...

onwards, pointing to examples of similar cases. As for the phrase "also constitutes a grave offense," this is also from the *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra*. The *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states:

"One who provides the means for killing—such as a place of execution in the secular world—and a bhikṣu goes there to provide a rope or cord so that the person may die by hanging, it is equally a grave offense."
Lizhen said: "Regarding 'following along with others,' there are monks who violate the laws of the king, and many other monks follow them;
these are called those who follow along. The *sengzi* (monastic attendant) seeks hand-towels and such from them. Lingshan said:
"Since one incurs a grave offense by using speech that has been sought out, what about using speech that has not been sought out? If that person says, 'I rely upon the king...'"
The Teaching: "For the time being, you should contemplate the Buddha’s words in accordance with the Path; by doing so, you will attain auspiciousness.

At that time, he incurred a *sthūlātyaya* offense because he further gave rise to discursive thought regarding the previous bhikṣu’s words, even though he did not immediately agree with them. Regarding the statement "five...

until 'conveniently'," it means that although the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* was cited previously to show that one may not harm oneself, this is now cited as proof to address whether one incurs an offense if one commits suicide or similar acts.
As soon as life ends, the *prātimokṣa* precepts cease; there is no formal sentencing for the offense, but one is merely charged with the *sthūlātyaya* of the preliminary effort (*pūrvaprayoga*).
Regarding the second section on non-offenses, there are two parts: first, the actual explanation; second, "In the case of laypeople," etc., which cites secular law by way of analogy.

First, regarding the statement "non-offense" and so forth: secular law states that those who commit various offenses involving killing or wounding others shall each be dealt with according to their [specific crime].

The legal petition argues for acquittal on the grounds that [the act] was beyond the reach of the senses and outside the scope of deliberation. For example, when several people together lift a heavy object and their strength cannot control it;

or when, while riding at height or treading on a precipice, a stone falls and kills someone; or when, in the course of capturing birds or beasts, injury or death results—cases such as these are all without fault.
Using worldly matters to illustrate the Way, this is the second distinct explanation of the six phrases of the precept text.

This is divided into six parts: first, the bhikṣu who is capable of killing; second, intentionally taking one's own life (clarifying the karma of suicide); third, the person whose life is ended (the object of the killing);

fourth, holding the blade (clarifying the division between the karma of self-killing and other-killing; this has two sections: first, raising the act of killing; second, concluding the preceding [section]. The first [section] has three parts:

first, holding the blade and giving it to another, which is providing the means for killing; second, praising death to another, which is verbal praise for killing; third, exhorting the one about to die—this refers to exhorting another to die through praise). Fifth, the conclusion of the offense; sixth, the funeral rites.

The fourth precept text has two parts: first, the designation of the name of the precept established; second, from "possessing nine conditions" onwards, the explanation according to the text. Regarding the phrase "the fourth... precept":
as for the origin story (*nidāna*), when the Buddha was at Vaiśālī, the price of grain was high and alms-food was difficult to obtain.

There were those observing the rains retreat on the banks of the Vāku River who, being praised by others, claimed to have attained the qualities of a superior person (*uttarimanussa-dhamma*). Their faith...
"Householder, you have reduced your own portion to give it to the Saṃgha. The Buddha, having perceived this, immediately rebuked him and established the prohibition.

Regarding the intent behind the second prohibition, the *Jieben shu* (Commentary on the Precept Text) states: "However, the unconditioned holy path is not realized by ordinary beings; because it has not yet been attained, they merely speak of it as empty talk."

Claiming for themselves that they have attained realization, they either disturb the minds of the multitude or deceive the world in their pursuit of fame and profit; this is a time when the net of the Dharma is being strangled.

This is the most extreme among transgressions; therefore, it is called the "ultimate prohibition. Regarding the threefold explanation of its name, the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: Its essence deviates from reality, hence it is termed "false" (*mṛṣā*).
The offense is grave and the deception is profound, hence it is termed "great" (*mahā-*) [lying]. Since the formation of karma resides in speech, it is termed "utterance" (*vāda*).
The precepts are the practices that serve as remedies; therefore, they are called the "precept against great falsehood.

The commentary is divided into three parts: first, an explanation according to the text; second, a specific explanation of the precept proper; and third, a detailed analysis of the precept. Within the second part, there are three sections: first, clarifying the object of the offense;

second, from "Furthermore, in the fourfold [classification]" onwards, clarifying the characteristics of the offense; and third, distinguishing the conditions for non-offense. The first two [sections] consist of: first, clarifying the completion of the offense.

Regarding the conditions (*pratyaya*): in the second quarter of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, the objects of transgression are distinguished. As for the statement "possessing nine [conditions] up to 'understanding' (*vijñapti*)," it is as the text explains.
Next, the deficiency of conditions is distinguished. The *Śīla-śāstra* states: "If the first condition is deficient—that is, if the person is a non-human, an animal, a stump, or a substitute."

One incurs three *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses; the second condition is missing. There are six *pāyantika* offenses; for each of "perception" (*saṃjñā*) and "doubt" (*vicikitsā*), there are three [offenses], as the third condition is missing.

If the object is false but one now treats it as real, there is no offense at all. This refers to taking the sublime Dharma (*āryadharma*) as the object, and falsely claiming to have attained what has not yet been attained.

Therefore, it is called "empty. If the fourth condition is lacking, it is merely overweening pride (*adhimāna*), and there is no offense. If the fifth condition is lacking, there is no intention to deceive;
because it is done in jest, it is auspicious. If the sixth condition is lacking—speaking of superhuman qualities (*uttarimanussadhamma*) regarding human qualities—there is no offense.

Question: Why is it said only that he "surpassed humans" (*atītya manuṣyān*), and not that he "surpassed devas"? Answer: As explained in the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, the Buddha established the precepts among humans;

therefore, humans possess the *prātimokṣa*. Because they cultivate wholesome dharmas extensively, those who enter the Path surpass the devas. Thus, it is said only that he "surpassed humans," as he had already surpassed the devas.
If the seventh condition is missing, it is not said that he "realized for himself," and there is no offense. If the eighth condition is missing... [text ends].

Regarding the statement "not understood": one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense for lacking the ninth condition. If the person before him does not hear [the words], or hears them but does not understand them, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.

Within the second section on the object of the offense, there are two parts: first, the formal explanation; second, from "If one says... onwards, the inquiry into the reason why the offense is established.

The passage from "The Four-Part Vinaya" to "is a *sthūlātyaya*" contains three points in full: first, the designation of the object of the offense; second, from "If one says... onwards, the characteristics of the verbal expression.

Third, regarding the present life: if one physically performs verbal acts, both the *Vinaya* and the *Śāstra* clarify that this constitutes the offense of claiming superhuman attainments (*uttari-manuṣya-dharma*).
Both state that from the attainment of the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) up to the realization of the four fruits of the path, these constitute the stages of such an offense.
As for manifesting physical signs, the *Sthiti* states: "When the entire assembly has gathered, if someone proclaims, 'Let those who have attained Arhatship rise,' and the bhikṣu [himself...]"

Regarding "knowing this and establishing oneself as an ordinary person": if the person before one has faith, one incurs a *pārājika* offense; otherwise, upon completion of the fifth [act], one incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

As for the statement "ten up to entering," it refers to the impure minor dharma of advancing; that is, the five *sthāpanā-citta* contemplations of the external ordinary person (*bāhyapṛthagjana*). This refers specifically to those with a predominance of sensual desire.

One who practices the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*), one with much anger (*dveṣa*) practices the contemplation of loving-kindness and compassion (*maitrī-karuṇā-bhāvanā*), one with much delusion (*moha*) practices the contemplation of causes and conditions (*pratītyasamutpāda-bhāvanā*), one with much attachment to a self (*ātma-grāha*) practices the contemplation of the eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśa-dhātu-bhāvanā*), and one with much discursive thought (*vitarka-vicāra*) practices the contemplation of counting the breath (*ānāpāna-smṛti-bhāvanā*).

Since these are shallow and minor dharmas, why is it said that one immediately incurs a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*)? Answer: Regarding "the initial gateway to the nectar" (*amṛta-mukha*): "Nectar" refers to...
This refers to *nirvāṇa*. It means that those who eternally sever the afflictions and realize great *nirvāṇa* all first travel through the land of the five contemplations.
Thus we know that the five contemplations are the initial gateway to *nirvāṇa*; hence it is said that all sages enter the Way by means of these.

Regarding the second section on the characteristics of offenses, there are two parts. First, citing the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, it states that if one speaks [of such matters] to devas, nāgas, or spirits, all constitute an offense.

Second, "one should receive" and so forth; if one claims to be a Buddha, one incurs only a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense). As for the statement that "the words are also extremely grave," regarding the arrival of devas and nāgas, the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) says:

"Because they surpass ordinary people in possessing signs and in their proximity to the Holy Path, they are equalized as being of one grave category. Lì (Lìzǔ) says: "Originally, one intended to speak toward..."
Zhang Yue. Furthermore, regarding the case of speaking to a royal messenger: although Zhang and Wang are distinct, they are equally human;
therefore, to say "I am a Muni" or "I am a Buddha" constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* offense, because people would not believe it.
If one says, "I have regressed from the four fruits of the śramaṇa," it constitutes a *pārājika* offense, as the words involve a claim of spiritual status. (10)

The recitation states: If a person writes a letter stating for himself that he has attained the first fruit (*srotāpanna*), and shows this letter to others, claiming in the letter that he has attained the fruit when in fact he has not, he commits a *thullaccaya* offense.
The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* states: If one says, "All those in such-and-such a place are not ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*)," it is a *vinayātikrama*;

if one says, "I am also among them," it is a *thullaccaya*, because it does not specifically designate [the attainment]. If one says, "I have also attained this Dharma," it is a grave offense (*pārājika*).
Regarding the phrase "because it is not [actually] reached," it is as stated in the text.

Second, the specific explanation of the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* follows the original commentary (*Ben-shu*) and is divided into seven parts: 1. "If a bhikṣu" (referring to the person who commits the offense);

2. "Truly having no knowledge" (clarifying that the object is false); 3. From "claims for himself" onwards, this correctly reveals the essence of the transgression (the note states: within this, there are two parts; first, "claims for himself").

This is a general enumeration of the noble dharmas (*āryadharma*). Second, "I have entered and abide below" refers to the specific enumeration of the noble dharmas. As for the statement "furthermore, noble wisdom" (*āryajñāna*), it means that one has attained the wisdom of the emptiness of persons (*pudgalanairātmya*); therefore, it is called "noble wisdom. It is termed "noble" because it accords with reality; it is "noble" because by contemplating selflessness, one attains the state of a noble one.

Regarding "superior dharmas," this refers to attaining the realization of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*); because one penetrates the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth as being non-existent, they are called "superior dharmas. "I know this, I see this" is a repetition that concludes the two preceding phrases. Fourth, "at another time... and so forth.
"Clarifying his own statement" refers to the time when he must speak after having made a formal declaration.
"If questioned, even to the point of false deception" refers to looking back at the original offense. "Excluding the increase of pride" means excluding the opening conditions;

that is, the untainted noble dharmas are called "superior" because they transcend [the world], while claiming to have attained what one has not attained is called "pride. This is the instruction for the deluded.

There is no ignorance, because no offense is incurred; therefore, it is said that [the rule] is "excluded. Six: the incurrence of offenses. Seven: the treatment of the funeral rites; these may be understood.

Within the section on the incurrence of offenses, the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) divides [the text] into two parts. First, there is one sentence which informs the assembly of their sentiments.

"If a bhikṣu commits [an offense] below... excludes doubt and attachment. "Now, I ask the venerable ones... and so forth, serves to quiet the assembly before expounding the subsequent chapter. Next, the exclusion of doubt.
The middle section has two parts. The first states: "If a bhikṣu commits any one of these offenses, he shall not dwell together with others as before.

This explains the doubt regarding communal residence. At that time, people harbored the suspicion that anyone who committed an offense would simply not be allowed to live with others, yet they did not know what kind of non-residence was meant.
Therefore, it is now explained: prior to committing an offense, because the person is pure, one is permitted to abide within the two types of dharmas.
"Living together": Since one has now committed an offense, one may no longer live in accordance with the Dharma as before; therefore, it is said that "one may not live together as previously.

Regarding the phrase "the same applies to subsequent [offenses]," this explains the doubt concerning repeated offenses. People at that time might have thought: "The first offense resulted in decapitation because there was a precept to be broken;
although one commits further transgressions later, these are not considered offenses. Therefore, it is now explained that subsequent offenses [are likewise grave].
It is likewise. That is to say, when a formal confession has been completed, such a person is one who dwells together with others through the shared practice of these two kinds of dharma.

If they commit the offense again now, they likewise do not participate in the previous instance of communal dwelling. The same applies to one who has not yet repented if they commit the offense later.
Such bhikṣus all constitute pārājika offenses; in total, they should not dwell together.

The second section concerns the *Saṃghāvaśeṣa* (Saṅghādisesa) offenses. Although the Nanshan tradition employs eight topical gates (*dvāra*), I shall now provide a brief overview. To explain this section, I will first set forth the meaning of five topical gates.

This is divided into two parts: first, a general classification by means of topical gates; second, the formal explanation according to the specific section. The first part is further divided into five sub-sections: first, the origination through the three poisons;
second, the correlation with body and speech; third, acting oneself or instructing others; fourth, the explanation of prohibitions and intrinsic natures (*prakṛti- and prajñapti-śīla*).

Regarding the five categories of the first section: as for the initial arising through the three poisons, there are seven precepts at the outset that arise due to three factors and are accomplished through a mind of greedy attachment.

Next, there are two precepts that arise and are accomplished through a mind of hatred. Next, there are two precepts that arise due to three factors and are accomplished through a mind of delusion and pride.
Finally, there are two precepts that arise and are accomplished through hatred and delusion. Regarding the second point, the assignment to body and speech, this refers to the first two.

Regarding the offenses involving the body: next are two concerning coarse speech, two concerning slander, four concerning admonition, and eight concerning the precepts; these constitute the primary transgressions committed by the mouth, with other factors serving as auxiliary causes.

Next are two concerning dwellings; these constitute the primary transgressions committed by the body, while the mouth serves as the auxiliary karma. Next is the one precept concerning matchmaking; this constitutes the primary transgression committed by both body and mouth.
Third, regarding those who act themselves or instruct others, the categories are divided into three. First, there are five precepts, namely: coarse speech, flattery, and matchmaking.

Regarding the second category of offenses, there are two precepts, namely the two types of slanderous precepts (*paiśunya*). Whether one acts on one’s own or instructs another, whether it is for one’s own sake or not, and regardless of the specific object of the offense, the conditions for the transgression are identical.

If one commits these five [acts] oneself, they benefit oneself; therefore, by instructing others to do so, one likewise incurs the offense of *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. However, if one instructs others in a general sense such that no personal benefit accrues to oneself, one incurs only the offense of *sthūlātyaya*.

As for the second category, there are two precepts, meaning the two slanderous precepts: acting on one’s own and instructing others, whether for one’s own sake or not, as the conditions for the disturbance of the object are the same.

He and I have committed the same offenses. Regarding the three categories and six precepts: namely, emission and physical contact constitute a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (offense requiring suspension) for doing it oneself;

inciting another constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense). Because there was no personal gratification, [the offense is mitigated]. Regarding the four admonitions: if one commits the actual offense oneself and incites another to violate the admonition, one also incurs a *sthūlātyaya*.

As for the fourth category, the prohibitive and the essential natures: matchmaking and the two types of rooms are prohibitive evils; the remaining ten items of majestic deportment are, by their very nature, [essential virtues].
It is unwholesome; therefore, it is of an inherently evil nature. Regarding the fifth category, the miscellaneous types: according to the *Śāstra*, they are divided into four.

First, there are the five precepts, which belong to the category of passionate attachment and are of the same class as sexual misconduct. Second, the two precepts concerning the two dwellings (the two *kuṭī* rules) are of the same class as theft.
Third, the act of defiling a household is of the same class as killing. Fourth, the remaining five precepts are of the same class as false speech. Second...

Regarding the second part of the "Correct Explanation" according to the chapters: first is the heading of the chapter; second, from "Therefore, [regarding] transgressions... onwards, is the detailed explanation based on the precepts.
The phrase "From 'The Sangha' to 'In the Middle'" refers to the heading of the chapter.

In the second explanation, there are thirteen differences, which are divided into thirteen sections. Now follows the first. Within this, there are two parts: first, the designation of the name of the precept established;
second, from "This precept" onwards, the explanation according to that name. Regarding the phrase "deliberately... up to one [measure]":
as for the initial origin story (*nidāna*), the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. Kāḷodāyin’s lustful intent was intense, and he followed his recollections.

[The monk] committed an offense. The bhikṣu informed the Buddha, and the Buddha rebuked him and established a precept. Regarding the intent of this regulation, as cited from the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra* in the *Vinaya-piṭaka-saṃgraha*, the *Śīla-shu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states:

"When one employs skillful means to initiate movement and sets the mind upon the ultimate goal, it is termed 'intentional' (*saṃcetanika*). As for its essential nature, it is complete when the conditions are fulfilled."

Therefore, it is termed a "transgression. This is that which is to be prevented; the precepts are the practice that serves as the remedy. Since both the object [to be remedied] and the subject [the remedy] are presented together, it is so called.

The commentary is divided into two parts: first, an exegesis according to the text; second, a detailed explanation of the *Prātimokṣa* (Precept Text). The first part has two sections: first, clarifying the intent of the regulation; second—
"Endowed with three [factors]" and below explains their characteristics. There are three initial points: first, clarifying the original intent of this precept;

second, "The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* (多論)" and below, correctly discerning the intent of its formulation; third, "The four-part Vinaya (*Caturvargika-vinaya*)" and below, recounting the words of reprimand. One recitation states:
"From 'this' to 'the donor,' because one violates this precept, one loses the ability to maintain it through one's own playful conduct; therefore, it causes the Buddha-dharma to exist..."
[Otherwise, the Dharma] would perish quickly. Now, because of these regulations, the individual practitioner remains pure as ice, and the community looks up to them for maintenance;
thus, the True Dharma abides for a long time without perishing. Regarding those who slander in their hearts, the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states:

"Worldly people and non-Buddhists will say that the Śramaṇas, the sons of Śākya, engage in impure conduct and are no different from the laity. For those who wish to inspire faith in devas and nāgas, the treatise says: "If one acts..."
Although this matter takes place in private, devas, nāgas, and benevolent spirits all see it. Ling Shan said:
"If you do not act now, it will cause the devas and nāgas to give rise to faith and reverence."
