since the pleasure of touch and the intention are distinct, one incurs the remainder (*śeṣa*) offense of *thullaccaya*.
The second section has three parts: first, a man; second, "or beneath the robe," touching an insentient object; third, "down to... touching one's own body.

Regarding the single exclamation, "The Vinaya reaches the *lǎ*": within the Vinaya, robes and bowls do not [distinguish] between self and other. The *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: "Robes and bowls are both the ultimate limits of restraint.
Since the mind is the root of transgression, the regulations are established according to the objects of engagement so as not to allow [transgressions] to arise."

Regarding the *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offenses: speaking in general terms, they are distinguished by the depth or shallowness of the object (*viṣaya*). Even that which does not involve physical contact is grave. Second, regarding the two cases involving hair and nails:
first, according to other schools (*nikāya*), if one is unaware of the contact, it constitutes a *sthūlātyaya*; second, if one relies on the lower [text], it is a *sthūlātyaya*.

According to our own school (*sva-nikāya*), if one is aware of the contact but unaware [of the specific nature of the object], it constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. One recitation says: "The term 'well-arrived' (*śubha-prāpta*) refers to this one."
Section on the Meaning. According to the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts): "Hair" refers to the teaching for dispelling doubts. At times, there may be doubt, saying:

"When grasping the hands or the flesh of the body, there is a sensation of pleasure and smoothness; since hair is part of the body, what karma could it possess that would result in the incurrence of an offense?

This arises from a defiled mind. The *Sifenlü* (Four-Part Vinaya) does not differentiate its characteristics; one should clarify its gravity or lightness through four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*), distinguishing between conscious and unconscious acts.

Regarding the object (*viṣaya*): Thus, the *Sudarsana-vinaya* states, "If hair touches hair, or nails touch nails, one incurs a *thullaccaya* offense in every instance because there is no mutual awareness (*saññā*).
If they touch one another [with awareness], then by principle, it constitutes a *saṅghādisesa*. As for the formulation of the four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*), Master Li establishes them as follows:

first, awareness of contact but no awareness of the remainder; second, no awareness of contact but awareness of the remainder; third, no awareness of contact and no awareness of the remainder (this corresponds to the conclusion of the *Jieshu*; fourth, no awareness of contact and no awareness of the remainder—this corresponds to the *Sudarsana*).
Regarding the *dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana* (the fetter of views): there are four cases of *śeṣa* (residual offenses) arising from intentional contact. These consist of two *śeṣas* and two *sthūlātyaya*s.

Although these are unintentional, they constitute a *śeṣa* offense because this part of the body is not the same as [other] clothing. If that is so, why does the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* state that intentional and unintentional contact results in a *sthūlātyaya*?
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* says: "If one touches a woman's body with a sore that has no flesh or bone, it is a *sthūlātyaya*. This applies to the woman's body."

The same applies when the sense organs are destroyed. The answer is: A wound is a state of destruction; although there is mutual contact, because the mind of defiled pleasure is slight, it constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
If one touches that woman while lacking flesh, bone, hair, teeth, or body hair, for that bhikṣu, it constitutes an unintentional act.

[The offense] is obtained as a *thullaccaya*. If a bhikṣu touches a woman’s hair or the like with his body, he immediately incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. To exclude this [case], the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* is cited;
thus the *Caturvargika-vinaya* says: "If one seizes the hair" means that the touch is conscious [on the part of the bhikṣu] while [the woman] is unconscious.

The second section, "Various Explanations from Different Schools," has three parts. First, regarding contact while in storage: according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, touching [a woman] does not constitute male-female contact.
According to the *Saṃghāṭi-vinaya*, this refers to one who was originally a woman and perceives her as a man or a *paṇḍaka* (eunuch) while making physical contact.

One recitation states: "Regarding 'reaching the object' in the *Saṃghāṭi-vinaya*": it means that if a bhikṣu suddenly touches a woman without a lustful mind, it is a *duṣkṛta* (minor offense). The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* says: [as follows].
If one touches the body of an incapable woman, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense. If a bhikṣu touches an incapable man who is a woman, he incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
This "incapable man" refers to the bhikṣu’s own body; it does not mean there is a separate male entity. Regarding the "incapable bhikṣu" among the ten types:
this refers to those schools that permit [contact with] an incapable person; because a bhikṣu uses such a person for contact, he incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense. — *Saṃgha* (The Monastic Community).

Regarding the meaning of "only the intention" (*zhǐyì*): this refers to the case where one possesses the nature of the precepts (*xìngjiè*), yet because one does not acknowledge the mental state of suspicion regarding the preparatory effort (*xiǎngyí fāngbiàn*), one incurs the *śeṣa* offense.

That Vinaya states: "If a woman is touched while perceiving her as a man or with suspicion, it is a *śeṣa*. It also says: 'If one perceives a hermaphrodite (*pandaka*) or touches them with suspicion, it is a *śeṣa*. The *Chao* (Commentary) says:"

This refers to those who previously possessed the preparatory mind and thus came [to the offense] because they had definitively understood the Vinaya texts. Nanshan said: "The holy regulations have their reasons;

it is impossible that the texts would omit anything. How could a wise person persistently hold to [the rule] and yet not touch upon [its implications]? If one realizes the transgression through a specific circumstance, may one not incur the *śeṣa* (saṃghāvaśeṣa) offense?"
This refers to what is grave (*guru*). In the preceding preparatory act (*pūrvārambha*), one intends to touch this woman and raises a hand toward her;

even if there is the perception or suspicion that she is a man or a *paṇḍaka* (eunuch), with respect to the subsequent mind, it stops at a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing). How could the preceding preparatory act not be grave?

It is not that the Master of the South Mountain (*Nanshan*) was unaware of the nature of the Vinaya precepts—that they do not open up [the offense] based on perception or suspicion. Rather, it is because the text of the Vinaya is not explicit. Therefore...
There is this definitive ruling. From this second point, regarding physical contact, since one may incur five offenses, it is established as a companion rule.

As for the statement that "good [conduct] leads up to the *thullaccaya*," this is discussed in the eighteenth chapter of the *Śāriputra-vinaya-vibhāṣā*. Śāriputra asked Pūrṇa: "Does physical contact result in a *pārājika* offense?

He replied: "It results in five offenses: first, if a nun touches [a monk], she incurs a *pārājika*; second, if a monk touches [a nun], he incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*; third, if they touch while both have clothing on, they incur a *sthūlātyaya*."

Fourth, there is the offense of both being together with a robe; if a bhikṣu touches a woman, he incurs a *duṣkṛta*. Fifth, if a bhikṣu strikes another bhikṣu with his finger, he incurs a *sthūlātyaya*.
These are called the five offenses. Since this act of touching pertains to all five categories [of offenses], it is established as a companion rule to them.
Regarding the second section on non-offenses, there are three parts. First is the heading. Second, from "The Vinaya says" onwards, the various schools provide specific explanations.

Third, from "In the *Triṃśaka* and the *Dharmaguptaka*" onwards, this collectively refers back to the preceding text to exhort one to understand the meaning of urgency and laxity. The first part is as stated in the text.

The commentary has three parts. First, it raises the point that according to our own school (*svasamaya*), there is an object of apprehension (*grāhya*) and contact occurs; this is established by citing the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*. Second, from "If [it is] one's mother, etc.

onwards, it clarifies whether it is permissible to seize women such as one's mother under exceptional circumstances when they have been separated for a long time. Third, from "The *Mahāsāṃghika*" onwards...

The *Zami* (Compendium of Clarifications) states that one should establish the ritual procedures according to what is appropriate and not contrary to the meaning. Regarding the statement "the Vinaya reaches the *thullaccaya* (grave offense)": playing is not a transgression. The *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) says:

"If one does not employ a lustful mind but engages in other forms of play, it may be considered an opening for [avoiding] the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (offense requiring suspension); therefore, it is not a non-transgression. This is the interpretation of the characteristics of the ritual procedure.

This is for the purpose of rescuing and liberating those in distress. It does not mean that one does not incur other offenses. *Huayan* (Flower Ornament) says: "This refers to [offenses] other than those concerning precepts, decorum, and auspiciousness.

As for the statement that if a mother reaches such a state, one incurs a *thullaccaya* (sthūlātyaya), the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations Vinaya) states: "There were various [people] who went toward the Ajiravatī River to bathe."
The river water suddenly rose in flood. The women were being swept away by the current, yet the bhikṣus did not dare to rescue them.

The women said, "O Venerable Ones, have compassion and pity! Where are these śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas? Seeing us being carried away by the water, why do you not rescue and grasp us? The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "I permit you to rescue and grasp them. Thereupon, the bhikṣus grasped them; however, when lustful thoughts arose, they released them again. The women...
It says: "Do not let go; you must wait until reaching the shore; you should not intentionally touch [her]. Regarding the phrase "the Sangha knows," it is as stated in the text.

Regarding the phrase "in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations)," the *Ji* states: "There was a bhikṣu walking by a riverbank when a woman fell into the water and cried out in distress, seeking rescue from the bhikṣu.
At that time, the bhikṣu perceived her as another person (thinking she was not his wife) and took hold of her to pull her out; he did not commit an offense. If he gave her bamboo or wood..."

If one is pulled out by a rope, there is no offense in pulling them out. Regarding the degree of force—whether it be gentle or urgent—if it is truly a matter of life-and-death suffering, one must rescue them immediately.
However, if they can free themselves once the rope is cut, one must not seize hold of them.
The second part provides a detailed explanation of five phrases from the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*: first, the person who commits the offense; second, the defiled mind; third, the object of the offense;
fourth, physical contact, which explicitly clarifies the performance of the karmic act; and fifth, the formal determination of the offense (the male counterpart being understood).

The third precept on harsh speech is divided into two parts: first, the designation of the name of the precept being prescribed; second, from "seven conditions" onwards, the explanation according to the text.
Regarding the phrase "up to three": first, as for the origin story (*nidāna*), the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. Kāḷodāyin...
Having heard that the Buddha had established the first two precepts, he then directed lustful thoughts toward a woman in her presence.
